div.head: RUDE AWAKENING.
div.p: A RUDE AWAKENING.
(C alright.)
By FRED. WHISJIANV,
Author of "Adventures of a Stowaway," "Boris, the Bear-Hunter." "A Romance of the Woods," "A Czar's Grat it 11 de," At.

On December 4th I dined alone with my old school chum, 'l*(aniny Arim4l, at. his house in St. Petersburg. Arnold - had lately some in for his father's Cusineps in that city, and I should say .it 's a very good bitsines4, if one may judge from the «yle in which Tommy lives. Tommy :1 does" himself cery vell indeed—to use a homely expression—and auring may fortnight's experience of the Czar's ppital 1 learnt the ways of wicked luxury. , We dined at home, that night, because we wished to discuss an ice-yachting excur.ion we intended to make on the following day, the weather being of the particular kind which is favourable for this sport.

One can only enjoy a spin in an ice-yacht while the winter is still young and the masses of snow - which are sure to (some afterwards have not as yet smothered the smooth ice of the frozen Gulf of Finland a yard deep in their sport-spoiling embraces. The wind blew from the north-east. "We shall run down the gulf at forty miles an hour," said Arnold. "You're in luck, sonny; I haven't had a decent run for three years ; there's always snow or thaw, or a dead calm on the only day. But, to-morrow--Great Scott! how we shall spin, if the wind holds!" Tommy spoke in joyous tones; it was clear that such a spin as he described was a thing to delight the heart. I, too, began to feel joyous in antici- pation. I had tried most, forms of outdoor amuse- ment, but never this ; Tommy's enthusiasm infected me, and dinner ran its course merrily. In the midst of it the servant announced that one Platonof had called, finding the office closed, upon v a matter of importance. I expected that Tommy would begin to curse and . to swear, for he is one who does not like to be disturbed at meals, but he received the announce- ment without emotion. "Ask him into the study," he said.

Presently Arnold excused himself and left the room. "This chap owes me a goodish sum of money," he explained, "which was to have been paid in to-day, but wasn't; he may have brought it. Excuse me a second, will you ?" si He was not absent long; in five minutes or less he reappeared, carrying a great bundle of Russian bank-notes.

"Look at that!" he said, with a laugh. "I suppose I ought to thank Heaven I've got my money; but look what the silly fellow's done—not content with bringing it after hours, he must needs pay the whole sum in notes—ten thousand roubles! What .am I to do with it? It's a thousand pounds —too much to have knocking about in the house." "Send for your cashier, and have it locked up in the safe," I suggested, and Arnold adopted the idea.

"It'll give you an opportunity of seeing atypical Russian faithful servant," he said. "Pavlof has been fifteen years in our office—much longer than I have, in fact—and his devotion to me is doglike." "That's all right as long as he's honest," I said. Tommy turned upon me. "Honest?" he said. "He'd cut his throat with a sharpened sixpence rather than rob me of it!" "You're in luck to have such a chap," I told him.

• "Yes, it's nice to have someone one can trust absolutely, isn't it?" said Tommy. "Now, we had a clerk—another Russian—who had been swindling us in a small way for years. We only found him out a few months since, thanks to this same Pavlof."

The gentleman in question appeared half-an- hour later; he was a civilised-looking person, correctly dressed, and he sat down and smoked a cigar with us. after going through the formality of making a slight demur as though the honour were almost greater than he ought to consent to; but the fellow was too gushing for my simple taste. When Tommy crossed the room to count and fetch the bundle of notes, Mr. Pavlof launched out into a description of his employer's virtues and of his own devotion to him. "I would lay down my life for him," he declared, speaking fair English, and not so softly, I thought, but that Arnold must hear very plainly if he happened to be listening. " Our relations are so pleasant," he said. "Imagine, now, the trust he must have in me: here is one thousand pounds; I give no receipt—he ask none. Very wood. It is a large sum of money—how know 'he I run not away with it to-night? Ah, bemuse he know my devotion to him is rare, is true, is beautiful." "The Russian police are wonderfully clever, too, I have been told," I could not help saying. "It would be an extremely difficult thing to leave St. Petersburg with a large sum of stolen money; and to remain in the city undetected would be, I suppose, impossible." "If there were no crime, there would be no police "he replied, sententiously. "And if all masters were like Mr. Arnold, there would be no crime."

"Yet I hear/that he was swindled by one of his employes only last year," I said. "Pfuie!" said Pavlof. "That man of wrath and of wickedness ? A child/ of evil, indeed! Such .a master, and to cheat him! Oh, fie, fie!"

"Ah, if all employes were such paragons of virtue as Mr. Pavlof, 1 said, "the police would grow fat for want of occupation." I thought this would be enough for my friend, but hei took the dose as a compliment, and as his simple due at that.

"Yes," he said, "if we all could trust one another, there would be no dishonesty." "Here you are, Pavlof," said Tommy, bringing the notes; "ten thousand exactly. Pop them into :he safe to-night, like a good fellow, and let the artelshik take them across to the bank to-morrow."

"Well, what have you been talking about?" he asked, when Pavlof had retired with the parcel of money. "You seemed to be making tremendous friends." "Mr. Pavlof was explaining what a wonderfully honest fellow he is because he has never robbed you of a farthing!" I laughed. "lie seems to be pretty fond of you, how'ever, in his sickening, gushing way." "Oh, don't be hard on old Pavlof! You wouldn't be down upon a dog for licking his master's band; and his devotion towards me partakes of the canine. As a cashier, he's a treasure."
Then we began to talk about our ice-y,achting trip, and thought no more of Arnold's faithful servant.
The morning broke fine and cold, the wind almost due east, the sky as clear as a blue marble, and not a vestige of snow among the possibilities —an ideal day for an ice-boat spin.

Tommy mit; preparing to mike an early start. "I shan't go to the office," he said; "I've nothing particular to do there." "Aren't you going to look in for a minute, just to see whether that cool thousand is all right? " I asked, in surprise. "Oh, dear, no! Pavlof had it, that means as much to me as though I had paid it in over the counter to my own banker."

Well, I happpened to be taking a message across to O'Connor, and the office lay between this and his house; 1 therefore took the liberty of calling in, on my ltwn initiative, and asked the arteishik in charge whether Mr. Pavlof had been in last night. Michael, the artelshik, looked blandly effete. "Mr. Pavlof went to his dinner at six last night," he said. "Ile does not come to the office of an evening." "Has he been here early this morning:?" I inquired. "Mr. Pavlof takes a tumbler of lea in the office a nine each day," said Michael. "Why should become earlier?"

This was very awkward. I ought to tell Arnold I that his cashier had not, as yet, brought that bundle of money and deposited it in the safe. Yet if I did, Tommy would laugh me to scorn, if not lecture me as a person with a tendency to interfere in Matters which did not concern him. . But circumstances ranged themselves upon my side, and I was able to give in my piece of information without anxiety, for half-an-hour before the time fixed for our ice-boat spin the servant announced-"ilie-inspector;" Now, the inspector is an officer of the police department who would not dream of calling upon a private individual excepting upon matters of I considerable impoftarice,:and his arrival somewhat ! surprised Arnold. "What in thunder does the inspector want? he asked, and, receiving no reply from the obviously anxious servant, he added; "Shew him in. That inspector's interview with Arnold was a memorable circumstance, and gave me a very high opinion of the alertness of the Russian police: When he was seated and busy with one of

Tommy's cigars, our friend plungsa kilt° the m' 115 of things. "You have a cashier called Pavlof?" he began. Arnold bowed affirmatively. "Does lie bear a good character ?" "The very best possible," said Arnold. "Ah, utterly above suspicion, no doubt?" "Entirely." "You are satisfied of this ?"

"Absolutely, Mr. Inspector; Pavlof has served my father and myself for upwards of fifteen years. Ile is a devoted servant. I should consider myself the most ungrateful of employers if I were to permit him to be suspected. To what do your inquiries tend ? " "I should be sorry to break down idols," said the inspector; "but if Mr. Pavlof has permitted the suspicion of the police to rest upon him he has no one to thank but himself."

. "Pleitse explain, Mr. inspector," said Arnold. "Twice within a year Mr. Pavlof has excited comment by spending more money than, in his position, he would seem to be able to afford. The first occasion was about twelve months since ; the second was last night. Mr. Pavlof entertained a party at supper at Pivato's restaurant, parting very freely with large sums of money. May I ask the amount of Mr. Pavlof's annual salary?" "Two thousand roubles," said Arnold.

"Ah, he spent last night more than half his annual income; one year ago he entertained three times in one week on this scale. In a man who enjoys a salary of two thousand roubles, but who— in the course of business--comes in contact with large sums of money which do not belong to him, this is suspicious." Arnold bit his lip with annoyance. "I will l•selt into it, Mr. Inspector," he said; "though I do ,not care for interference in the private affairs of my employes. "Take my advice," said the inspector, "and let your books be carefully examined by an expert; meanwhile, Mr. Pavlof is under our surveillance. This morning, doubtless fatigued with the dissipa- tions of the night, he has not repaired to the office."

"Do you inean to tell me," I said, when our friend had departed, "that the Russian police always act the Guardian Angel in this fashion, watching the private expenditure of peaceful inhabitants and warning all those who might by any possibility have been robbed by them, in case they should seem to be spending too much?" "I know a case where, quite lately, a fellow robbed his employer, who knew nothing about it until such a warning as this from the police caused him to look into matters; then he examined his books and found that the rascal had been quietly robbing him for years, and might have continued to do so unsuspected but for the police observing that he spent too much money." "Then you suspect Pavlof ?" I asked. Arnold laughed. "Not the least bit in the world," he said. "If he chooses to bumtnel ,around occasionally, it isn't my business." "Well, I don't want to alarm you, Tommy," I said; "but I had the curiosity to call in at the office while I was out, before nine o'clock, and [was told there that Ilsvlof never called in last night." "The dickens, he didn't!" exclaimed Arnold. Evidently this information hit his faith in the cashier somewhat hard.
"No, he didn't. I'm very:much afraid there's something in the suspicions of our wonderfully astute friends."

Arnold considered awhile. "No, I don't believe it," he said; "not of Pavlof. The chap is really fond of me; he wouldn't rob me. He had that party on last night, you see, and—and I daresay it was beastly inconvenient for him to go to the office in the evening. I don't know what pre- cautions he may have taken, but the money will have been all right in his rooms or on his person. He's accustomed to handle lots of money—perhaps not quite such large sums in cash, as a rule—but still he could rob me at any time. No, it's all right, I don't suspect him; the police have been a little bit too clever this time. A chap needn't be a thief and a hypocrite because he drinks a couple of glasses of champagne with his friends one night I Come, we must be off. I ordered the trap for eleven, and it's ten past. We've three miles to drive to the yacht club, and the breeze is too good to waste." "Aren't you ;going to the office?" I asked, surprised. "Certainly not I" said Tommy. "Why should I ?"

Sol drove down to the yacht club with this prince of employers. Innocent or guilty, I reflected, Pavlof was a fortunate man to have such a chief to deal with. Then we boarded the ice- yacht, and in the delirious delight of scudding along before the wind at forty miles an hour, I soon forgot Pavlof and suspicion, and everything else in the world that was not connected with the ice-yacht. The vessel was a mere triangular framework of strong wood set upon three steel skates, and fitted with a mast and one large sail. The skate at the stern of the ship worked upon a pivot and formed the rudder. There were no seats ; one stood or squatted where one conk!, holding on for dear life to mast or rigging. For the first five minutes I thought ice-yachting a poor sport; there was half-a-mile of river to negotiate, and we were sheltered from the wind, or may be it was in our teeth; at any rate, we dragged and shoved the boat instead of tearing with it over the surface of the ice. But once we reached the open and encountered the wind rushing on its way seaward, "Jump in quickly!" shouted Tommy, and we had scarcely scrambled aboard when, with a scrape and a great heave, the boat launched out into full career. The strong wind caught us '• it filled our sail and carried us with it at the speed of an express train. "Well," shouted Arnold, at the top of his voice, for the whirr of our skates on the ice and the merry shriek of the wind would have drowned ordinary speech, "how d'you like it?" It was too perfect to be expressed in mere words. I sang out in the joy of my soul, a wild war whoop that was half a mad hulloo and half the triumphant yell of the barbarian warrior. Through the freezing air we flew—flying must surely feel like this I A minute ago we were close to St. Petersburg town, and now we approached Peterhof, fifteen miles away. •Hold on!" shouted Arnold. "She's going about."

Heavens! What a wrench to one's arms! She went about with a pitch and then a spring forward, which went near to uprooting me, though I clung to the mast, at Tom's warning, like a limpet to its rock, and away we sped actoss the gulf towards Cronstait. It was superb. Let any man inclined to depression, or in need of a nerve tonic, climb aboard an ice-ship and be swept before a forty-mile wind through the champagne air of the frosty latitudes! In five minutes he will laugh and sing, in spite of himself. I guarantee it! Twice across the gulf we sped and twice back again, and exhilaration was at the flood, "Great Scott! old man," I shouted to Arnold. "It is simply supreme!" Then we took a diagonal course that would carry us out past Cronstadt. "We might just as well have a run up the Finnish coast," said Tommy; "the wind would be blowing a gale, or near it, out in the very open. My goodness! How we should fly!" We passed at a quarter of a mile distance a man skating—or rather, we saw hifli from afar, skating, but be had now been brought up by a crevice. We had cleared many crevices in our stride, so to speak; cracks in the thick ice caused by the intensity of the frost. This one that had stopped the skater seemed a wide one.

_ "We must step and .have a look before we fly it," said Arnold ; "we mustn't commit suicide for the sake of a good jump, thOugh the little ship's Safe for anything up to six feet or so!" So about we went, both of us clinging with grim determination to anything we could grip as the yacht brought up in the wind's eye. The crevice proved a wide one—five feet at least. "We can easily rush that much !" said the skipper. "Drag her back a bit, and we'll take the brook at full stride! Stop, I'll offer,to tarry that skating chap across. Just run over to him and tell him he can jump aboard, if he likes." The fellow had skated up the crevice and down it, but seemed nonplussed. I hurried across the ice to give him Arnold's invitation. As I drew near, lie turned and saw me. I noticed him give a great start, and stand a moment irresolute. Then he skated towards me. It was our, friend Pavlof.

.... My first impression was that I ,would give any odds that the rascal had Arnold's thousand pounds about him, and had devised this ingenious way of decamping with it. "Is it you. Mr. Elliot?" he said. "What a happy chance! Would your friend take me over the crevice, do you think? I am anxious to get on." "My friend is Mr. Arnold," I said, watching his face. He did not start this time, or change countenance. "He sent me to offer to take you across," I added. "How like kind Mr. Arnold," he said, "to offer assistance to every stranger—for, of course, he did not know it was I _

"No, that lie didn't," I replied. "It is, indeed, a happy chance, as you say He glanced quickly at me, but I think my smile was successfully bland and childlike. - When Arnold saw whom I had in tow, his face underwent a change, and I could see plainly that his mind was going through certain struggles and —I hoped—tergiversations. He must surely discern that this rencontre was an extremely fortunate one, and that fate had placed certain oppk)rtunities in his hands which, perhaps, lie did not quite deserve. "What, you, Pavlof ?" he said. "What are you doing here?" "I hope you will excuse my absence from the office," said Pavlof. "You received my note this morning, of course?" "I received nothing," said Arnold. "I note, sir, to say that my mother is very ill, and desires to see me. I learnt the news by telegraph early this morning. My mother lives near Wyborg, on the Finnish coast, and that is why I am skating across the gulf; it occurred to sue that this would be the quickest way." 1 "The 10.45 train to \Vyborg. would have taken you home in three hours, or little over." "To \Vyborg, sir, yes; but there would then be ' a two hour's drive." _

"Well, get in," said Arnold; "I'll take you across, anyway." "My goodness!" thought I. "Is he really going to let the man escape out of his hands when fate has dropped him, like a ripe fruit, into them ? " I could not say anything now, however ; but determined that when once he had gone and was skating away from us for all he knew, I should convince Arnold that he was more than an ordinary idiot to 'let him go, or perish in the attempt! We dragged ,the ship back a couple of hundred yards, 'Pavlof assisting. I could see that Arnold's mind worked. Was the germ of truth taking root, the suspicion that this man was a hypocrite and a swindler? AS we laboriously dragged the ship through half- an-acre of cat-ice, which had formed just in this place from an overflow at the lip of the crevice, I saw, a mile away, between us and St. Petersburg, a body of about half-a-dozen horsemen. I guessed in a moment that these were mounted gendarmes, and that they were after Mr. Pavlof, thanksefo the vigilance of our friend, the inspector. "Hallo! What are those chaps doing out on the gulf?" said Arnold. "They're gendarmes," I said, looking hard at Pavlof, to watch the effect upon him. He started and uttered an exclamation. I saw that Arnold observed this also. _
"What's the matter, Pavlof,?" he said. "Why do you start and grow pale?" Thank Heaven, thought I, Tommy is beginning to come round.

"When I cough, hold on lute grim Cietim, • Arnold suddenly murmured. "No talking there!" shouted the ruffian in the bows. "I'll have no confounded plotting." Tommy coughed and I held on; I saw his game, and prayed for its success. About went the ship, and my arms were nearly wrenched out of their sockets.

But Pavlof flew off at a tangent, exactly as it was intended that he should. He found ice some twenty feet from the ship, alighting heavily, and spinning round and round on his coat-tails with inconceivable rapidity. His pistol flew out of his hand, and I jumped out and secured it while he was still spinning. Up rode the gendarmes. Pavlof sat upon the ice cursing and swearing like a madman. Arnold never said a word, though he looked very black; he felt the villainy and ingratitude of the man—this rascal whom he had treated like a gentleman, and who had shewn himself the worst of cads; he had trusted the fellow and believed in him, and hero was a sorry return! As for the police, they did exactly as might have been expected. The Russian detective police are marvellous in organisation; they detect a crime almost before it is committed, and bring it home to the real criminal with unfailing certainty; but when it comes to arresting the delinquent, and the executive police—the gendarme, or the gorodovoy —have their turn, the work is often bungled. Pavlof had been suspected, watched, followed; thanks to us, he had been captured. But, in spite of our protests, these gendarmes arrested us as well as the delinquent. We must be accomplices, they pointed out, because we had carried him off, and had only given him up to justice when the ice- boat upset and we had all fallen out and hurt ourselves. So we returned to town, dragging our boat, prisoners, and under the escort of six gendarmes. However, that didn't matter at all; and, in fact, the thing was quickly set right at the police-office. "What matters," said Arnold, wagging his head at Pavlof, "is that chap! A bite from one's own dog is by far the most painful." [Tule END.]

A telegram from Asheville, North Carolina, states thar G.E. Smith, well known in the racing world as "Pittsburg Phil, the King of Plungers," has died of consumption. The value of his estate is estimated at a million dollars.

On Wednesday afternoon a loud explosion occurred in the Tambowle Distillery, at Milngavie, near Gifts] low. The bonded store was immediately Involved in flames, and was completely destroyed. The damage is estim- ated at £15,000.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

This Council held its monthly meeting at Homey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon under the presidency of Mr. A. Brooks. There were also present .—Aessrs. J. W. Knowles, G. Mather, G. Thompson, R, Forshaw, W. Houghton. J. Backhouse, P, Longton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer of health), F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Burnage (assist- ant surveyor). IVINWICK IMRROV.PIENT. The Council sealed an agreement with the Ecclesiasti- cal Commissioners with regard to the widening of Hollins-lane, Winwick. The Clerk said legal charges to the amount of ten guineas had been incurred.

div.head: WATER SUPPLY QUESTION.
div.p: WATER SUPPLY QUESTION.

The CLERK read a letter from the Warrington Water Engineer with reference to a notice served upon the Corporation by the District Oouncil to supply water to Pear Tree Farm, Houghton. The farm, he stated, was about 800 yards from the main and the 009 L of extend- ing the main would be about £l5O. He presumed the District Council would give the usual guarantee,namely 8 per cent, per annum for seven years on the cost of the work.

The CLERIC said he had replied stating that the notice was purely a-notice served upon the Corporation as owners of the property to supply their tenant with water, and had no reference whatever to any agreement between the Council and the Corporation to supply the parish of Houghton with water. The INSPEcTort said a second notice had been served upon the Corporation, but it had not yet expired. It was decided to defer the matter until the next meeting.

div.head: FEARNREAD SEWERAGE.
div.p: FEARNREAD SEWERAGE.

The CLERK said the Medical 01110Efr made further reference to this questiun in his annual report which would shortly be issued. The Surveyor had already explained that the only practical arrangement, in his view, would be to connect with the Warrington Corporation sewers. It was reported that preliminary negotiations with the Borough Surveyor had been entered upon.

div.head: CUERbLEY WATER SUPPLY:
div.p: CUERbLEY WATER SUPPLY:

The CLERK said he had had a long correspondence and interview with Sir Richard Brook's agent on the sub- ject of Cuerdley water supply. He had also seen the Town Clerk of Widnes and had ascertained that all the Widnes Corporation wanted was that the Liverpool Corporation should agree with them as it was previously understood they would agree with the Warrington Corporation although no formal agreement was drawn up. The affect would be that wl en the Wines Corporation could supply the water to Cuerdley themselves they could call upon Liverpool to discontinue the supply. PLACE : The outside of one of the smartly ap- pointed omnibuses plying between Layswatel and the City. INTERLOCUTORS : The driver, and the occupant of a front seat, Mr. "lazeldean,—a country gen- tleman farming his own land, of enTuring mind and of enlightened principles, up in London from Mangelwurzelshire, on a visit to friends in -Westbourne Terrace.
Driver: Want to know what I think about ! neve 'ere elections we've had lately ? Well, I don't think nothing about 'ern at all, and that'. the truth.

llazelfleah (with the Socratic meekness, which the example of his •old Oxford tutor has told him is the best way of eliciting information) : But, • My friend, you see and talk with nian people of different kinds. Driver: That's exactly how it is, sir. spore the rod and spoil the child, as the warder with Ow hirch-rod said to the youngster in the deforma- tory. The fact, is, sir, nobody takes any .inter- tatt in lections, since all the pickings and per- kisits were taken away. Hazeldean (somewhat sententiously) : 3lean- ing, I suppose, that the stringency of the latest laws against bribery divest a citizen's element- ary duty to choose his representative of the main immcement to its performance. Driver (With a thoughtful and puzzled air) : That's not exactly how I should- put it, sir, but maybe it's what I mean. I'm a conntryman..l am, from Essex. Down in my fold home, every- one Used to look to lections to pay the rent. Nobody thought of promising his vote till the dibs was paid down, gold, silver and 11'-pun' notes. They was rare times, they was. Tit- two candidates s'eemed to be running neck and neck, when the news went round that the man in the moon was coming, and would like a word or two with the free and independeats (mean- ing of course the electors), on the strict. They had every public in the place, and if any man went to bed sober, why, it was his own fault. '

/laze/dean : But, at least, as matters are, if you (.16't make such a good thing out of it. the cost of choosing a member bap been so rednes.d, that working men can be represented by one if themselves if they wish. • Driver (with a knowing look and a suppressed' whistle', half addressing his .conductor at the other end of the vehicle) : Here, .Bill, here's ii gent says I can send you to Parliament ne,kt 'lection (the individual Bias accosted, ignoring what he regards as, a bad joke, the speaker con- tinues). No,' sir; everyone to his own trade is my motto. Parliament men must learn their own laisiness as well as 'bus-drivers. I've heard speak of drivin' a coach-and-four through an :set of Parliament. Tait that don't make the driver a proper Parliament man. Hozeldeon : Then, my friend, you are content to leave things as they are, and to pay taxes. without a vo,ce in their spending being raised at Westminster, by any of your own class. - Driver': As for that, sir, I always heard that taxes went to pay the cost of government. It's all done above-board. We've no cause to com- plain, and we shnuldn't make less a mess of it, if we did it ourselves. Them as ought to know gets what they think the right men for the work. It's a fight between the ins and the outs, but I could never see there was a pin to choose be, tween them. The Buffs is always going to give us what they call a free breakfast table, if we'll , only put them •in the place of the Blues. We does so. They claps another twopence on, and says those before them have got things into such a precious mess that. it'll take, heaven knows, how long, before nkatters are put straight and they can begin again. But in my opinion, ,sir, it's the old story of the two niggers who was 'zactly like each other, especially Sambo. Hazeldean : Do you find that view borne out by facts yourself ? Driver : Turn and turn about's fair play. Them's my sentiments, sir. Give both a try, and see which aloes. best. Can you tell me why, sir, there are any Parliament men at all? • Hazeldean Why ! Because you and I, like all Englishmen, may enjoy the inestimable bless- ings of representative government, and of the rule of the people by themselves. Driver : Then I'm a Dutchman, sir. So far as I see the business of every Parliament man is to say and vote just as he's told to do. There's the boss on both sides, who gives the word. The others have to play "follow-my-leader." Hazeldean In that case, where, do .those you call the ".free and independents," I menu the electors come in? Driver: Nowheres that I know in 'lections, it's a regular put up job. Havldean: It would follow, my frieuld, from your doctrine, that ours is not after fill, a free country, and that elections, bye or general, are farce. _

Driver : And that's the truth, as many of the likes of us think. I never vote at an lection in all my born days, and I'll tell you why. I reads my paper, the Morning Earthquake, reg'ler every day. Here, in articles, letters to the beditor, or what not, I sees heverythink on hevery side, wot was, or can be, ever thought or said, and in the long run I find Parliament men doing pretty well as the Earthquake tells 'em. What call have I, therefore, or the likes o' me, to trouble our 'ends about 'lections:

Haze : It seems my friend, you are some- what of a fatalist in politics. .Driver : 1"r aps I be and p'r'aps I bain't. .All I know is, we working-men don't think any- thing about 'lections at all. Fust they took away the hustings. There were no more bands playing, dead cats or rotten eggs flying. No more shouting or polling at the booths. Only a sneaking- of something into a covered box, with a hole in the side. A reglar hole and corner affair, as quiet and dull as, in a figure of speech as one might say, a chapel service on Sunday afternoon. That's not the English way. And then, sir, we finds them as stands for Parliament, whichever colour they be, make the 'dentical promises at the time, and thinks nothin' about 'em afterwards. Tections used to mean fun and money. That's all gone. Why should me and my mates bother ourselves any more about them. They've got rid of all that make 'em worth anything. My opinion is .lections of any kind, and p'eaps Parliament too, vill soon be as ifead and gone as 'osscs and vehicles of every kind.—Nothing but motor-Fteam . engines in the streets. and the 'Oases of Parliament. nut no to Let oi„.e Dioty, as they were when Oliver Croni- Well..httudied them all out, neck and crop into the street. lint here we are at the 'Bank.

Our friend yonder, like thou- sands more, is at heart too full of the novelties attendant on a. reign that Is only just beginning, even to recognise the issues periodically sub- mitted to the electorate. And yet this is called a self-governed country. Our constitutional monarphy.. yelled dp.rancracr. lave we

Well may the Government, as the papers enarge it with doing, miss the moral, and be deaf to the warn- ing of the elections they have lost. In the popu- lar temper, reflected by our omnibus friend, a much less clever man than King Chamberlain might snap his fingers at all demonstrationl against his uncrowned sovereignty.

div.head: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION. Burns Supper.
div.p: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION. Burns Supper.

On Friday last the members of the Warrington Cale— donian Association and their friends, celebrated the anniversary of the birth of Scotland's national poet, Robert Burns, by the holding of a hot-pot supper and social evening, in the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street. The President of the Association Mr. J. Monro, Latchford, occupied the chair, and there were present Mr. W. Skinner, vice-president, Alderman Francomb, Councillor J. Fulton Smith, Dr. Leadbetter, and Messrs. J. A. McGregor, T. May, J. Finlayson, R. Dunn, J. L. Daven- port, J. Hunter, G. Bowman, G. C. Miller, J. Richardson, D. R. Hodge, J. McDermid, J. Tennant, W. Mitchell, J. Barlow, N. Taylor, R. Essen, J. Carruthers, J. Leah, S. Ellison, C. Wells, J. Grounds, J. Bate, P. Bate, J. Emson, H. Currie, Sze. An excellent supper was per- veyed by the popular Host, Mr. Lee. On the tables being cleared the Chairman proposed the usual loyal toasts, --hich were duly honoured. The President also later on, submitted the toast of the evening: "The Immortal Memory of Robert Burns." Mr. Monro said he would ask all present to concentrate their thoughts, just for a few minutes, on Robert Burns, that great personality whose memory they had comp there that night to revere and perpetuate. They came there full of ardent and boundless admiration, and appreciation of the beauti- ful writings of that lad who was born in Kyle, on that stormy night, 25th January, 1759. Although the unco gnid had all along said nasty things of the poet and ignored his good points, the great jury of humanity had given its verdict in his favour, and no traducers, no sneers, no ridicule' would ever affect or attaint in the very slightest degree the immortal memory of Robert Burns. . . . .

The roast was drunk with the usual silence. Mr. THOMAS MAY made a few remarks d..aling with recent antiquarian " finds " in Scotland, giving an account of an important discovery which has just been made in connection with the Scottish Regalia. Mr. May said that the old chest, in which the crown and other articles comprising the regalia of Scotland had been deposited in Dunottar Castle during a troubled i period n history, had just been found t I aye a false bottom under which, on search being n.Aae, there had been found an ancient and interesting locket, bearing a representation of the Virgin Mary, and believed to have formed part of the regalia now preserved in Edinburgh Castle. This find, Mr. May 'explained, was so recent that the particulars had not yet been made public. The evening's proceedings were enlivened by an excellent selection of Scottish and other songs, and musical and humorous items, submitted under the superintendence: of Mr. J. L. Davenport, a member of the association who renders local Caledonians yeoman service in providing entertainment for their periodical gatherings. Mr. H. Currie, a young Scotsman fulfilling a short theatrical engagement in Warriegton, gave a fine rendering of "Asnie Laurie " and being encored responded with "Conlin' through the rye." Mr. Currie also contributed several other songs and humorous items which were much appreciated. Mr. J. Bate sang "Alice, where art thou?" and Mr. P. Bate, "The Bandelero," both gentlemen being heartily applauded. Messrs. Bate also favoured the company with a duet. A fine old Scottish song by the President is always con- sidered a treat at the Association's gathering, and On. this occasion Mr. Monro sang "The Lea Rig," and in response to a hearty encore gave "My Nannie's Awa. " Mr. J. L. Davenport's contribution was "Jessie the flower o' Dunbland," while Mr. J. Fin- lsyson sang "O' a'othe airts," and Mr. J. Hunter, "There was a lad was born in Kyle." Mr. T. May recited "Burns Epitaph," and also gave a humorous recitation. The humorist of the evening was Mr. J. Emson, whose mirth-provoking selections were much appreciated, Mr. Emson having to respond to repeated encores. Mr. J. Grounds acted most efficiently as accompanist, On the motion of Mr. J. Fulton Smith, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the singers for their services, Messrs. P. Bate and J. L. Dayonport responding, and acknowledg- ing the company's indebtedness to Mr. Currie for his valuable assistance as an entertainer. On the motion of Mr. Alderman Francomb, a hearty vote of thanks was given to the President, Mr. Monro, for his services in. the chair, and for his efforts in making the gathering such a. thorough success. At the close the company joined hands and sang " Auld Lang Sync."

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

A MAYORAL "AT HOME," The Mayor and Mayoress of St. Helens (Councillor and Mrs. Martin) held their annual "At Home" on. Tuesday evening at the Town Hall. About 1,.100 invi- tations had been issued. It proved a most enjoyable. function. The guests were received by the Mayor and Mayoress at the entrance to the Assembly-room, which was beautifully decorated. The corridors .and steps• were adorned with plants and flowers. The large hall was used for dancing. Mr. Ernest Hastings and Mr. Tervy Routledge gave a series of entertainments which, were greatly enjoyed. Refreshments were served in the Council Charnbcr and committee-room.

div.head: NEW SCITOOL FOR Sr.HELENS
div.p: NEW SCITOOL FOR Sr.HELENS

Colonel W. W. Pilkingt'on presided at the monthly meeting of the St. Helens Education Authority, when a number of important recommendations were made with regard to new schools at Thatto Heath, Park-road, Windle, and the Cowley Schools, North-road. The architect had received instructions with respect to new schools to be erected on the site of the Cowley Schools. North-road, which would provide infants' and mixed departments and a mixed higher elementary department. Alderman Gamble moved the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, and said the plans of the new school at Thatto Heath were before the meeting. A deputation bad been to interview the Education Depart- ment last week, and their views wqrc favourably received in regard to the school.—Councillor Rudd asked as to the tcheme for the alteration of the British Schools in Waterloo-street, and the doing away with the half-time school. Was that to be laid before the Council ?—The Chairman : No.—Councillor Rudd said there was no information on the minutes, and he would like to know if they could discuss the scheme which it was proposed.—The Chairman said the whole matter would be brought forward when the scheme and plans were completed, and the whole matter would be laid before the committee. It would not be a council school.—The minutes were then passed.

div.head: WONDERFUL DISCOVERY.
div.p: A WONDERFUL DISCOVERY.
Skin-Healing, Past and Present.

Two thousand years ago, the usual way of healing was to anoint the body with some oil or balm made from the extracts of certain valuable herbs and roots. In modern times, however, there has been a gradual departure from the laws and ideas of nature; and to-day we find the majority of ointments and salves composed not of pure- vegetable extracts, but of courser and less effective ingredients in the shape of rancid animal fats and mineral poisons. Such latter preparations are either too coarse to get absorbed into the skin, with the result that they utterly fail to heal and dispel disease as they profess to be able to do ; or their mineral ingredients have a positively harmful effect. It was for long the conviction of an eminent chemist that inasmuch as the instinct to nib comes from nature then Nature herself probably had secreted away some- where the precise article to rub with. He therefore set to work with a view to finding this substance, and turned all inquiries in the direction of the herbs and shrubs in Nature's own storehouse—the forest and bush far removed from the borders of civilization. At length, after a wearying search,certain rare plants were found from which could be extracted juices pos- sessing the astonishing power of creating new, healthy skin! When applied to a cut or sore, inflammation and disease would be at once taken. out, and new sound tissue grown completely over the affected place. To this unique extract were added other juices and balsams of high medicinal merit ; the whole was refined and concentrated so as to increase the potency of each ele- ment, and Zam-buk, the great healer, thus came into existence.

It is, therefore, entirely different., from, as well as superior to, any ordinary preparation. Housewives and mothers particularly value Zam-buk for its purity, reliability, and wide range of usefulness. Robbed well in, Zam-Buk is invaluable for sore throat and chest, colds, chills, rheumatism, neuralgia, tic, sciatica, &c. All chemists sell Zam-Ruk in one-and- three-halfpenny' and two-and-ninepenny boxes (large. size contains nearly four times as much as the one-and- three-halfpenny), or it may be obtained post free from the Zam-Buk Company, Redcross-street, London, E.C. The Biggest Diamond.—The discovery in a Transvaal mine of a diamond three or four times as large as any ever before known, suggests the possibility that diamonds may some day become so common as to lose their monetary value. The famous Koh-i-Noor weighed in the rough state 900 carats, but this new giant diamond is over 3,000 carats in weight, and if it is of fine quality it would be almost beyond the resources of the greatest American millionaire. It may however suffer in the cutting like, the Koh-i-noor, which now weighs only 103 carats, or like the "Excelsior" diamond, also found in South Africa, it may be cut up into a number of smaller stones of marketable sizes. In its present state it is something of a white elephant, though no doubt it will ultimately prove of great value to those fortun- ately interested in its possession. div.head: St. James' Church, Latchford.
div.p: St. James' Church, Latchford.

Success attended the annual congregational tea and entertainment in connection with this church, which took plabe in the schools on Monday evening. About 400 members of the congregation and friends were pt.( sent, At the entertainment an admirable programme was submitted, songs being rendered in a highly credit- able manner by Msss Mollie Spencer, Miss Maud Hill Mr. Turner, and Mr. Hill. The choir contributed two part songs in a manner which showed careful training. The humorous 'part of the programme was supplied by Mr. Alfred Grounds, whose sketches were most laughable and called forth encores. Mr. E. Davit - discharged the duties of accompanist. During the interval the Vicar (Rev. H. B. Firth) alludc I to the genuine interest of parishioners in the church ard thanked all who had rendered assistance, the choir, the artistes, and especially Mr. E. Davies for the excellent , programme of music provided. The Rev. A. Eglingtop,l vicar of St. John's Church East Dulwich (an old college friend of the Vicar's), addressed the me3ting and con- gratulated the congregation upon the improvement which had been effected in the Cturch services since his last visit on March 10th,1904. He urged the parishioners to work with enthusiasm From 9.30 to 11.30 dancing was indulged in.

THE ALLEGED WIFE BURNING. At Runcorn, on Tuesday, John INl'Alahon, 'arm labourer, Aston, was brought up for the third time on a charge of setting his wife on fire on Christmas Day. It was stated the woman was still in hospital and unfit to appear, and the prisoner was remanded for a further seven da) s.

div.head: LOCAL COMMERCE.
div.p: LOCAL COMMERCE.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON CHAMBER.
The Ship Canal Lay-by.

Matters of considerable importance affecting local commerce were touched upon at the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce which was held at the Town Hall on Monday morning under the presi- dency of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, the retiring president. There were also present :—Messrs. John Fairclough, F. W. Monks, Holman Kingdon, H. Thornton, J. H. Smethurst, A. itathbone, F. A. Mosse, H. Chambers, F. Webster, and Arthur Bennett (hon. secretary).—A letter was read from Mr. Fulton Smith,regretting his inability to he present owing to an engagement out of town.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: THE ANNUAL REPORT.

The twenty-eighth annual report was submited by the hon. secretary and stated :—The Council have pleasure in being able to say that in several ways, the chamber is giving evidence of increasing usefulness. Mr. T.H.Barker, Secretary of the Liverpool Chamber, has been approached with a view to giving a lecture on the Siberian Railway, by which route he returned from Canada after the Conference. IMPROVEMENT OF BANK QUAY STATION, At the suggestion of the President, the London and North-Western Railway Company were written to again upon this subject, and they replied as follows : "London, 4th March, 1004. Dear sir,—ln answer to your letter of the 26th ult. as to the Warrington Bank Quay Station, you may rely upon it that the company have not abandoned thqir intention of enlarging and improving the Bank Quay Station, but, as you will readily understand, in the present depressed condition of trade they are not anxious to press forward the carrying out of works involving large expenditure which can possibly be deferred for a time, and I am afraid, therefore, I should not be in a position to name any definite period within which the alterations are likely to be completed.—Yours faithfully, F. HARRISON. A. Bennett, Esq." The Council are also pleased to report that, partly as the result of their representations the company adopted in February last, a uumber of very desirable improve- ments in the local train service.

div.head: SHIP CANAL LAY-BY.
div.p: SHIP CANAL LAY-BY.

Perhaps the most important work which the chamber has undertaken since the last annual meeting has been its attempt to secure the utilization of the Warrington lay-by. The Council have always felt that Warrington is not obtaining all the advantages which it has a right to expect from the proximity of .the Manchester Ship Canal. They have from time to time, urged various measures calculated to promote this object, and to sc3ure the improvement of the river. Whilst they regard the proposal to build a weir below Bank Quay, and so secure a river channelalmost coterminous within the borough, say ten feet in depth, which has now received the sanction of Parliament, with approval, they regret that the time allowed for the construction of the Warrington Dock has expired without any effort to secure an extension, or to prevent the site at tValton from being turned to other uses. Bat they realize that the most practical method of creating a local shipping trade is to make the best use of the existing facilities, believing that these, if taken advantage of, would inevit- ably lead to others. The lay-by built in 1897 has hitherto been practically unused. The matter has been frequently discussed, and the chamber appointed in November last, a Lay-by Committee, consisting of Messrs. John Fairclongb, E. L. Fleming, Louis lienshall, F. A. Mosse, C. E. Parkerand the Secretary (ex-officio), with the express object of ascertaining whether War- rington cannot make use of it with advantage. The committee have met twice, and sent out a circular to all the leading local firms asking if in case of a saving in cost being shown,they would be willing to make use of London, Glasgow, and Belfast steamers if they would call at the lay-by, and stating that any other suggestions in connection with the canal would, be welcomed, as we are strongly of opinion that War- rington is not at present deriving from it the benefit which was anticipated, and which could prob- ably be secured by co-operative effort.' A large number of replies have been received, and they are almost uniformly favourable to the idea. They have been sent to the Canal Company, and the Council confidently believe that, if the local public who are in- terested in the matter will back them up in their efforts, the lay-by may soon be in regular use, with un- mistakable advantage to the numerous industies associ- ated with the town. AFFILIATION OF LOCAL TRADE SOCIETIES.

The questions briefly touched upon are typical of many others in which chambers of commerce may inter- vene With great advantage, and we are very anxious to obtain the cordial co-operation of all our present mem- bers and of any other firms in the town or district not at present members of the chamber. An important step in this direction has been taken by the recent adoption of a new rule, which reads as follows: " Any local society of a commercial or industrial character may be affiliated with the chamber on payment of an annual subscription of two guineas, which shall entitle each such society to nominate one member to attend the general meetings of the chamber as their representative." We trust that local bodies of this character will promptly take advantage of the rule, and so increase their influence and our utility at the same time.

div.head: DEATH OE MR. THOMAS TUNSTALL.
div.p: DEATH OE MR. THOMAS TUNSTALL.

The Council very regret to record the tragically sudden death, in the early part of the year, of Mr. Thomas Tunstall, chartered accountant, for many years one of the hon. auditors of the Chamber, [but they are glad to be able to intimate that his partner, Mr. C. D. Parkinson, has kindly undertaken to act in 'his place.

div.head: FINANCIAL
div.p: FINANCIAL

The financial statemen'CSY;;;;Wci an adverse balance of £2 2s. 4d., but the Secretary explained that it was due to the fact that one or two members had unfortunately left them, and to exceptional expenses incurred during the year. Generally their income and expenditure about balanced. THE CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS. Tflq NECESSITY FOR STATION IMPROVEMENTS.

The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the•report said that when he accepted the office of president for another year, at their kind suggestion—he was almost going to say kind compulsion—it was on the under- ing that his presidental duties should be merely formal, and that the practical work of the association should be committed to other hands, • more conversant with commercial matters than he was, lie noticed that a further communication had been received from the London and North-Western Railway Company. They would all hail with svlisfaction any improvement in the railway accommodation in the town, and he hoped what the company had already done was only a first instalment of what they were prepared to do. For two years past the chamber had pointed out the in- convenience and evert danger of the present Bank Quay Station. The platforms were so low that frequent accidents happened from people stepping out of the carriages and, miscalculating the distance from the platform, falling headlong to the flags. The platforms, also, were so narrow that with a congestion of luggage ; and passengers it was a matter of difficulty and danger !to get along them. If his memory served him rightly, ;after a complaint from that chamber two years ago, they were assured that the plans were out for remodelling the station, and that the work was to be commenced. Now they got an answer that " they were not anxious ; to press forward the carrying out of works which could possibly be deferred for a time," which he snpposed meant that it would not be done until some serious accident obliged them to do so. Be thought Warring-
The Examiner, Saturday, February 4, 1905. WOMAN'S REALM.

ton had a right to expect a much better passenger I station,and it ~as the duty of the chamber to press the matter. (Ilear,hear.) They must all rejoice in arbitration treaties taking the place of the fearful arbitrament 1 of war, and recognize• with pride and pleasure that our peace-loving King had been instrumental in smooth- I ing many difficulties and obliterating the ill-feeling which existed between us and some of our Continental neighbours. (Hear, hear.) The utilization of the lay-by on the Ship Canal might, and they hoped it would, be productive of great advantage in the future, and the energetic action of. the Chamber should merit the approval and thanks of all interested in tha future of Warrington. Hitherto the Ship Canal had not brought in that golden harvest they were led to expect from its promoters. Let them hope the Chamber would be suc- cessful in attracting the attention of some of the great shipping companies to the facilities they coeld offer, and that Warrington,instend of being left in the could as she had been hitherto, would become an important place of call for the ships of our great mercantile navy. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN FA.IRCLOUGH seconded the adoption of the report and balance sheet. The SECRETARY said that with reference to the lay-by he might say,that they had received about 30 letters in reply to their circular, and the firms were almost unani- mously favourable to the idea of utilizing the canal. Many promised support if suitable terms could be arranged. The letters had been forwarded to the Canal Company, who had written stating that they were being considered. The importance of the matter could not be exaggerated, and he felt that if the members of the Chamber who were representatives of leading industries would work together they would very likely be able to secure conditions which would be of incalculable advan- tage to the commerce of Warrington. The report and statement of accounts were adopted.

div.head: EDUCATIONAL MATTERS.
div.p: EDUCATIONAL MATTERS.

As Mr. HOLMAN KINGDON has only represented the Chamber on the Education Committee for a very short period, he intimated that he would reserve his report on local educational work for some future meeting. With regard to the Advisory Board in connection with the Faculty of Commerce, Victoria University, Manchester, he had attended two functions, one being the official reception by the Lord Mayor. It should be remembered that these Boards were collected from various towns around Manchester, and they were only invited to express opinions on matters of general interest. Mr. Kingdon alluded to the university extension lectures on social questions being held fortnightly at the Co-opera- tive Hall, and asked the Chamber to support such a commendable educational effort.

ELECTION OF PRESIDENT. In accordance with a recommendation of the Council Mr. F. W. Monks proposed the election of Mr. Fulton Smith, the vice-president, as president of the chamber for the ensuing year, remarking that that gentleman had shown considerable ability in connection with their transactions. He was eminently suitable for the office. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. H. SMETHURST seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. VICE-PRESIDENT.
On the motion of Mr: FAIRCLOUGH, seconded by 61 MONKS, Mr. Kingdon was elected vice-president. HON. TREASURER AND AUDITORS.

Mr. William Skinner (Parr's Bank, Limited) was re-appointed hon. treasurer, and Messrs. T. and J. L. Tunstall and Co., hon. auditors. Or the motion of Alderman BENNETT, seconded by Mr. KINGDoN, votes of thanks were .accorded to the officers for their services during the past year. The PRESIDENT briefly responded. THE COUNCIL.

The Council was elected as follows :—Messrs. James Fairclough and Son, Ltd.. W. Lrm,T. and Son, the Long- ford Wire, Iron and Steel Company, .NLwiie and Com- pany,Monks Hall and Company, the National Telephone Company, the Penketh Tanning Company, Pierpoint and Bryant, Andrew Rathbone, J. H. Smethurst, J. C. Parr, Fletcher, Russell and Company, Mr. Fulton Smith (the new president), Mr. H. Kingdon (vice-president), and Mr. Skinner (Parr's Bank, Limited)

• LOCAL STATION ACCONIMODATION. The meeting discussed the question of accommodation at the Bank Quay and Central Stations. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH observed that Bank Quay Station was in a bad state especially on the London platform. The CHAIRMAN said that occasionally when a train went a good way out of the station steps had to be provided to enable passengers to enter the. carriages. He proposed that the Chamber should forward the com- pany another resolution similar to that theyhad already sent. There was no harm in reminding the company that promises had been made which had not be kept. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH seconded. _

Mr. CHAMBERS drew attention to the condition of the Central Station. which, he said, might very well be improved. The PRESIDENT observed that a driving access was needed to the near platform. He proposed thata letter be sent to the Cheshire Liaes Committee als ). Mr. CHAMBERS suggested that the Chamber should recommend that the platform should be widened and the whole place covered in, but several members pointed out that if it were covered in a nuisance would be created because the smoke could not escape. The resolutions were carried,but it was decided not to ask for Central Station to be covered in. MINISTER OF COMMERCE NEEDED.

The Hex. SECRETARY read a letter from the British Iron-Trade Association asking the Chamber to write the Prime Minister suggesting the creation of a Depart- ment of Commerce and the appointment of a Minister of Commerce as a member of the Cabinet. The Board of Management of the Association had already written Mr. Balfour on the question and they were inviting the support of all Chambers of Commerce. Mr. MONKS proposed that a letter be sent to Mr. Balfour as suggested. A Minister of Commerce was really badly wanted in this country, and there were many ways in which such an individual could help commerce and the traders as a whole. Mr. I:INGDON seconded and endorsed Mr. Monks's remarks most thoroughly. Such an appointment was one of the crying needs of the present time. In this respect we suffered very considerably compared with other nations.

The proposition was agreed to. Alderman BENNETT said that this step was entirely in harmony with the views of the Associated Chambers of Commerce. RAILWAY COMPANIES AND CANALS. Mr.MoNKs said the question of the canals of the country came up for discussion at the British Iron Trade Association meeting. If they could do something which would have the effect of improving canal naviga- tion it would do a great deal towards helping trade generally. The railway companies had bought up the canals with the idea of throttling them and preventing competition. If they could get the Government to buy the canals up at their present depreciated value and run them as a Government department, or have some public trust created for the management, it would be a great benefit to all. After discussion a resolution was adoptod in favour of the formation of a public trust to control the canals and give increased facilities. Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. Parr for pre- siding, and to the Mayor for the VISO of the room.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH
OF WARRINGTON,
WEEK ENDING JANUARY 2Sth, 1905.
During the week, the following births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 55, deaths, 20. The excess of births over deaths was 35.

The birth-rate was equal to 41.3. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 15.0 per 1,000 against 21.9 the average f the previous 4 weeks and against 224 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 7 per 1,000, against •55 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 3.6 the corresponding period of 1004. The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Total 4 2 2 1 9 2 20 The deaths included-1 from diphtheria, 3 from phthisis, 1 from cancer, 4 from lung diseases, 11 from all other 'causes. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during t'lb wee:: :—Scarlet fever, 6 cases ; diphtheria 1 case. Total number of patients in hospital, week ending 28th January, 1905, 67. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 37 Fah. and therefore 4 deg. higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 47 F., was recorded on the 28tb inst., and the minimum temperature 21 F., on the 25th inst. The rainfall measured •15 inch. The general direc- tion was N.W.
J. GUEST GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: Superintendent Monaghan's Capture.
div.p: Superintendent Monaghan's Capture.

At Runcorn on Monday, Jack Liptrot, a youth of 17 years, with a very had record was sentenced to a month's bard labour on a charge of stealing a silver watch and chain,value..c.;2llelon,,ing to James Shackleton of the canal boat France. The prisoner bad worked on the boat for a fortnight. On Friday he decamped and within four hours of the discovery of the robbery Superintendent 3lonagban had found the watch in a Warrington pawnshop and had arrested the prisoner- : very smart capture. The prisoner also pleaded guilty to deserting from the West Riding Regiment at Halifax, and he was ordered to await an escort at the expiration of his sentence.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
ROYAL GOD-CHILDREN.

There is often a complaint nowadays among the rising generation that it is no good having sponsors, for they forget all about them. This is not a view held by the Queen, who has a wonderful memory for her god-children. Thus, remarks the Onlooker, she sent for the younger boy of Colonel Dalrymple Hamilton, who has just got on to the Britannia, and presented him with a watch.
EVENING DRESS OF CHINE-DE-SOIR.

The evening dress depicted in the sketch war. composed of chini-de-soie, which is a particularly delightful material, being more durable than crêpe- de-chine, and not easily crushed. The gown from which this illustration was sketched was of a pale maize yellow, and boasted a berthe of point de Venice lace, cut in large tabs, and strapped across with tiny straps of yellow velvet finished with

steel crystal buttons. The full bodice was arranged in four deep tucks, being slightly pointed in the front; the lowest tuck hangs over the wide belt of folded velvet. The sleeves correspond with the bodice, and are finished with two frills of accordion- pleated chinei-de-soie; each frill is edged with a narrow ruching. The skirt was closely gathered over the hips, the lower part of the skirt being trimmed with lace and straps of velvet, the hem finished with three flat tucks. The foundation was of pale yellow taffetas having a deep accordion- pleated flounce, which held out the skirt well from the feet.
Gossip.
Countess Howe, with Earl Howe, has left for the East. She is still far from well, and has gone out with no less than five nurses and maids to look after her.

Miss Van Wart is still at Ditton Park, her place near Slough. She has again been very unwell, and suffering from severe neuralgia, but she hopes to do some entertaining later.on in town. Mrs. Hervey has left Guilsborough Hall for Monte Carlo. Later on she is going to Japan, and will return to England by way of California. Mrs. Hervey is an American, but very English in all her tastes, a straight rider to hounds, and a great traveller. She has many pets at her home in North- amptonshire, one of her favourites being a large white Russian hound.
WINTMIR HATS AND TOQLS.

Winter hats and toques are the very first, of all the things that belong to the cold season, to give place to more spring-like models, while the last wintry garments to be reluctantly discarded are the furs. Knowing this, we must be accustoming our- selves to the new models which we are so soon to adopt for our personal head wear. Our first sketch shews a most sensible theatre toque. It is of palest mauve chiffon, and is quite small. The strings of large Parma violets with which it is wreathed lie close to the chiffon, and a clump of small shaded mauve plumes are the only adornment. The

second is also a toque, composed of white and greenish tinted violets. It is flattened up at the sides, and ends in a sharp peak in front. The crown is swathed in shaded green tulle, and wings of the same tulle are used as a trimming at the left side. Our third and largest model is a cream lace hat, criprned with cream panne. The brim sweeps sharply up on the left side above a panne bandeau supporting a spray of pink roses, and is out- lined with Banksia roses; and a beautiful black osprey, attached to the edge of the upturned brim, showers itself over the crown of the hat.

div.head: AUDACITY OF UGLINESS.
div.p: THE AUDACITY OF UGLINESS.

Englishwomen, it has recently been pointed out in a daily journal, do not make the best of them- selves. Despite the fact that, as a nation, we possess physical advantages that in the natural order of things should give us a long start, we are nevertheless outdistanced by other women when a decision has to be arrived at as to who are the most attractive women in the world. And the secret of this, declares "Ambrosia" in the World, is that we do not possess the audacity of ugliness. The American or the Frenchwoman never allows herself' to be daunted by the fact that she has not been endowed by Nature with good looks or a good figure. She dresses as carefully, carries herself as grandly, as her beautiful sisters, and indeed assumes rather more of an air than they, with the happy result that America and France seem to have no ill-dressed and no really plain or ungraceful daughters. We Englishwomen are too modest, and fancy we are altogether hopeless unless we have good material on which to work. Dressed abso- lutely to date, with every detail correct, and with a perfectly confident air that she looks well, I will guarantee that a really plain woman will triumph over her far better-looking sisters who are less audacious.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

- PARTRIDGES EN CASSEROLE. —MIS recipe is by "Madge" of Truth: Have ready three picked and cleaned partridges. Scrape and pound 6oz. of white veal. Sauté three or four chickens' livers with the livers Of the partridges, 20z. of butter, loz. of scraped fat bacon, a sprig or two of parsley, a sprig of thyme, and a chopped shallot. Drain them from the butter and herbs, and pound them with the veal. Add 2oz. of breadcrumbs that have been boiled until thick in Stock, the yolks of two eggs and one whole one. Season all with salt and pepper, add a pinch of cayenne, and then rub it through a wire sieve: Fill tie crop part of the birds with the farce, forcing a little of it betweer the skin and 'the breast, and trues them into shape. Fry them quickly in a stewpan with butter and vegetables. sprinkle them with flour, add a gill of cooking sherry, and sufficient stock to cover them stir them together, and braise them for an hour. After which remove the string, cut the birds it halves, and place them in an earthenware casserole. Strain the sauce over them and simmer them half. an-hour, serving them in the casserole.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND GLEANINGS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND GLEANINGS.
THE Flaherty carboy inelinator is an American device for tilting carboys in order to pour from them into vessels. It is of simple construction, and worked by a handle.

lilmrrnm.oT, the eminent chemist, has found Uri- variations of humidity do not influence the length of the stem of plants, but they influence the surfa( e of the section of the stem, and the thickness of its tissues.

div.head: EARTH'S MAGNETISM.
div.p: THE EARTH'S MAGNETISM.

According to a writer in Science, the source of the magnetism of the earth is a complicated problem. It seems caused by an internal magnetism (perhaps of lodestone) as well as by earth currents of electricity, and some emanation from the sun appears to influence it.

div.head: TO HEAR THE FISH SWIM.
div.p: TO HEAR THE FISH SWIM.

A French scientific magazine mentions a German patent for a micro-telephone detector of herring and other schools of fish in the water. The microphone in a box is lowered into the water and connected with a telephone on board the fishing boat. The noise of the fish in the water is thus reported.

div.head: FROZEN AIR-BLAST.
div.p: A FROZEN AIR-BLAST.

Mr. Gasly, of the Carnegie Steel Works, Pittsburg, United States, has caused the air blast to pass through refrigerators which cool it to below zero, and make it give up its moisture. It enters the furnace at the freezing-point, and this improvement has effected an economy of 20 per cent, in the coal used.

div.head: RADIO-ACTIVE GASES.
div.p: RADIO-ACTIVE GASES.

MM. Curie and Laborde having observed that the gases from certain hot springs are radio-active, M. Moureau has found both helium and argon are present in such gases. The fact is interesting in connection with the observation that helium is pro- duced from the emanation of radium. The presence of argon also tends to explain the therapeutic action of some springs.

div.head: TO OBTAIN INTELLECTUAL REST.
div.p: TO OBTAIN INTELLECTUAL REST.

According to Dr. Fischer, of Berlin, the most effective position of sleep for obtaining intellectual rest is to keep the head low and the feet slightly elevated. Failing all this the body should, at any rate, be horizontal, so as to irrigate the brain well. The habit of sleeping with head low and feet high is, according to the doctor, a remedy for brain troubles and some internal maladies. It can be adopted gradually.

div.head: WHEN THE LEOPARD CHANGES COLOUR.
div.p: WHEN THE LEOPARD CHANGES COLOUR.

The black leopard has been regarded by many as ' a distinct species. A naturalist in India, however, 1 reports having found a pair of leopard cubs, one of which was black while the other was of the ! ordinary colour, thus proving that the black colour is simply an instance of melanism, in which an • animal turns black in the same way as the albino turns white. This tendency to blackness, it is stated, is most marked in hot, moist climates.

div.head: RADIUM AND THE DIAMOND.
div.p: RADIUM AND THE DIAMOND.

In the course of some experiments concerning the effect of the emanations fm radium upon diamonds, Sir William Crookes made a curious discovery. When a diamond was placed in the path of the radiations it was converted from the carbon crystal into the common form of graphite, while in addition its colour was quite changed. As I a result of this strange metamorphosis, Sir William Crookes suggests that the radium rays may prove of great commercial value to the jeweller, since by this means diamonds which are of an indifferent and defective colour may be appreciably increased in their commercial value by treatment under the radium rays. He also observed that prolonged action of the radium increased the intensity of the pale-coloured gems.

div.head: IS THERE ANOTHER PLANET?
div.p: IS THERE ANOTHER PLANET?

When the moon is interposed directly between ttie earth and the sun, the brightness of day is temporarily exchanged for the gloom of night. If the sky be free from clouds the stars spring forth, and can be seen around the obscured sun. Even if a planet were quite close to the luminary it would be visible, says Cassell's "Story of the Heavens," on such an occasion if its magnitude were comparable with that of Mercury. Careful preparation is neces- sary when it is proposed to make a trial of this kind. The danger to be specially avoided is that of confounding the planet with the ordinary stars, which it will probably resemble. The late dis- tinguished American astronomer, Professor Watson, specially prepared to devote himself to this research ! during the notable total eclipse in 1878. When the ; eclipse occurred the light of the sun vanished and the stars burst forth. Among them Professor' Watson saw an object which to him seemed to be the long-sought intra-Mercurial planet. We should add that this observer also saw another object, which he at first thought to be the star known as Zeta in the constellation Cancer. When he after- wards found that the recorded place of this object did not agree so well as expected with the known position of this star, he came to the conclusion that it could not be Zeta, but must be some other unknown planet.

div.head: "LIVING CRYSTAL."
div.p: THE "LIVING CRYSTAL."

The researches of Dr. Otto von Schriin, Professor of Pathological Anatomy in the University of Naples, says a writer in Knowledge and Scientific News, gave meaning some ten years ago to the ex- pression "the living crystal." He shewed that living matter, largely albuminous in character, takes the crystalline form, and, while still living and crystalline, obeys so many of the laws, and manifests so many of the properties of inorganic crystallisation, that its crystalline character may be said to be estsblished. From these experiments he drew the inference that crystallisation in its terrestrial origin was a manifestation of life—of vital energy: in short, that a crystal grew for the same reasons that a plant grows, or the brain grows, or an amceba grows; that the vital forces stirring the one are no more than a different form of the forces that develop the other. The "living crystal," the "vital crystal" which, for example, he dis- covered as one of the products evolved by various of the bacilli that he examined, became thus, in his theory, the bridge between what had heretofore been called living matter—animal and vegetable— and dead matter—mineral. The first crystals which set him on the road to this theory were the crystals of the Asiatic cholera bacillus, which he examined as long ago as 1886. They were long, needle- shaped prisms. Other bacilli examined exhibited distinct crystals of different forms. The bacillus subt:lis, for instance, formed bayonet rhombs; the bacillus tenueefortnis hexagonal prisms; the tubercle bacillus develops square rhombs ; anthrax, elongated rhombs ; any given bacillus being immedi- ately identified by its crystal, which never varies in the shape assumed in its original formation. These objects are perfect crystals in form; yet, as anyone may see, they are alive, and their life, their motion, and their reproduction are as visible and undoubted as their death when it ensues is un- doubted. Their death occurs when all the living matter which originally formed part of the crystal has eliminated itself. On death they become the crystals that we know, ordinary mineral crystals.

div.head: UTILITY OF RADIUM.
div.p: THE UTILITY OF RADIUM.

While scientific men have been descanting on the marvels of radium, and calculating with minute accuracy the amount of energy stored up in the smallest fragment of this extraordinary substance, the man in the street has been persistently asking, What is the use of radium? At first sight, the prospect is, says a contributor to a contemporary, most encouraging. It has been calculated that, on the lowest estimate, the heat stored up in any given bit of radium bromide is 300,000 times as great as the heat stored up in an equal weight of coal. In the case of coal, however, we can use its energy at whatever rate we please. We may con- sume a ton of coal in half-an-hour to drive a locomotive, or we may spread out the expenditure over many weeks if we only want to drive a three- horse-power engine. But radium gives out its energy at its own rate, which we have no power to change. And the worsireof it is that this rate is provokingly slow. Our little gramme of radium bromide will take several thousand years to yield up the energy that is stored in it; and, conse- quently, the amount available at any moment, is so insignificant as to be of no use for practical pur- poses. Again, we can use the energy of coal when we want it; and when we do not want it the energy will remain stored up and ready for use. But radium is perpetually giving out its energy, whether we want it or not. Its incessant activity never relaxes for a moment: and we have no means of stopping the prodigious waste that is always going on, day and night, week after week, for years and centuries almost without end. Indeed, until we consider some way of controlling this energy as we control the energy of coal, there is no prospect of radium bromide being turned to useful account as a motive power.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
FRBRUARY 4th. 1905.

Mr. CFIAMBERLAIN'S THE GAME IS UP. speech at Gains- borough betrays a consciousness that the game is up. There was little trace of the confidence and spirit with which he began his fiscal campaign. He is full of warn- ings to the perverse generation which will not heed his counsels. There is only one way of pre- serving the Empire. He has pointed out the way and yet the people will not take it. "Hold fast to the Colonies," he cries, 'for you will lose your most promising market." Nobody has any desire to quarrel with the Colonies, but it does not follow that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S plan is the only one that will keep them. "It is easier to do business with our kinsmen," he tells us," than with foreigners." But our foreign trade is of considerable importance to this country, and we see no reason why we should not maintain it and do business with our kins- men as well. This attempt to set up an invidious distinction between our kinsmen and the foreigner is unbusinesslike to the last degree. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN maintains that it is upon tha Colonies we shall have to rely in a time of I stress, but the growth of uur exports scarcely points to this conclusion. It is upon the whole volume of our trade that we must rely, and that volume increases under a fiscal system , which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN denounces as antiquated. He denies that he has any desire to make food dearer. Of course lie bee no such desire; but the question is whether dearness will not follow the adoption of a policy which means a protective tariff all round. Manifestly it is the predorninent opinion, after eighteen months of ardent debate, that such a consequence is inevitable, and that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S scheme of Colonial pre- ference offers no advantage commensurate with such a sacrifice. Some of the Prime Minister's friends are now assuring us that he has foreseen Mr. Cliemnsar.kix's failure from the outset, and has laid his plans with a view to throwing the "Missionary of Empire" overboard, or rather not the missionary, but the mission. For it is argued by these hopeful apologists that Mr.CHAMBERLAIN himself must see that he has failed, not temporarily, but finally, and that he will have to co-operate with Mr. BALFOUR to rally the party on some other issue. Has not Mr. BALFOUR said that it will take two General Elections before any mandate can be seclred for a commercial union with the Colonies. What does this indicate but a deter- mination to shelve the whole business? It is pretty certain that the Unionists will be smitten hip and thigh at the next General Election, and it is more than doubtful whether they will ever appeal to the country again on the issue raised by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN.

All this is very plausible, but it neglects the consideration that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN commands the allegiance of more than half of the Unionist party, and that he is counting on the great things he will be able to do in opposition. It is also over- looked that while Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has repeat- edly claimed Mr. BALFOUR as an adherent, the Prime Minister has never disputed the soft impeachment. His own avowed policy, moreover, is pure Protection, and he is pledged to take the judgment of the country upon it. The idea that, when it is rejected at the polls, Mr. BALFOUR will inform his party that so far as he is concerned, the whole matter is finally settled, and that they must get out of the lurch as best they can, seems to us a very poor compliment to his character.
