_ A successful smoking concert arranged by a com- mittee of the regimental institute was held in the new Volunteer quarters last evening. Lieutenant-Colonel Edlesten presided over a large gathering of officers and men. An excellent programme' was submitted, the artistes including Messrs. Lante4berg, Lebarrow and Taylor (Widnes), Messrs. Grounds, Bate, Lloyd, Aukland, and linsworth (of Warrington) who acquitted themselves very creditably. Mr. Lomas accompanied. During the evening opportunity was taken to elect representatives of the corporals and privates' rooms to serve on the General Committee of the Regimental Institute.

div.head: Eo be tet.
div.p: Eo be tet.
The L.N.W.R. at St. Louis Exhibition.

Last night's Liberal meeting was probably the most inspiring event of its kind in the Radical his- tory of Warrington. Mr. Lloyd-George is the man of the moment, and the enthusiasm of the dense crowd of electors who flocked to grset him was invigorating in the extreme. And what a speech they listened to! Mr. Lloyd-George has singled out Mr. Chamberlain as his spacial foe ever since his entry into Parliamentary life, and never yet has he failed to worst his famous opponent. Last night, the champion of Wales—and of England too—fastened upon "Joe" with the tenacity of purpose which is perhaps his most distinguishing characteristic. Step by step he dogged the great "Missionary" through every phase of the Pro- tectionist campaign and left him not a leg to stand upon. A more crushing indictment of the suicidal foolishness of Protection was propably never uttered. "Facts are stubborn things" as the speaker said, and with them, fresh-cull ad from unanswerable blue books, he administered such a flagellation on behalf of Free Trade that he con- vinced the doubters and shook the faith of the most ardent tariff reformers. The speech itself was a masterly piece of oratory, full of scathing criticism, and scintillating with a wit as sponta- neous as refreshing. The Free Trade cause will date a big advance from last night, and the testimony of Warrington to the eternal principles of Cobden and Bright seems more and more assured.

We notice that some of the Junior Conserva- tives are getting despondent with regard to the prospect at the corning Parliamentary election. They admit that the contest in Warrington will be a keen one, and such an admission from such a quarter is striking testimony to the weakness of their own cause and the strength of the opposition. The effect of recent by-elections has obviously been to make even our Tory friends place very little faith in the 1200 m ijority they obtained during the war. And if the juniors are getting pessimietic, what of the seniors in Sankey-street? The younger generation is usually supposed to be more optimistic than the older. There must be something akin to a panic in the local Protectionist party. At any rate there is plenty of confidence among the Liberals and Unionist Free Traders that Protection and privilege are in for a knock- down blow at Warrington.

Considering all the talk about retaliation recip- rocity, and binding the colonies to the Mother Country, it is wonderful how little evidence there is that the colonies are enamoured of a closer union and prepared to sacrifice something for it. On the contrary we hear an outburst every now and then about the tariffs they put up against imports from the Mother Country itself. In all probability only a small proportion of the people in England who are bitten with the Pro- tectionist fever and overflowing with a grand imperial sentiment, realise that our Australian cousins have not yet learned what reciprocity means. Each day that passes brings fresh evidence of the irritating restriction upon trade involved in the import duty of threepence per pound now charged upon all trade catalogues and prise lists entering Australia. Practically every firm export- ing to the Commonwealth is experiencing the annoyance of finding that the catalogues they are in the habit of sending, and through which so much business has hitherto resulted, have failed to reach their customers through the operation of this irritating tax. Naturally enough a customer often rejects a catalogue rather than pay the duty on it, just as we, in this country, return to the postman the sur- charged missive which looks suspiciously like a circular. Heuths are being taken to over- come the difficulty by paying the duty at this end, and getting the distribution of catalogues attended to in the antipodes, but the fact remains that in so small a matter as this, one at least of our colonies inflicts a tariff bearing harshly on the home manu- facturers. The sentiment is all on one side, apparently. We are not only to purvey the im• penal flavour, but we are to pay for it in addition, Monday's Labour demonstration was very well attended, and the personality of Mr. Keir Hardie, M P., aroused considerable interest. The speezhes, however, were decidedly more Socialistic than Labour, and after hearing them one could not help coming to the conclusion—if it had not already been formed—that Socialism is the doctrine of the discontented A more even distribution of the world's wealth was the sum total of the demands when crystallized. "You have too much. There- fore give me of what you have" seemed to be the burden of the cry, and it was supported by argu- ments which,in many cases, will not bear examina- tion. Free breakfasts for poor school children was one of the planks in Mr. Seddon's political plat- form, and a section of the audience warmly greeted the proposal—it would save themselves and their wives both money and trouble. The individual responsibility of the parent was never considered, but it will have to be, and very seriously. Mr. ' Keir Hardie made light of the poverty produced by drink. It was less than 20 per cent he said— a statement which he will have a difficulty in making people believe. We should imagine that ' 50 per cent was much nearer the mark. There are I few cases of poverty and wretchedness into the cause of which intemperance has never entered. Mr. John Burns. who is probably a truer knight of labour than :Mr. Kier Hardie says: "The undoubted fact that two thirds of :the total drink bill is due to the working classes is not mitigated, in my judgment, by the fact that they are seven- tenths of the total population and only receive less than half the total wealth." It does not seem to us that socialism anct labour can go hand in hand, and the sooner they take different ways the better for the future of the democracy.

It would be a good thing, we think, if our local legislators immediately went into training for the Council meeting on Tuesday. Judging by the bulkiness of the agenda paper and the controver- sial nature of a good proportion of the business, the sitting will either last until" the small hours" or have to be adjourned. The February meeting is an annual meeting in the sense that the recom- mendations for increases of salaries are always considered at this date. Usually one or more of the increases is objected to by some economist, and considerable argument required to carry the point. This year there are no very big advances proposed, and there is a reasonable prospect that this part of the proceedings will not cause very much trouble. Altogether there are ten officials, including two under the Education Committee, who are applying for an increase of salary. The total of the proposed increases only comes to £194 per annum—not a very exorbitant demand from so many applicants.

Somewhat late in the day, the thanks of the C ouncil " for valuable services," and for" prepar- ing the satisfactory report," are to be offered to the six gentlemen who at different times acted as Commissioner's for the Corporation on the recent Non-Trading Inquiry. We should imagine that the recognition. somo six months after the event of services rendered, will hardly be appreciated to the fullest extent. But, better late than never! Why, however, have the thanks of the Council not been given also to the three Non-Trading Commissioners? They worked even harder than their confreres in the production of l' their report, and likewise submitted the same to the Mayor. Perhaps he fact that th ir report was not so "satisfactory " from a Corporation point of view has something to do with this apparent discourtesy. We should have thought that His Worship the Mayor would have recognised that all the Commissioners had a single eye to the public weal!

For twenty-eight years the Chamber of Commerce hes played a useful part in the com- mercial life of Watrington. Jadging from its present activity there is reason to believe that it will in the future exercise a greater influence in the forwarding of measures which make for the pros. perity of our many industries and continue to take a lively interest in questions of great import to the commerce of the nation. The repert presented at the annual meeting on Monday formed interesting reading. Of matters more immediately local, by
MINN

far the most important dealt with was the effort to promote a general utilization of the Ship Canal lay-by at Walton. The retiring I president summed up the position to a nicety when he said that "hitherto the Ship Canal has not brought in that golden harvest we were led to ' expect from its promoters." It is indeed high time that Warrington obtained some advaitage from the great waterway and if our traders woulki unite in making the fullest use of the facilities at Walton we have no doubt the results would quite justify the experiment. It is encouraging to know that ' the majority of the firms approached have expressed themselves favourable to the idea if a saving can be shown, and there should be no difficulty on that score. The undertaking would be fraught with great possibilities to the industrial progress of Warrington and we hope the Chamber of Com- merce will persevere in keeping it to the fore. The Chamber passed a resolution in favour of the formation of a public trust to control the canals of the country and provide increased facilities. It is a notorious fact that these water- ways have been bought up by the railway corn panies and rendered practically useless as a means of transit for manufacturing concerns, simply to restrict competition. After all the Chamber's resolution only touched the fringe of a big ques- tion. The nationalisation of railways, which in itself would be an incalculable boon to industry, could be followed as a matter of course by a development of canal traffic. It is only reasonable that British manufactures should benefit by the undertalcings which took years to engineer success- fully, and reform in this direction is urgently needed. We are glad the Chamber has shown itself to be alive to the injustice of the present system, and as the cheap is being advocated by many influential bodies which have very few points in common, there is an indication that the reform may in course of time come within the range of practical politics.

What electricity is nobody knows. That human beings are able to harness and utilise this mysteri- ous element is therefore the more remarkable. The might of the element will be realised when it is understood that the new power-house in London, erected at Lot's-road, Chelsea, will supply various underground railways with a motive force equal to that of 80,000 horses. This power-house is the largest in the world. Experts who have seen it go, into raptures over the scientific ingenuity of the plant. But so much electricity cannot be origin- ated in London save at great cost. To produce 80,000 electric horse-power 8,000 tons of coal are needed. In other words, one ton of coal is equal to 10 h.p. This, in the course of twelve months, will mean an enormous total. It implies also that if, by reason of war or strikes, the coal supply fails, the entire underground system of the metropolis will be at a standstill. Against this, if we turn our attention to South Africa, we will find a still more wonderful power- house being erected shortly at the Victoria Falls. That magnificent volume of water, which naught except an earthquake can divert, will enable ten timss as much electricity to be made as is required for the London subterraneous system. When the cost of erecting the machinery and laying down the cables has been defrayed, the I supply will be almost automatic, without any expense. For making the electricity the water will furnish all requisite force. This will light towns and drive tramcars within a radius of some 300 miles. Wonderful as the London power-house may be, it will be totally eclipsed by its South African rival. ConsiJering how local rates mount up in this country for water and lighting, it is to be regretted that the ZAmbesi Falls cannot be removed bodily to Great Britain. As the moun- tain cannot come to IVlahornet, it is advisable that lyoung Mahomet should go to the mountain ILatest news indicates that things are looking up in South Africa. E iterprising youths in this over- crowded country may, therefore, well keep an eye on new Rhodesian developments.

The meeting was presided over by Mr. W. H. Sherburn. Recitations were given by Florrie Starkey, E. H. Bibby, Alice Heesom, Martha Riley, Auce Starkey, Ethel Wainwright and John Henry Bibby. Mr, F. Riley gave a Lancashire reading. The following musical items were given: Concertina solo by Mr. William Bennett, selections on the auto-harp by Mr. F. Miss Elizabeth Gallop sang "The Beautiful City," a very pleasant evening being brought to a close by a dialogue entitled "Matthew Brown's Vow," which was given by the friends of Workingmen's Mission.

Warrington Spiritualist Lyceum. The annual tea to the members of this institution took place in the Druids Hall on Tuesday evening. After tea a programme of songs recitations &c., was opened by Miss Lee and Miss Bowyer, with the pleas- ing duet " Angels are whispering," and afterwards they gave" The Gipsy Countess," and in response to an encore " Where are you going to my pretty maid." " My heart is your heart," was nice!y sung by Miss Harrop. Miss Lily Moffat recited, The New King- dom," and Master Dobson " The Village Blacksmith,' and both were loudly applauded. A number of boys caused roars of laughter by singing in character " Macnamara's bard," and had to respond to an encore. Three of the lads also sang " Mr. Dooley." Great fun was created by " Dick " Scarisbrick with his old friend Judy," his solos on various singular instruments, a stump speech, and a song and dance made up as a dwarf. Mr. Monks officiated as accom- panist. At the conclusion of the programme. Mr. Stout presented a good number of prizes for attend- ance. One family of five have never missed or been late since they commenced to attend the Lyceum, except when overtaken by illness. The remainder of the evening was spent in games, &c. PURLICIBENEFIT. Tanners Heavy Failure. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday before 'Mr. Registrar Ridgway, Robert William Pierpoint, 40, Sark-road, Green-lane, Liverpool, but lately of 213, Prescott-road, Fairfield, Liverpool, and Thomas Bantock Pierpoint, 91, Halton-road. Runcorn, carrying on business as tanners, curriers and leather dressers under the style of "Robert Pierpoint and Sons " at Halton Old-road Tannery, Runcorn, appeared for their public examination in bankruptcy. I—The statement of affairs showed liabilities expected to rank at £2,095 Is. and assets to the amount of £272 Is. 11d., leaving a deficiency 0f41,822 198. id. The bankrupt attributed their failure to "want of capital, depression in trade, and heavy business expenses in proportion to turnover." They com- menced business sixteen years ago in partnership and conducted the business which had been carried on by their father for twenty-eight years. In August 1902 they executed a deed of assignment, paying a composition of ss. in the £, having borrowed money from their friends to enable them to do so.—Robert William Pierpoint, was subjected to a searching examination by the assistant ;official receiver (Air. Johnson) and Thos. Bantock Pierpoint was also questioned.—The examination was adjourned until March 3rd.

Grammar School Old Boys' " Dinner. The third annual dinner in connection with the Boteler Grammar School Old Boys' Union took place at the Lion Hotel on Tuesday night. Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., presided, and there were also present, the Revs. E. J. Willcocks (headmaster), Canon Willis, E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. Henry Roberts, and Mr. C. , Sawkins Burgess (governors), the Rev. W. Hollowell (a former master), arid Messrs. E. R. Pickmere,Travers Pickmere, James Hepherd, Arthur Browne, and about 70 " Old Boys." Letters of regret for non-attendance were received from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. F. Monks, Mr. W. P. Rylands (governors), Rev. 0. H. Cary (former headmaster„ the Revs. T. Schonberg and Lucius Cary, Mr.. Henry Greenall, Mr, Vera B. Davies and others. The following was the toast list:—" The King," proposed by the presi- dent ; "The pious memory of Sir Thomas Boteler," proposed by :Mr. C. Sawkins Burgess (chairman of the committee) ; "Prosperity to the school," proposed by the president and acknowledged by the Rev. E. J. Willcocks ; "Prosperity to the County Borough of Warrington," proposed by Mr. Arthur Browne, and acknowledged by Mr. James Hepherd ; "The Governors," proposed by Mr. E. It. Pinkmere, and acknowledged by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, and "The president," proposed by Mr. James H. Smethurst (secretary to the committee). The musical programme, an excellent one, was arranged by Mr. W. H. Payton, who was assisted by Messrs. R. E. Warburton, J. Babbitt, F. Fieldhouse, and A. Grounds.

H. Ar. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY ST., WARRINGTON.—Advt. A Newsagent's Bankruptcy. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, William Thomas Dickinson, newsagent's manager, 3, Scotland-road, and formerly carrying on business as a newsagent at 3: and 39, Scotland-road, appeared for his public examination. The statement of affairs showed liabilities amounting to .£255 3s. 4d., assets expected to realise 2s. 91, leaving a deficiency of .Z 254 Os. 7d.—Dickinson stated that he commenced business in April, 1903, with :£3O free capital and agreed to pay £l5O for the business he had take d over. He had only paid :£5O, however. In June, 1904, he sold the business to his wife for .C. 50 and re-commenced business at 30, Scotland-road. In November his stock-in-trade and fixtures were sold under an execution and he became manager for his wife who carried on business on her own, separate account as a retail tobacconist and newsagent at 3, Scotland-road. Having kept no books of account he could not explain exactly how the deficency had arisen, but he attributed his failure to " bad trade and insufficient capital." He became aware of his insolvency about the end of last November.—No creditors were represented, and on the application of Mr. Johnson, the deputy official receiver, tbs examination was closed. LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. A grand concert is to be held at Parr Hall on Satur- day evening next under the auspices of the Warrington 1 Male Voice Choir when a first class musical pro. gramme will be given consisting of items by the above choir and also in combination with the famous Manchester Orpheous Glee Society who have made a name in the musical world. We trust the Warrington public will give encouragement to this society on this their first appearance in Warrington.They have scored many victories, notable among these being the National Eisteddfod held at Bangor in 1902 where they took the first prize, also an International Eisteddfod held at Cardiff in 1903, where also this society took the first .prize of 100 guineas. Mr. Thornley Dodge, humorist, who will be remembered as the dramatic instructor to the very successful Musical Society's Operas will also appear. Other vocal and instrumental items will be given by the artistes whose names appear in our advertising columns.

The annual tea and concert in connection with St. Paul's Church will be held in the Parr Hall on Mon- day evening. There will be a dance in the same building on Tuesday evening A sale of work in aid of Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission Building fund will be held in the mission on Thurs- day and Friday next. Mr. A. H. Crosfield will per- form the opening ceremony on the first day, and Mrs. Henry Roberts will open the sale on Friday. The Warrington Market Tenants' Association will hold their annual ball in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. Personal. Mr. Ernest Hatton, general manager of the Salford Tramways and formerly in the service of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, Warrington, is one of the final three from whom the Newcastle Corporation will select their new tramway manager. The degree of Fellow of the Royal College of Organists has been conferred upon Mr. F. M. Darby, Mus.:Bac., organist at the Parish Church.

' Musical Society's Forthcoming Concert. The third subscription concert of the season in connection with the Musical Society which is to be held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday, February 28th, will be of a particularly interesting char- acter, as practically the whole of the programme 'will be supplied by the members of the society. The orchestra will be augmented for the occasion and the items will include Mendelssohn's " Loreley " (soprano solo, Mrs. A. Booth) ; Tschaiko wski's " Casse Noisette" Suite ; Wagner's march and choruS from" Tannhauser " ; Sextet from " Lucia di Lammermoor" ; Quintet from " Morrie England quartet from "The Yeoman of the Guard " ; the following members of the Society taking part: Sopranos, Mrs. A. Booth, Miss G. Pemberton, Miss A. Daunt; tensrs : Mr. J. Rabbit, Mr. J. H. Draper, Mr. J. E. Hannan; contraltos : Miss E. D. Jeans, Miss M. Henshall, Miss M. W. Collin; basses: Mr. W. H. Wallington, Mr. J. W. Bibby, Mr. F. Fieldhouse. Mr. I Alfred Ross will be the solo violinist. Mary War- ringtoniana who have had the pleasure of hearing the vocalists mentioned in the amateur operas given by the Society will no doubt be anxious to take the opportunity of attending the concert,and there should be a large attendance,

div.head: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.
div.p: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.

[By Godfrey Dean.] The War of the Roses. This month lam five-and-twenty years of age. Yet, since Phyllis' advent into my life, I begin to feel buoyantly youthful again. The elusiveness .of her nature only adds to her attractions. She is an unknown quantity. Different, she would not be Phyllis. When last I saw her—she was never more charm- ing. But her character is all contradictions and complications. If one advances„ she eludes—`-only to approach when danger is past. That, at least, is my experience ; but I hope no one else can say the same. This afternoon I am to see her again, and maybe— I must have smiled at my thoughts, for a lady, driving by, looked at me with cyriosity. Just then—oh, wicked Fate—Phyllis passed and chilled me with a glance. It is dangerous to smile in public— in the Row, particularly. The stranger was pretty, too, which makes it worse. I watched Phyllis along the drive as far as possible. Toe Vaughan's coachman has a broad, muscular back, but really, those big-blooded hays require some holding in. I must caution Phyllis against such risks —though at the right time. I rather expected Phyllis would have something to ' say to me about this incident, and did not know what ' to think when she made no mention of it. Knowing , that I cannot bear uncertainty, she, doubtless, wished to punish me. I considered what course to adopt. Though I had not smiled at the lady, would it be wise to tell Phyllis so ?—for I am capable of doing so in uncertain cir- cumstances. And Phyllis might reasonably conclude I was not telling the truth. No, I would confess what was not true, and, as she would resent the statement, I could show repentance. Women love to forgive. "I did not know you were to be in the Park this morning," I said. "So I should have thought." She was smiling. "You took me quite by surprise ! " " So it seemed "—still smiling. This was not what I bargained for. " One does unaccountable things at times," 1 observed. ic yes." "For instance, I smiled at a lady in the Park to- day." I guessed as much," she said in a low tone, as if to herself. " Whom I have never seen before. I am sure now I do not know her." "Of course," Phyllis commented. A shadow seemed to pass over her face. Either Phyllis is jealous, or she is a wonderful actress. There was silence for some time. Only the ticking of the clock was to be heard. Then Phyllis rose. On her face was an expression of resignation. "I guessed as much," she said." feared it with that I fear which is ever present to the woman that the man —she stopped abruptly. "Ah !" The exclamation escaped me. " What were you going to say ?" I asked. "Oh, merely that the man is never to be trusted out of sight ; that any pretty face can win his attention. Jam speaking generally, of course; not blaming you." "I had rather you did." " Why ? "—wonderingly. "Because—well, because it is you," I answered lamely. ,1 "It is impossible that a woman should ever thoroughly understand a man," Phyllis observed. As if a man could not say the same of women! with more reason, too. But I did not voice my thought, of course. "I am referring," she said (guessing that I thought 1 she was speaking of the Park episode), to your desire to be blamed. But how.can I blame you when you can't help it?" ' "Phyllis, lam awfully sorry. Won't you forgive me?" "Why should I—what is there to forgive ? " "My being so—" I hesitated to put it. " Oh, there is something else that you've not told me of?" " No, really." Phyllis stood near the fire, with her back to me. "r thought there was." The words were half whispered, and she looked disappointed. I left my seat and stood by her. She was looking into the flames. Near by was a slender vase, holding two roses—one white, the other red. "If it be possible," I said, "the white rose would improve you." I took it from its place. "No," Phyllis said. I turned to replace it. "Not that," she added. I was too late to see what her eyes said, for she was looking into the flames again, apparently quite abstracted. I offered her the other, but she did not seem to see me. " Where shall I fasten it?" I asked. "In its proper place." " That is near the heart." " Yes, of course." Pinning that rose was an embarrassing pleasure under fire of Phyllis's eyes. " The white one," I said, still engaged in my task, " would have been in fine contrast." " The red one is in harmony," she remarked. "But your dress is black," I pointed out. (And by-the•wav, Phyllis looked superb.) 'That I am aware of "—with dignity. I can be very stupid, but I caught her meaning this time. I informed Phyllis that I had told her an untruth. " Oh," with a whimsical expression of reproof. I like to bring confessions to you," I continued, firmly. Personally, I don't believe in the confessional (Phyllis is a Catholic), but the woman one loves is a proper confessor. "It's nice to do wrong —I don't mean anything very wrong—then I can come to you for absolution." "You are a Philistine," she said, insocently enough. "and what you say is heresy." "I am a Phyllistine, of course, rind your lover.', " That doesn't justify you," Phyllis said ; but she did not look angry." "I don't care, I said, defiantly. " Besides, I did not smile at the woman." "I knew it," she remarked. That's Phyllis all over. I might have guessed it. (To he continued.) (These articles originally appeared in the "London Echo.")

A Clergyman's Wedding. An interesting local wedding was solemnised at St. Benedict's Church, Ardwick, on Wednesday morning, the contracting parties being the Rev. George Alfred Dearden, who has been for some time assistant curate at the church and was recently appointed to a curacy at the Warrington Parish Church,and Miss Katharine Frances James, a well known worker in the parish, and only daughter of Mr. J. James, Clowes street, West Gorton.—The church was crowded,and suitable voluntaries were played by the organist as the bridal party entered the building. The I bride, who was attired in a dress of white silk crepe de chine, and wore an old family veil, was I given away by her brother (Mr. R. F. James), and I was attended by Miss Flint. She also wore a gold curb bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom, whilst Miss Dolly Stinton distributed lilies of the valley amongst the guests. Dr. Dearden officiated in the capacity of best man.—The ceremony was conducted by the Rev P. Gethen, rector. The newly-married couple sub sequently left for Lytham, y,here a portion of the honeymoon will be spent, the bride wearing a travel- ling dress of dark grey zebeline,faced with white, and a black beaver picture hat. On his return the Bev. G. A. Dearden will take up his clerical duties at War- rington. There were a large number of presents.

div.head: LION HOTEL.
div.p: LION HOTEL.

The centenary of the establishment of the works of Messrs. Rylands Lins., Limited, Church-street, was fittingly celebrated by a dinner at the Lion Hotel on Friday evening. The occasion was one of great interest in local industrial life for from small beginnings the concern has flourished nntil it now holds an honoured place among the iorernost manufactories of the town. From an interesting souvenir booklet issued in cele- bration of the centenary we learn that it was in the early part of the seventeenth century that the firm was founded by John and William Rylands, the first-named having been born in 1619. They and their immediate dc%cEmdants employed weavers in the neighbourhood of Culcheth, to weave linen threads into fabrics which were sold in the Manchester market, even then the leading market in England for linen cloth. Mr. Peter ltylands, a direct descendant, about the middle of the eighteenth century, removed the business to Wigan, and, with his son, John, also opened a business in Warrington, where they added sail cloth to their other manufactures, being contractors to the Admiralty for sail cloth for the fleet. A generation later, in the year 1805, Mr. John Rylands, of this firm, which was then known as John Rylands and Son, introduced the manufacture of wire into Warrington, and subsequently discontinued all their other manufactures. The original wire mill was situated upon a part of the site now occupied by the present works. The business ultimately passed into the hands of Mr. John Rylands's three sons, John, Thomas Glazebrook, and Peter, who largely developed the wire trade, taking up all classes of wire, and manufactures made from wire, and establishing a reputation for superior quality of work, which has made Warrington wire a household name wherever wire is bought or sold In 1868, the firm was converted into a private limited liability company, under the style of Rylands Bros., Limited, and this company has largely extended and increased the business of the old firm in all the various classes of wire and wire manufactures. _ _ _ _ _ _

At the centenary dinner Mr.J. Paul Rylands presided over an attendance of between seventy and eighty. The vice-chair was occupied by Mr. W.Peter Rylands, and sitting at the cross table were Messrs. J J. Bleckly, W. H. Blackly, John Bleckly, jun., H. H. Field, E. W. Bindloss, and Aubrey Tatham. Apologies for non-attendance had been received from Mr. Temple, Mr. Clifford Temple, Mr. A. Doughty (Messrs. Alexander Doughty and Co.), Mr. A. Doughty, jun., Mr. Herbert S. Bleckly, Mr. Arthur Bleckly, Mr. William Atherton, a.r. James Dodds. Mr. E. V. Walker, and Mr. H. Harmood Banner. The last-named gentleman wrote to the Secretary of the firm (Mr. T. J. Hulse :—"I should much like to have been with you to show my in- terest in the firm, and wish them `God-speed' in the new century. May the vigour, energy, and open-mindedness which are the distinguishing features af the firm at present, remain with them during the ensuing years, and keep them, as they are now, in front of their competitors." An excellent repast having been served by Mr. John Lee, the ldyal toasts were honoured. Afterwards, Mr. JOHN J. BLECKLY proposed "The firm" and gave some interesting reminiscences of the beginnings of the concern. He contrasted the rapid methods of production of to-day with those which existed when the firm first commenced business in War- rington. He wondered what John Rylands the elder would have thought if he could have received an order for 1,000 tons of galvanized netting to be delivered inn few months, as sometimes happened now, ^.nd he (the speaker) could only imagine his astonishment—to reverse the picture—being equalled by that of his grandson, Mr. Peter Rylands if his manager were to come into the office to consult with him on the possi- bility of producing a piece of wire six or seven pounds weight out of the hand hammered strips of metal that did duty for wire rods in those days. (Hear, hear.) It was a far cry from those days to these, and the interval which had elapsed had witnessed development in every direction of engineering, chemistry, and metallurgy. The invention of railways, telegraphs and steamships had in fact not only altered the methods of manufac- ture, but the face of the earth, and in all these changes the wire trade had had its share and there was no pro- cess they put in operation that day, except the old draw plate—there was no other operation in use 100 years ago that was in use now. Through all these changes Messrs. Rylands Bros. had been abreast of the times and ahead. Theirs had been no mere mushroom growth like they saw in America and in other places, but a steady development upon a good and sound founda- tion; and if he mistook not, the leaders and their assistants to-day were resolved that Messrs. Rylands Brothers should maintain the place they had always occupied, in the front rank. (Applause.) He had much pleasure in coupling with the toast the name of Afr. W. Peter Rylands, than whom he wished for no better representative of the firm and the name. Cheers were given by the staff for Mr. and Mrs. Peter Rylands. Mr. W, PaTER RYLANDS, in reply, said that as Mr. John Blackly had reminded them, they lived in an age of rush, and frequently companies were of mushroom growth and, he was sorry to say, sometimes subjected to rapid decline. It was, therefore, no mean achieve- ment for a firm to have arrived at the age of 100 years without reckoning the long period of 150 years during which the same family, the predecessors of the firm, carried on business, although of a somewhat different character. When they looked back upon the 100 years of the life of a firm, they were all proud to think that that day it was as full of vitality, or more, than at any other period. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Two or three of their largest and most important competitors were really offsprings from this great firm of Rylands Bros., but they were not jealous of them. They were pleased to see their children growing and flourishing, and the mother, he was pleased to say, cosld still stand against the attacks of the competition. They found 'there was room in the world for all, and they must look lupon them not as competitors, 'nit as offsprings, and be proud to think that they were doing well. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Od behalf of the firm he hoped and trusted that another 100 years would find someone standing in that place returning thanks for the same toast on its hi-centenary. (Loud applause.) Mr. NV. H. IlLiicHLy proposed "The health of the President," and alluded to the remarkable progress of the flrm,stating that they were now turning out GOO tons a week in one mill. He could say without fear of con- tradiction that there was not a better mill in the world than theirs. The Germans could undersell them, not because they had better mills or because their work was better, or because their workmen were better educated. They had as good tackle, and Rylands Bros. were able to turn out wire as cheaply or cheaper, if they only had fair play, than anyone else in the world. This year was the centenary of the establishment of the firm. It was 100 years old, but he had no hesitation in saying it was younger to-day than it was 100 years ago. It had been gradually progressing. He did not mean to say it was better than it was going to be, but it had gradually progressed and was still in its youth, and had the tenacity and enthusiasm of youth The staff who were assembled that evening were the men who were doing the work and it was ,to them they must continue to look. (Applause.) Cheers were then given for Mr. and Mrs. Rylands. The PRESIDENT said he was proud to stand before them as chairman of the company, and he remembered that 41 years ago that month he began life in the office as office boy. Forty-one years was a good slice out of the hundrea years they were celebrating that night and a great many of the changes which Mr. John •Bleckly had spoken about had come within his own knowledge. It seemed as the years went on that they got stronger and stronger. If he felt proud of being the lchairman of the co ropany,he also felt proud in being associated with men who possessed such wonderful business knowledge, such keenness to do business on the right lines, and who seemed to think that nothing was too much trouble to turn out a good article that would keep their name and their trademark in the position it had always occupied. With regard to the antiquity of the firm, as an antiquary, he might be excused saving a few words. (Hear, hear.) The firm although it had only existed for 100 years as manufacturers of wire, had been handed down from father to son for 250 years. He had seen many changes in the concern. He bad seen many good times and many had ones, but he felt confl- dentlthat whether they regarded the quality of their manufactures, the condition of tbeir machinery, or the estimation in which they were held in the trade, they had never been in anything like the position they were now. (Applause). There was another matter he would like to mention, and that was that during the last 100 years, there bad never been one stain of bankruptcy 'upon the firm, nor had there been any great dispute with the men all differences having been settled amicably and satisfactorily. There had been no fire and there had been' no discontent, and the whole business worked smoothly and honestly. (Applause). The toast of "the staff," was proposed by Mr. W. I PETER RYLAND,.. It was, he said, a great pleasure to 11 him to be at the head of such a staff as that of Itylands Bros. In every department they had heads who were inspired with loyalty to the firm, and had the keenest desire to do their best ' • and, as a result of those exer- tions, they had been able, first in one direction, and then in another, to economize in many ways, and to make it possible to hold their own, in spite Oi the ever- lasting keen competition with sshich they had to con- tend. (Applause). Mr. FIELD, in responding, said one saw a spirit in the ‘c orks which promised very well for the repetition of that gathering 100 years hence. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. J. NIELD also responded. He was, he said, very optimistic, and he had greater faith in the success of Rylands Bros. to-day than ever he had. Much as they had extended in the past, and much as they has spent in bricks and mortar, and much as was the land they had covered, they still found themselves cramped fo: room, and had still to go on building. Rylands Bros.' staff could boast of a leader which few concerns could boast of. (Applause.) He (the speaker) knew Mr. Rylands was much interested in the proposed change in the fiscal policy, and he was at one with him in his views. They were all prepared as English- men to fight on equal ground, and prepared, also, to stand or fall on their merits. They were not afraid of being hit so long as they were not hit below the belt. He thought it was the duty of a Government to stand '

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: by any proportion of the community which was struggling hard against means which were unfair— means which did no credit to any country or any com- munity. He firmly believed that the Government would realise its responsibilities to manufacturers, and would see that in their struggle they were allowed fair play. The toast of " The London Office " was submitted by the PRESIDENT and responded to by Mr. TATHANt. Mr. T. J. HirrAF. (secretary of the company) proposed " The visitors."

In responding Mr. E. W. Bri-mcoss said he could take off his hat in volnntaryadmiration to Rylands Brothers, which had had such an unparalleled record during the past 100 years. It was a firm in existence months before Nelson won his great victory at Trafalgar, and many years before Wellington won his crowning glory at Waterloo. It was something to be proud of, for a firm to celebrate its centenary, and to be surrounded on all sides by such faithful and willing hands, everyone intent on doing his best to keep afloat and well to the fore this grand old firm. (Applause). They all knew that the times in which they lived were particularly strenuous, and every one in a firm, down to the lowest person in the works, must be deterraked, not merely to earn his daily bread—the wherewithal to keep and main- tain his family—but to do his best to keep the ship going, knowing how they were handicapped by the most unfair conditions in the shape of tariffs. (Applause.) Mr. C. E. BUNCH supported the remarks of Mr. Bind- loss. (Applause). As they were perhaps aware, he had just returned from a short visit to America, in which ' he was accompanied by his friend, Mr. Atherton, and he would tell them what impressed him more than anything else with regard to the iron and steel industry of America. They had all heard times out of number of the great bustle of American business life, the struggle for the almighty dollar, and how business men and workmen, too, were continually hurrying and bustling to see how much work they could do in each day. Having had the advantage of visiting most of the lead- ing iron and steel works of the States, it began to dawn upon one that there was something else besides the bustling of the workmen in the success of American manufacturers. He might say at once that as regarded the actual work done by the American work- man, in his opinion, he worked no harder than the same workman in this country. The secret lay here ; that, although he did no more actual labour, he produced, he thought, more work per man than his fellow on this side. That was where the bustling came in It was not physical bustling, but bustling of the mind. From the manager downwards, output was the consider- ation, and in increasing it, they looked not to driving Ithe men, but to the improvement of the machinery and the introduction of labour-saving methods. The fore- man or manager of an American workshop must demonstrate that his department was in some way benefiting by his presence. Everybody was compelled to use his brains, and being attentive, respectable and quiet—virtues which carried one on in this country— would not do in America, unless accompanied by originality and progress. (Applause.) During the evening an enjoyable musical programme was submitted songs being rendered by Mr.T.Humphreys, Mr. W. Moores,and Mr. T. Reddish. Mr. T. Taylor gave a pianoforte solo, and Mr. J. Stanley an oboe solo. Humorous songs and sketches by Mr. William Whittle reated great amusement,

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.
OPENING OF THE NEW ORGAN.

Saturday was another day to be long and well remem- bered in the history of the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. Hardly had the efforts of the workers to erect a new and more commodious chapel been crowned with success, when a scheme to obtain a new organ was launched. The congregation entered heartily into the project and on Saturday had the pleasure of witnessing the formal opening of an instrument which, in addition to enhancing the effectiveness of the services, will when the ornamentation is completed still further improve the appearance of the chapel. The organ which will cost over R2OO, consists ,of two complete man ials and an independent pedal. The action to the manual is mechanical; and that to the pedal organ is improved tubular pneumatic. The interior work is of the highest quality, and also the whole of the materials. The exterior is specially designed tn suit the position and surroundings. lhe casework is of selected pitch. pine. The "recess" fittings (i.e., the key frames, book desk, draw-stops, and jambs,) are of polished walnut. The drawknobs are of ebony with ivory facings. The total number of pipes is 586. The instrument has been designed and built by Messrs. J. Hardy and Sons, Hanover Organ Works, Stockport. At the opening service on Saturday afternoon, Councillor JAMES EVANS presided over a large attend- ance. He congratulated the people at Bank Quay on haviqg been successful in their efforts to obtain an organ which would not only be an ornament to the place but would add considerably to the efficiency of the services. The Crosfield family had been deeply interested in the mission since its formation and as Mrs. Crosfield was present, he had very great pleasure in asking her to turn the key and formally open the organ. Mrs. Crosfleld then performed the little ceremony, and Councillor EVANS called upon Mr. W. H. Payton, , Miss. Bac., to give an organ recital. The recital was very much appreciated and served to demonstrate to the full the good qualities of the instrument. Mr. Payton submitted the following pre-' gramme in his usual masterly style:—Sonata in A Mendelssohn; (a) "The Question" (b) "The Answer,' Wolstenholme; ;Toccato in G. Dubois; Descriptive piece "The Abbey Chimes," G. E. Lyte ; Postlude in F ()Linuet), W. H. Payton; "Jerusalem the Golden" ( with variations), Spark; March Ponti ficale," Lemrnens. At the close Councillor EVANS ekpressed the obliga- tion of the members of the mission to Mr. Payton for the services he had so willingly and ably rendered. CONGREGATIONAL TEA AND CONCERT,

The annual tea meeting which followed the recital proved a great success, a large company attending. The following ladies assisted at the tables : Mesdames J. Hassall, T. Taylor, D. Hill, J. Taylor, R, C. Tanner, R. E. Jones, G. Strange, \V. Backhouse, H. Buckby, and F. Atkinson, Messes bobbins, T. Hassan. and A. Cook.

The schoolroom was filled to its utmost capacity for the enjoyable concert which brought the day's proceed- ings to a close. Some disappointment was experienced when it became known that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who had promised to preside, had sent a cablegram from Smyrna, where he was staying for a short time, regret- ting his inability to be present and wishing the mission every success. The alai! was taken by Mr. Thomas Dale, the leadar of the mission. REPORT ON THE YEAR'S .WORK.

The SECRETARY (Mr. A. Tilling) presented the annual report on behalf of the committee. The past year, he stated, had been a very important one in the history of the Mission, for it had witnessed the pro • vision of a new chapel. They took possession of the building on the 27th February last, the chapel being formally opened by Mrs. Crosfield. They were indeed a thankful people, for they were able to look upon their new home without any fears of a heavy debt hanging on the same, Mrs. Crosfteld having, on the day of opening, very generously offered to pay the balance owing. He might mention that Mrs. Crosfield's total donatiqn to the mew building amounted to the magnificent sum of £1.05 is. 2d., for which the corn- inittee felt it quite impossible to find words to adequately express their thanks. When the chapel scheme was first set on foot, it was thought advisable to try and arrange for a new organ. The old instrument was far from satisfactory, and it was felt that a pipe organ would greatly help the singing and add to the effectiveness and solemnity of the services. The large sum required to erect the chapel would no doubt have delayed the organ scheme very considerably, had it not been for Mrs. Crosileld's generosity. However, seeing that they were not to be hampered with a debt on the chapel building, they considered they were quite justified in getting to work to provide funds for a new organs They had had special collections in the chapel for some months, and the lady members of the mission had been and were still making preparations for a sale of work. They had obtained the instrument some months earlier than was anticipated, for instead of taking six months to supply the order, it had only taken one month. They had been able to pay the organ builders (Messrs. Hardy and Son, Stocknort), £5O on account, and they had in , ' hand £6 Gs. The old organ had just .been sold for £2O and that, together with the profits from that day's , ceremony, the collections to be taken in chapel during the next month or so, and the profit from the forthcoming se'e of work, should enable them to pay the major portion of the total cost---£205 ibefore ve-y long. They hoped, with the continued , assistance of the members, to be able to settle the Aide account before the end of the year. The chapel accounts (apart from the organ fund) stood as follows : —Balance from 1903, £5 is. ild.: lucerne during the year, £42 ss. 31d. ; expenditure, £45 ss. Id. ; balance in treasurer's hands, £2 2s. 2d. The collections daring the year forall purposes amounted to just over £lOO, being far in excess of the colleations taken in any previous year since the mission was founded. The poor fund was still in the able hands of Mr. T. Dale, and there was a credit balance of £2 18s. Open-air mission work was carried on during the summer months, and they trusted and believed that the efforts put forward had not been in vain. During the year a rather important step had been taken with regard to the preaching appointments. Their pulpit had for many years been filled three Sundays out of four by their •independent Methodist friends, the name of the chapel appearing on their circuit plan. That arrangement was come to 'between their late patron (Mr. Crostield) and the Independent Methodists. On their eitering the new chapel, the Independent Methodists thought it an opportune time to ask if they would become fully affiliated with that denomination. As that was against the wis'ies of the founder of the mission who repeatedly expressed his wish that the ells pel should always be unsectari in) they could net see their way to grant the request, the c in eqne .ce being that the chapel no longer appeared on the denominational plan. They still,however,claimed the Independent Methodists as their friends, and while not assisting them as a de-

nomination, they promised their help as individuals, so that the committee felt sure they would have no diffi- culty in filling the pulpit in the future. They had de- cided to try an experiment by having students, fairly frequently, from the Manchester Denominational Colleges. They were hoping and praying that the year upon which they had entered might witness a spiritual revival in connection with their own mission, and throughout the whole land. The committee and officers entrusted with the carrying on of the work during the year were :—President Mr. N. Hough ; Vice-President, Mr. George Dale ; Treasurer, Mr. T. Taylor; Secretary, Mr. A. Tilling;committee,Messrs. T. Dale,J. NVoolley,D. HiII,J. H. Edwards,F. Atkinsou,W. Worrall,W. Johnson, and W. Dobbins.

The CHAIRMAN said that those who had heard the sweet music played by Mr. Parton that afternoon would be satisfied as to the suitability of the organ. They were sorry Mr. Crosfleld could not be present at the concert. His absence was not due to any unwillingness but simply to inability to attend. They all knew how he sympathised with the work which was being carried on there and how readily he helped them. (Applause.)

div.head: AN ENJOYABLE PROGRAMME.
div.p: AN ENJOYABLE PROGRAMME.

The musical programme must rank as one of the most enjoyable ever submitted at the mission. Master Tom Barton's juvenile band was in attendance and gave several selections in a manner which showed that it is making gratifying progress. Miss M. Davies very sweetly sang An old garden " and " The birds go north again I' and was warmly applauded. Mr. E. Pearce gave very effec- tive interpretations of "Bedouin love song" and " Revenge." He was enthusiastically encored for the latter and responded with " Off to Philadelphia." The Lyric quartette party added much to the pleasure of the evening with expressive renderings of "Killarney," " Moonlight and music," and" Come back to me," the voices blending admirably. Miss L. Fairhurst, a member of the party, had the honour of a recall for the solo "The enchantress," and later she gave "Sing me to sleep" very creditably. Mr. J. Corrin, who had been announced to sing, was unable to attend but an efficient substitute was found in Mr. Greenough who acquitted himself well in "The Holy City" and "Alice, where art thou ?" A popular item was the humorous song "Soldiers three," by Masters Tanner, Swain, Atkinson. and Smith (scholars of People's College) which created considerable mirth. A duet "Love and war" by Nfessrs. Greenough and Pearce was well received. Hr. E. A. Sind?rs, who happened to be in the audience, obliged with the humorous recital "Nomination day," and so well was it given that an encore was the result. The duties of accompanist were discharged by Master T. W. Pearce. A hearty vote of \Oianks to the artistes concluded a successful gathering. OPENING SERVICES.

There were large congregations on Sunday when the opening services were continued. In the morning the preacher was Mr. J. Irish, of Patricroft,and the organist Master T. W. Pearce. In the afternoon a special musical service was held, when the chair was taken by Mr. H. Roberts, who congratulated the members of the Mission upon the enterprise they had displayed in procuring snch an organ as they now possessed. He referred to the important position music occupied in public worship. iThe complaints that they sometimes heard with I regard t,o the poor attendance at their churches , and chapels wouLl be far more frequent if lit were not for the musical parts of the services. I There were certainly some people (the Covenanters. or I "Wee Kirkers "—wee in more senses than one) who did I not permit any musical aids in their churches. lie (Mr. ! Roberts) believed that not only did music appeal to the musical ear of man, hut, through emotion, the spiritual side was very often reached. Were there any of them there that afternoon who could hear certain tunes (learned in the Sunday school, the Church, and the home) without feeling betiefited because of the memories they brought to one. He hoped the new organ and the building would be used for many years to I come for the uplifting of many souls, and that many, I under the influence brought to bear upon them in that • chapel, might find the " peace which passeth all under- ' standing.', (Applause). I Mr. T. DALE, on behalf of the mission workers, ' heartily: thanked the chairman, singers and the organist 1 for their services so willingly rendered. The organist was Mr. F. Hickman. An admirable musical prograirnme , was gone through choruses being rendered by the corn- ' bined choirs of Legh street Primitive Methodist and I Working Men's Mission Churches, and sacred solos by IMrs. A. Booth. Mr. Irish again preached in the even- ing and Mr. Hickman presided at the organ,his rendering of The Hallelujah Chorus "being very effective. The choir under theconductorship of Mr. Atkinson, sang very creditably an anthem entitled " Sing unto God. The total collections amounted to £l2 12s. 4id.

div.head: WAGES IN TNE MIDLAND IRON TRADE.
div.p: WAGES IN TNE MIDLAND IRON TRADE.
Serious Crisis Narrowly Averted.
REDUCTION AVERTED.

Although the slidiug scale has been suspended, and so far very little progress seems to have been made in the direction of replacing, it, the Standing Committee of , Midland Iron and bteel Wages Board on Thursday I notified a reduction in ironworkers' wages. The follow- ing notice was posted on the Exchange :—" At a meet- ing of the Standing Committee held on Thursday, February 2nd, at the Grand Hotel, it was unanimously resolved 'that the rate of wages for puddling be fixed lat Bs. 3d. per ton basis price, and millmen's wages in I proportion, to commence from Monday, February 6th. ' and to continue until Saturday, April Ist,l9os:—Daniel Jones, employers' secretary; William Aucott, operatives' secretary. The reduction thus made amounts to 3d. per ton in the case of puddlers, and 2A per cent in that of millmen. There were no local figures pre- suited to show eithor output or average selling price, and it became a question whether the committee should continue the policy which has been purs led for close upon three years past and follow the North of Enchnd ascertainment which had given a reduction of 3d. and 124 per cent, in the wages paid in that part of the c mntry. The proposal to do so was very strenuously fcMght by the operatives' representatives, and we Idorstaad that a prolonged and heated discus- sion ensued. The difficulty of ' agreeing was so great that the operatives asked permission to retire I for private conference, and xere absent an hour or so before they returned to the committee room to give in their adhesion to tho proposition to reduce wages. Such a state of affairs (says the "Birmingham Post ") is ominous, and it reveals again the absurdly lax manner in which the Board's affairs are now being conducted. The sliding scale has been cast away, and, until Thurs- day at any rate, there had apparently been no agreement as to the alternative policy to he pursued and thus the difficulty experienced in coming to an arrangement to follow the north. This, however, is but typical of the chaotic condition of the Board's affairs at the present time. Four or five months have passed since the opera- tives gave notice to terminate the sliding scale, and, so far as can be gathered, little if anything has been done to devise a new working arrangement There is said to be some difficulty in devising a method of wages adjustment which will be acceptable to manu- facturers of steel shapes. &c. In this branch of industry there have been great modifications of works practice, and equally important extensions of plant, and it is pointed out that the old conditions are no longer appli- cable to the regulation of wages. The obvious reply would seem to be that Ira sliding scale is to be of any use at all it should be framed on lines sufficiently com- prehensive to deal with new processes as well as old ; but instead of accepting this commonsense scheme, which ought not to be beyond the ingenions contrivance of members of the Board, there is actually talk of leav- ing steel outside the scope of the Board's operations. It is to be hoped that the difficulties of providing for steel rolling, however great they may appear, will not be shirked. If they are it will prove a further source of weakness to a Bo rd one of the chief defects of which is that in the pAst its arrangements have not been suffi- ciently comprehensive.

• The Late Mr. Henry Milling. The Rev. E. E. Farrar, curate of Grappenhall made allusion to the late Mr. Henry Milling, of Summerville, Latchford in the course of his sermon at St. Wilfrid's hurch on Sunday morning. He said that the district had suffered a great loss by his death, as Mr. Milling had always been a good Christian, and had led a very straightforward and generous life. Two special hymns were sung.

To a London saleroom 3,200 guineas was paid for a Re nbrandt portrait, which in 1854 was bought for twelty guineas. In New York £9,040 was paid for a Dutch painting by Mauve, which twenty years ago changed hands for £4OO, In Florida a motor-car ran ten miles in a fraction over six and a half minutes—a world's record.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalist.";

Saturday was the last day for qualifying players required for the Northern Union Cup-ties. Very few new men have been signed on by any of the clubs recently and there were probably not half a dozen making their first turnout on Saturday. Warrington's resources are practically the same as they have been all the season, or if anything, rather less seeing that Dickinson and Harris have both been out of action for some time. With the exception of Brookes and Kenyon coming into the threequarter line the team is substantially the same as throughout the season, and it ought to give a good account of itself when the cup tournament commences. The reserves are a capable and tried lot of players, and with J. Davies Dickinson and Harris fit again there shnuld be no anxiety on this score.

Last week probably the strongest team Warrington can put in the field opposed Leeds at Wilderspool and succeeded in wiping off the slate a stain which has stood since October 1, when Warrington sustained a severe reverse at Headingley. The Leeds men came down in full strength and with .a determination to record their first success at Warrington, but they found the home lot rather too clever for them. The margin at the close was not large, but Warrington were quite six points the better team. So far only one visiting club has taken the maximum points from Wilderspool, and that one was Leigh, who were remarkably fortunate. Warrington must see to it that the feat is not performed by any other visitors and they will finish the season with a, league record which will bear some comparison withipast perform- ances.

Warrington spectators who expected a display equal to that of the Hull match were mostly disappointed. There was not the same brilliance displayed by either team on Saturday as in the previous game at Warrington, btit an interesting and ex- citing struggle for supremacy it was, never- theless, between Warrington and Leeds. The defence all round was far superior to that shown in the free-scoring game with Hull, and this is probably one reason why the match was not so attractive. But good football is not all attack-, and Saturday's game could not be considered a poor one by any means. Play was of an open character throughout and very even. In fact, only the superior play of the home halves and Fish's cleverness on the wing gained War- rington the day. Leeds were more powerful in the pack and had numerous opportunities to score, but they lacked originality and initiative behind.

Play opened with Warrington facing wind and sun, and for sometime they were pressed back on the line. Leeds had numerous opportunities, but poor combina- tion prevented them ever becoming very dangerous. Naturally the home lot took the earliest opportunity of removing play to a more congenial sphere. Fish quickly changed gefence into attack and kicked past the Leeds full babk, but someone else was handy and cleared. The home forwards now seemed to find their feet, and the backs quickly showed the Leeds men the way to handle the ball. Once more it was sent across to Fish, who got away down touch and kicked clear. There was an exhilarating race, Llewellyn and Fish both going down for the ball. Neither secured it, but I3oardman coming up at a great pace picked up and went over the line easily with a try. Preston failed at goal. Leeds ought to have equalised after this. for Llewellyn got away at top speed only to spoil the effort by passing badly to the wing man. He might easily have gone on and scored himself. Practically this was the only time Leeds looked like breaking through the home defence.

Though only leading by a try at the interval, Warrington were einected to pile on points, once they got the elements ia their favour. The Leeds forwards however, showed their mettle in the second half. Playing against the wind they kept the ball close and certainly beat the Warrington eight for possession. Still it came out on the home side every now and then. After a lot of very poor punting by the Warrington backs, Hockenhall dodged cleverly away from the centre and smart combination between Isherwood, Thomas and himself resulted in tha County half-back scoring near the posts. It was a very fine try, and Fish was unfortunate in failing to improve the point. Luck has deserted him, for the ball hit the cross-bar instead of going over.

A warm "A " team has been chosen to meet Runcorn" A," and the crowd will be pleased to note the re-appearance of Dickenson, Harris, and J, Davies. The three-quarter line is particularly . strong. Team: Knight, full back; Harris, Dicken- son, Berry and J•irdan, three-quarters ; J. Davies, and W. Bate. half backs ; Forster, Ashton, Lunt, Morrison, and Harmer, farwards.

The Runcorn team will be: Houghton, full back; Harrison, Butterworth, Hesketh, and Williams, three- quarters; Jolley and Walton, half backs; S. Walker, Dobson, J. Walker, C. Houghton, Richardson, Padbury, Messenger and Dixon, forwards.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

Last week the Stockton Heath club first eleven played South Manchester at Grappenhall-road. The day was perfect so far as the atmospheric conditions were concerned, but the ground was very soft after the recent thaw. Both teams were fairly welt represented, and a good hard game was expected, as the Stockton Heath eleven defeated the visitors on their own ground earlier on in the season by 4-1.

The game in the first half was very even, and the score at the interval of 1-1 justly represented the play. The goal for Stockton Heath was scored by IV. Longdin, with a splendid shot, after he received the ball from W. Richardson who had beaten the half back.

The South goal was scoeed by Mercer. who rushed between the home backs and scored with a good shot. The visitors won the toss, and decided to play both against the slope and the wind, so that when half-time came with the score equal, the South seemed to have a grand chance of avenging their defeat earlier in the season.

Well played, forwards! It is seldom that the forwards have been guilty of winning a match this season, but last week they won the game" off their own bat "so to speak, and it would not be fair to single out anyone for particular praise.

Of the backs little can be said, as they were not properly extended, but it was quite obvious that Eric Fairclough has not fully' recovered from his injury, received whilst playing against Sale six weeks ago.

The match between Latchford and Altrincham St. Margaret's was played at Latchford on Saturday and resulted in an easy win for the home eleven by four goals to one. Speusley soon opened the scoring in the first half and Pearson added two more before the teams changed ends, the score at half-time being 3 goals to I.

The event of the day on Saturday, was the defeat of Oldham at Widnes—a fate they have endured before. Bradford simply smothered Wakefield, and their win by 27 points to nil is about the best away performance ever recorded under the Northern Union. These two matches place Oldham and Bradford on an equality, with the Ran szers only a point behind and a match in hand. Warrington have again passed Wigan in the race.

St. Margaret's played up well in the second half, but with the home eleven in good form they were unable to make impression and Banks eventually added the fourth goal for Latchford, by scoring in a particularly clever manner' having to bent quite a number of the opposing side before being in a position to put the ball into the net.

Latchford 2nd simply crushed St. Margaret's 2nd at Altrincham. From the first bully off Latchford showed their superiority, and by good passing and com- bined play soon invaded their opponents' circle. Here they were very mull handicapped by the heavy nature of the ground and it was not until after a lot of scrim- mages round the oa.l mouth that the ball was safely netted. After bullying off they again made tracks for the home goal and although the " Maggies "strove hard to keep them out, they were not long before they added to the initial score. This was further augmented by three more in the first half the score at half time being Latchford 5, St. Margaret's nil.

Sankey Harriers and Athletic Club. Sankey Harriers ran their trial race from the Black Horse, on Saturday. The trail was laid across about seven miles of country, and as this run was practically to decide the team for the Northern Junior Champion- ship an exciting race ensued. The pack consisted of 20 runners, and after bt-ing absent 40 minutes, John Riley came lome first, followed by J. Stamps 2, and T. [Devlin, 3.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

WARRINGTON WONSAN'S SAD POSITION. At the Borough Police Court yesterday Annie Glover, Earle-street, was charged with stealing a nightdress of the value of 3s. from a clothes line, the property of Mary Rose, 14, Cambria-place, on Wednesday, and also with stealing from the shop of James Laslie, Pinnsrs% brow, on Thursday. two blacking brushes of the value of Is.—The Chief COnstable said that judging, from what he knew of her history, the proper place for the prisoner was an asylum. Certainly the case was one which battled him. Prisoner was the wife of a respectable working man, but had been for a long time an habitual dninkard. Now she had no moral control over herself whatever, and had periodical " sprees." During tnese she absented herself from home and seemed vacant in her mind. When she had not money to obtain drink she stole something. She had been before the court on many occasions in consequence of drunkenness and on one occasion a separation order was granted to her husband. She had been to a home for six months but it had done her no good. He did not think she really knew what she was doing at times, as she was not a badly disposed woman. As to the thefts she took the nightdress from the clothes line and sold it to a shop keeper named Clara Clarke, 13, Tanner's- lane, who said she gave prisoner ninepence for it, "out of sympathy." Re did not know whether she meant sympathy for herself or for the prisoner, inasmuch as she gave 9d. for a 3s. article. With reference to the brushes,prisoner was arrested with them in her possession —Prisoner was unwilling to go to a home, an I a tine of 10s. and costs with the option of n days imprisonment was imposed.

Detective Clough said he saw the two defendants with two other young men tossing for money round the electric lamp opposite the Farmers' Stores. Be caught the two defendants, but the others ran away. Tossing in this neighbourhood was becoming very frequent.— The Chief Constable sail this made Beckett's 16th appearance and the worst feature of his case was that he was a corrupter of other youths. Broderick had not been before the Court, but he was one of the gang.— Beckett was sent to prison for a month, and Broderick was lined .ss. including costs.
