iILABOUR DEMONSTPATION. efficiency. Unfortunately for those who made the state- ment the facts were against it. Major Seeley, who was a good Conservative member of Parliament turned Free Trader or rather remained Free Trader, used some MR. KEIR HARDIE, MP. AT figures recently in support of his Free Trade position. They showed that the incomes of those who paid income WARRINGTON. tax had increased by £209,000,000 in the ten years from 593 to 1903. That fact, apart from any other, was suffi- cient to disprove the statement that poverty was due to The Poverty Problem. under-production. A more accurate statement would be that it was due to under-consumption. (Applause.) It remarkable fact that whilst we were roaming the ; QUESTION OF POLITICAL INDEPENDENCE. was a I world at large on the outlook for new markets, there ! was a market lying at our very feet waiting to be opened up end developed, and which was altogether overlooked and neglected. Take the case of the thirteen millions he had referred to. Add ss. per week to the wages of the wage earners amongst them, and they at . once increased their spending power by £50,000,000 per annum' and created a new market—without shedding one single drop of human blood or stealing anyone's terri- tory—greater in amount than that of all our colonial possessions put together. (Applause.) They might ask , where the £50,000,000 would come from, and his reply was that the money would come from the over- abundance of wealth which the few possessed at present. He put it to them, irrespective of their politics,whether it would not be good and well for our nation to add £50,000,000 a year to the comforts of the poor even if it should require to be taken out of the debasing luxuries of the rich. (Applause.) Socialism was inevit- able because the present industrial system was destruc- tive of freedom. They were all sympathising just now at the struggle which had broken out in Russia, and he for one from the bottom of his heart, hoped it would go on—(applause)—until freedom, industrial and politica', had been won in that much oppressed country. They heard much concerning Chinese slavery in South Africa, but many were forgetting that lack of freedom was not confined to Russia nor was slavery confined to the compounds in South Africa. In the newspapers on Saturday was recorded the fuct that some Welshmen who had the daring to join a trade union some years ago and who were locked out by a lord for doing so, when they had been starved into submission were refused re-employ- ment in the quarry at Bethesda. Their humble petition was spurned, rejected, and refused. IVhat was the use of pretending that we were free in this country when one petty lordling was able to treat six hundred of his 'fellow beings in a manner such as that? (Applause.) Nowadays men were no longer slaves or serfs, but they were hirelings, end between the position of a hireling and that of a slave there was but little to choose. The man who was not free to claim the right to be allowed to earn a living was not a free man in any sense of the word. (Applause). The old Free Trade doctrine stood for freedom, and the men who fought the Free Trade fight in the middle years of last century were inspired by great and true ideals. They claimed freedom of trade; they claimed free citizenship ; they claimed a free Press; and to a greater or less degree they won all along the line. Now in the process of time the very system these men had built up had also become tyrannical and it was as much to be feared as were the old restrictions imposed by the feudal lords in the days of their power. When the South African war was being hatched, the Press of this country was bought up and the opinion of the nation was poisoned and distorted to make war possible. The Press controlled by wealthy capitalists was as much a menace to the nation and its liberties as the Press controlled by a Government. Trusts and combinations, were growing, and these combines were all in restraint of trade and destructive to the very idea of free com- petition. Socialism, he submitted, supplied the change required to once more enable vs to realize our ideals of personal and common freedom. To-day the people ruled the empire through the House of Commons, and yet they could not rule or control the land , without which they could not live; they had neither rile nor control over the capital without which they could not labour ; mid until the people were supreme not only in things political but in things industrial freedom would remain a chimera to be desired but never to be realized. Socialism proposed that the land and industrial capital of the country'should be held in corn mon to be used in common for the common good. This second object of the Independent Labour Party was the creation of a distinct Labour party in politics, and here they got at cross purposes with many of their friends who told them that Labour was not necessary. It was charged against them that their principal object app eared to be to smash the Liberal party ,• that they directed all their attention to one party,and left the other unscathed and uncriticised. It was not a question of whether the Liberal party was better than the Tory party or whether the Tory party was worse than the liberal, but whether either of those parties was sufficient for their purpose. The experience of generations went to show that whether the party in power be Liberal or Conservative, labour and its interests were carefully ruled orirside the Cabinet mc eting place. Hitherto labour, the one section of the community most requir- ing to make its voice heard, had always had to speak through someone else. They wanted a Labour party if only to enable Labour to speak with its own voice and through its own organs. Mr. Hardie proceeded to con- , tend that the interests of labour had been neglected in regard to old age pensions end the unemployed ques- tions. He instanced how when the great American shipping combine threatened the Cunard Company the Government quickly took steps to preserve the independence of that company. The result of the subsidy arrangements UdS that in twenty years time the Cunard Company wor'd hive received £6,960,000 of public money without giving one penny- worth of service in return. Surely if the St .te could do that to preserve the independence of a shipping company it might do something to preserve the independence of unemployed workmen. They would not then be dealing with dead property, but with lives,—human beings who were suffering a degree of misery and hardship which, could it be communicated to the well-to-do people, would rouse such a revolutionary feeling as would compel attention to their case. The reason these questions were neglected was becarse there was no Labour party in Parliament to fight for the poor. They were criticised by the hirelings of the gutter press and their eiders and betters, lay and clerical for their independence. He wondered when independ- ence became a crime in England. He had always beard it lauded 25 IL virture to be cultivated and developed. The people who criticised them mostly did so from a mistaken idea of what they were aiming at. They did not simply want to send workingmen to Parliament 1 there to be absorbed by Liberalism or Toryism. They seeking to create a Labour party separate and were distinct ftom either Liberal or Tory, to take its place in the House of Commons just as the Irish party did—to be the watch-dog for Labour and to fight all who opposed and neglected it. One good thing Mr. Chamberlain was doing in his campaign was that he was producing the same disintegration in the ranks of the Tory party as he formerly did over Home Rule in the Liberal party. When the two parties got disinter- grated there would be an opening for Labour to step in. Mr. Reir Hardie went on to demonstrate that there was no antagonism between socialism and trade unionism. Trade unions were necessary to protect them under the existing conditions and socialism was necessary to sweep away the existing conditions and to make them free men. He had read with a good deal of irritation about the attempts which had been made in Warrington to find a Labour candidate to champion their cause. He could not understand the frame of mind of any trade union that was willing to, pay for Labour representation and that was not willing to fight for it, whether there be one, two,or three candidates in the field against it. (Applause.' tie asked the working- men of the town and neighbourhood to think afresh of their position, to remember that out of every ten voters in England seven were working met', and if those seven would only combine and stand shoulder to shoulder no pawer on earth could hinder them from doing what they would. (Applause.) The resolution was cal ried unanimously. QUESTIONS.

Reply'rig to questions from the audience, Mr. Hardie denied that the Independent Labour Party speakers attacked the Liberal patty much more than the Tory party. Which ever party was in office ruitrally came in for the brunt of the Independent I qbour Party criticism. He could not say how it was that not-.bour candidate had yet been found for Wart ington. One of his olkirts in coming hero was to make that speedily possible. In places like Warrington trade ur'onists should be able to find a candidate of their own. Whether it was too late for them to select a awl for the coming contsst was not for him to say. Mr. HAItDIE further as.orted that there was no great dividing principle between the Liberal and Tots, parties. As soon as Labour got strong enough to tttn sesta against both parties, the two parties combined in order to oppose the further advance of Labour. The speakers having been thanked, the meeting closed.

He well remembered, and recitations were given, Prizes being awarded to the he said, the scorn, vituperation, and malice which were poured upon the heads of Mr. Keir Hardie and his corn- successful reciters. rades when they started the Independent Labour Party. Fortunately for the politics of this sountry, the party had justified its exist snce by the creation of a larger party —the Labour Representation Committee. He noticed that in an address on Saturday the present member for Newton told his audience that the question of primary - importance for the people of this countly was the defence of our Indian empire. (Laughter.) That might be so for a discredited party, or a bankrupt politician, but he was afraid that Colonel Pilkington would find out speedily that the workers of this country had realized to their heart's fulness that it was only the fool who "had his eyes in the ends of the earth." (Applause.) The Labour party had sprung into existence because the democracy of this country were confronted with proelems which touched them very closely and deeply. Such for instance was the ques- tion of the unemployed which had been brought within the range of practical politics by Mr. Keir Hardie and his party. Another matter which touched the very heart and the very existence of the nation had been brought into prominence by the Labour party, and that was the question of unfed and underfed school children which would have to be faced. They said as true imperialists, as true lovers of their race, that that question was or tar greater importance than the frontiers of India. (Applause). Then, the Labour Party had also forced into the eye of the public the question of the distribution of wealth. The power of accumulated wealth was a real menace to the stability of our empire end the welfare of our people. One of the problems which could only be solved by the Labour party was the re-allocation of taxation. Mr. Chamberlain said Protection was going to do everything for them— increase their wages and the contents of their cupboards, provide them with old-age pensions, and Heaven knew' what it was not going to do. He (Mr. Seddon) was not so sanguine. The other week he was speaking to a gentleman who had spent a considerable time in Germany examining the condition of the glass workers there. He found that the great majority of them, who were skilled at tizans, had to sit making bottles for twelve hours a day for 12s. Gd. per week—and that was under Protec- tion. In America, another protested country, they had some of the most sanguinary battles between Capital and Labour. There they had the question of the unem- ployed to an even greater degree than in this country. The Labour party said to Mr. Chamberlain " However seecious may be your promises, there is no hope for the workers of this country from Protection." (Applause.) It was not the Neal policy which was on the backs of the people to-day On the contrary it was the people who adorned Mr. Chamberlain'splatform—the landlords the railway lords, the gold mine owning lords—these were the men who were bleeding the country, and not the fiscal policy. (Applause.) When Mr. Chamberlain I or Mr.Pierpoint.their member,carne down end advocated Protection as a remedy for their diseases, let them tell those gentlemen that they would prefer to seethe land, lord,the ra He ay lord,nnd the mine owner off their backs, arid then they would consider the tariff proposals. (AP- plause).What they wanted to do as a p ,rty was to focus their attention on home affairs. The vast proportioa of that audience, declared the speaker in alluding to the poverty question, was not above a month From the Workhouse. The men who were exploiting the workers were the men who were producing the appalling poverty existing on every hand. (Applause.) SPEECH BY MR. KEIR HARDIE.

Mr. KEllt. HARDIE, M.P., who had a hearty reception congratulated the Independent Labour Party on the very evident progress it was making in this town. They were asked by the resolution to approve of the principles and policy of the Independent Labour Party. The object of the party was two-fold. It sought primarily to propagate the principles of socialism, and secondarily to create a Labour party in politics. 130th the principles of socialism and the policy of labour repre- sentation w ere growing in a 3ceptance amongst the people. Socialists started on the assump- tion that socialism was inevitable for two reasons: First, because it was the only means whereby a civilized people could live free life and in addition because, leaving the ethical consideration out of the question, our present system was breaking down lamentably in all its works. They had heard the statement frequently that despite the wealth of the country and its growing position amongst the commercial nations of the world, we had from twelve to thirteen millions of the population living either under or on the poverty line. That meant that practically 30 per cent, of the people, when fully employed during a period of good trade, were not receiving wages to purchase them the same standard of physical e:ficiency as they would enjoy in the Work- house or in prison. Various reasons were assigned for that, the most popular being that poverty was the outcome of drink or drunkenness. In individual cases drunkenness undoubtedly caused poverty, and the drinking habits of large masses of the people in all ranks of society were a hindrance and a stumbling block to reform. 11 (Applause). It was not, however, true to say that drink II or drunkenness was the cause of poverty on the part of the people to whom he was referring. Sir Charles Booth and Mr. Rowntree, who had specially investigated the matter, agreed in their conclusions that less than 20 par cent. of the people who were poor, were poor because of drink. The cause of poverty, said Mr. Hardie, was that the wages paid were not sufficient to purchase a decent standard of living. Then it was also alleged that poverty was due to under-production. We were told that the wealth produced was not sufficient to keep the whole nation up to ['standard of comfort and

div.head: DREAM.
div.p: A DREAM.

There came to me a dream the other night, A world of wonders dawned upon my sight. I thought beyond the shadows of the tomb, In boundless space the Universe has room. For spirits when the dear old earth they leave, To wnich they do so often fondly cleave. The thoughts we see and feelings of the heart, Become of spirit life a conscious part. Not lost the joy or sorrow here we feel, Nor ought we do or ought we would conceal; This is the seed time and the harvest there, But the two worlds we cannot well compare. I hoard a voice me thought it answered me All life to man is veiled in mystery ; Untimely to that world we should not go, When lite is long then all its seeds we sow. When life is short the harvest must be less, From the best conduct comes our happiness; Results are there, death is another birth Of souls immortal when they leave the earth What is, in other changing forms has been, And the most conscious may the least be seen ; The p...wer unseen which guides the wandering star" Tho, gh ever with us is for ever Mr. To a blind boy I heard his mother tell, Of moon and stars and flowers we love so well. To sweetest notes he would her words compare, Yet deemed he not the world could be so fair. Ala like the poor blind child me thought are we, Though nature teaches us we cannot see. Whispering beyond is happiness and light, Slowly we learn the Universe is right. S. KEN YON.
THE NEXT LIBERAL PREMIER.

Lord Spencer, who has been much beneftted by his stay at Bournemouth, is going abroad shortly after the meeting of Parliament. Among Liberal politicians it is believed that he will be the aext Prime Minister. It is now an open secret that he would have succeeded the late Mr. Gladstone if that statesman had had his way. But Queen Victoria, though a constitutional monarch, had a very strong will of her own, and seldom yielded to Mr. Gladstone unless constitutionally compelled. Bence Lord Rosebery's summons. Lord Spencer's acceptance of office, though he is over 70, would smooth out many difficulties in the Liberal party. An officer belonging to a party of visitors from the Russian Army to Cabal has been shot dead in that town The murderer, whose nationality is not given, escaped. It is stated that the superior office- of the party has reportcd the occurrence to the Czar by special messenger, but this statement is not conarrneci.

div.head: BEAUTY DEAR,
div.p: BEAUTY DEAR,
MRS. L. T. MEADE (Author of" Stories from the Diary of a Doctor," etc.)

He was the most disagreeable man on board, and if it had not been for the child, there was scarcely another passenger who would have troubled to speak to him. His name was entered on the ship's Log Wi " James Stirling "—" James Stirling and child " .—but beyond the fact that Stirling was the Itlatl'N name, and that, a child was wh him, no one knew anything whatever about him. Our ship was the " Arethusa " of the P. and 0. line, and I was the ship's doctor. Stirling and the child came on board at Bombay. The man wore shabby clothes, and was very rough to look at. He was the sort of person who might have gone as steerage passenger, but strange to say, he travelled first. He bad a four berth state-room on the first dock for himself and the child, and this room was in the most central position. The child was se u.ce!y three years old, and Stirling made ltina4.ll a regular nurse to her. She was not a bit afraid of him, although he wa- us repulsive looking is man as I have ever seem His face was horribly mailed and seamed with small-pox, his nose was wide and turned up, his n.outh was still wider with great coarse lips. His eyes were so deeply mink into his head that they were scarcely visible, his forehead was very low, and his hair coarse and grizzly. In addition to the homely nature of his features he had a most forbidding expression, and a constant scowl between his brows.

The child was a very bright little creature, a perfect contrast to him. She was shrewd and clever for her tender years, and could talk quite well. It was the most pathetic and at the same time comical thing in the world to see her curling herself up in this ,ugly brute's antis, and calling him " beauty and " beauty dear." Then she would stroke his disfigured cheeks, and press Let velvet lips to his. As she sat on his knee, her baby chatter went on incessantly. Stirling was entirely devoted to the child—hc was her playmate, nurse, and father in one. When he entered the dining saloon little Victoria always sat perched up on his shoulder. It was useless to suggest that babies dined at a separate table. Victoria sat with Stirling and dined with him or not at all. During meals she sat on his knee while he fed her with the daintiest tit-bits he could lay hands on. She made a perfect picture seated thus with her fair head pressed against his breast. The man was dressed roughly, but little Victoria was dairsty in her clothing, and the ladies on board were all much attracted by the bright little ereature. It was useless, however, to lavish af- fectionate or friendly words on her. To all en- dearments she had but one form of eply. "No, no,—go way, natty lady. Vic 'tay with Bea uty- Dear. Vic not go to natty lady." Neither bon-bons nor seductive words would :mince her to stir from the safe shelter of 'beauty -leer,' and by and by the ladies on board the Aretlinsn left her alone.
But one day a strange thing happened. Little I.'ictoria lay and cried in her state cabin—she tried incessantly, and softly to herself, and at ftst I lie stewardess came in search of me.

" Dr. Grant," she said, " there is something wrong with little Miss in cabin 94. You know the baby child who belongs to Mr. Stirling? She 61 lying in her berth with her face turned to the and won't speak to anybody; she cries •dl the time and is quite alone." " TIM; where is Stirling," I asked. " I don't know, sir. I never saw the child .!-“erted before. Site won't tonal, her breakfte.t--- utev are a (peer pair, both of them." .; It is odd that Stirling should have forgotten !On child," I made answer. " I will go and look him—he is probably on deck or in the smok- mg-room." But though I searched the smoking-room. th-re was no Stirling, and though I went frem ,ittl to end of the deck, neither could I find hini. At last. just as I was about to return to inform Mrs. Harris of my non-success, a rough !elle] -retched itsalf out from an unexpected biding- betwea the upper and. the lower deck, and stilling, dragged me towards him. " For God's sake come and speak to me, Dr. Grant I did not dare to send a messenger foi von. I have ' got it, and the child must have no- thing more to do with me. Put me anywhere, easy front the other passengers. I an, sure .0 die, but that does not matter, I ant only think-. lug about the child. She is net infected so for. I hoped that we might have reached England tirst, but it was not the will of the Almighty. For God's sake find some corner for me where I my be isolated."
But what is wrong with you ?" I asked. There was no one near at the moment to list en-to our words.
"Look at me doctor," he made reply. " What do I look like? Healthy and handsome, aye." " You look ill, very ill," I replied. 60,:pat what Jo you fear ?" _

He bent forward and whispered a word. I slatted and felt myself turning pale. " No," I said, " iiiipossible !" " Possible, very. In fact—certain. I was expollted to the infection just before leaving for England. A friend of mine died of it. He left Ihe child in my care. The child was not infected then, and she is not infected now. Will someone else look after her f"

"Then she is not your child." An expression of agony crossed his face. " I am taking hr home to her mother," he said. " Once she is put into her mother's care my sorrows cease. I—l cannot tell you any more, doctor. No, she is not my child, but I love her as I love no other creature on earth. Let someone take care of her, and put me where I can be out of the way."

" Stay where you are for a moment or too," I liiwered. I rushed off to where Mrs. Harris, the slewardess, was waiting for me. "Do what you can for the child," I said. " I'll be back presently?" ' I saw the Captain in his state-room, and told him briefly what had occurred. .
" What'," he cried, "a case of Bubonic plague on board—Good God !"

" Whatever happens, Captain," I made an- swer, "we must keep panic at bay. There is that cabin in the stern of the lower deck which is unoccupied. State-room No. 4 ; it is quite out of the way. I'll have Stirling conveyed there." " He had no right to come on board after sub• jecting himself to infection," said Captain ROM. " The whole thing is disgraceful—and the child, —you say the child was subjected to the came in- fection P"

" He says the child is safe." "Safe," said the Captain, "he would say it to screen her. She must be closely watched, and if there is the slightest symptom of indisposition, she most be quarantined at once." • " I will do all that is necessary," I an- swered. " I have promised the poor fellow to ' look after the child, and I must keep my word. After all, be is terribly to be pitied. From ; what I have seen of him he is not likely to live." ‘• Ugly brute," said Captain Ross. "He has I put me into a fine mess. Well, do what you can, I Grant. I can depend on your discretion." Accordingly I had Stirling conveyed to an empty cabin on the lower deck. It was a large ,*roomy apartment, but seldom used on account of 1 its bad position. Having seen to the sick man's comfort, I went back to the luxurious state-room, where little missie queened it in royal fashion over the stewardess. " Come, Miss Victoria," I heard Mrs. Harris say. " You must get up; it is very naughty for I little ladies to lie in bed all day."
"Go 'way, natty ting," was little Vie's re- rponse.
" You will get up for me, won't you P " I said, touching her on her shoulder. t• Stirlhig would wish it.

The pretty blooming face was raised from the onlow ; the bright eyes were fixed on mine. " Vic go to beauty dear. Take Vic to beatify ',sir," and the mite stretched up her arms. " Get up then," I said, tenipraistng in quite a icick/1 fashion. " Let, Mr.. fiiirrim dr.7,44 y•an it once; I eon do uothing while von stay in bed.' At the tlaught of findiug fleauty Dear,' Vic- toria illoc,l lier Self to lie ,itt into her clothes. When she was 1111 ly (17.!.•,q1 Mts. Harris her in it passion of nr-ilierly love to her 'moo% " 'rake Vie to Beauty lle;er,'" said (lie ei.lll. Murmuring womo iii ulnlle relly, the steward- ess took her into the dining-saloon where OA ser- vants wevii cnjoi ing thiu hint ii breakfast, but although the good woulan eoaxed mid petted, little Victoria shut her lirs tightly, itld refitsed either to speak or to touch fowl.

At firlsti this conduct on the part of the child was put down to a tit of baby sulks, but when it continued all through the day, and no one could induce the poor mite to eat, or to play, or to be happy, matters began to look serious. he was a Yexy vatient baby. azd after thetret

tronble she ceased to cry. She crept back to the luxurious cabin, which she and Stirling had shared together, and crouching on the floor, clasped her broken doll in her arms. She sat there hour after hour, a most pathetic and hungry expres.ion in her eyes. Meanwhile, the plagite-strieken man grew worse. As the night approached, he began to get delirious. I resolved to sit up with him, and in company of a sailor, who lad already suffered from plague, and was supposed to be immune, kept watch dur- ing the long hours of darkness. Seldom had I spent a more dreadful night. In his mad delirium, the man was giving himself away, and his revelations of his past life were terrible. There were few deeds of lawlessness at which be had stopped. Ile had injured and oppressed most of those he had conic in contact with, be had lost his money by gambling, and defrauded his friends. In especial, there was one man- whom lie bated ; his bitter hatred of this man was apparent in his delirium and caused him sometimes to give vent to wild and terrible screams, and even shrieks. Beyond doubt there was a very black sin on his mold in connection with this man. .Ars Stirling raved and struggled, and tossed himself about, I hail to exercise all my force to keeft him quiet. By the morning, however, the fell disease bad to a great extent done its deadly work. The giant lay quiet as an infant, perspiration streaming off his face. "He is quieter now, David," I said to the sailor. " I can leave him in your care for an hour or two. I Will just go and have it disinfecting bath, and change any things—then I will come back and relieve you." I rushed off to my cabin; the dawn MIR break- ing. If all went well, we should arrive at Malta in twenty-four hours—we were now steaming across the Mediterranean, which i was smooth as glass. I had just finished my toilet when there came a tap at my cabin door. I opened it, and Mrs. Harris stood without.

"If you please, 4r," she said. "have you taken the child to Mr. Stirling ?" " Heaven forbid," .1 answered. " I hear, sir, that the gentleman is very bad." " But what about the child ?" I queried. " Little Miss is nowhere to be found, Doctor. I thought of course she had gone to the gentle- man's cabin."

"She must not go near Stirling's cabin—do you hear, Mrs. Harris i' You must keep the child in this part of the ship." " Well, sir, I'll do my best—but I can't pro- dee what may be impossible. The child is con- ttilry and a bit stunned. Never a bite did she put inside her yesterday, and last night, sir, when went into the state-room to undress her, she was fast asleep on the floor, her cheeks all I,tained with tears, and that broken doll of hers, she calls it, clasped in her arms. I took the poor mite up just as she was, and popped her into her berth, and I hoped she would be safe till the morning.. Will she slept, and I went. and had a bit of supper, and when I had seen to my ladies, I thought 1 would go and sleep in the cabin with little Mingle."

" Quite right, Mrs. Harris," I answered. " I went to I.wd right enough, sir, and to sleep, and the last thing I saw was the glint of little Missie's golden hair ()II her pillow, and I heard her breathing, gentle as a lamb, but to- wards niorning, I awoke all of a sudden, and I looked across to Mksie's berth, and she was not there. I went and searched for her and called her name, and so did the sailors and the stewards, but; v.:me of them could find her, and none of tli knew Where she was. One said that maybe she had gone to find that lisrum- searum man whom she is so taken up with, and I thought I would ask you, sir."

'6 Srie is not there, and what is more, she must not go there," I answered. " just speak to the Purser, will you F—lie will give you orders tc have every corner of the ship searched. Now I must go back to my patient." I suatched some food, and went downstairs to the large cabin occupied by the plague-stricken man.

The worst manifestations of this awful disease • were now making themselves apparent. The deadly weakness continued, and got worse, and strange to say, it had a sort of refining influence on the coarse face. The voice so rasping and loud I was reduced to the merest whisper. I gave a sigh of relief when I saw that little Viotoria was not in the room. Motioning to my smiler that he might leave me for the present, I I sat down by the dying man. " Come closer," I heard him whisper. " I have something to tell you." I bent towards him. • "How soon shall we reach Malta r. " By this time to-morrow," I answered " Twenty-four bourn," he muttered. " Shall I live till then, Doctor ?" " Hard to tell. I will do what I can for you, Stirling." "Thanks. I should like to know that the child was safe in port, and delivered over to her mother. She wail to meet us at Malta."
Can you tell me anything about the little one, Stirling; you may live, but you may not. you know—it is best to be prepared. At present I do not even know the child's name." _ _ _ _

He smiled feebly. " A lady will meet you at Msita, and will come on board, and if—if I am not there give her the child. The lady will be the child's mother. The little one's name is Angelo, Victoria Angelo." " And what am I to say when I give the child to Mrs. Angelo ?" " Say that Stirling brought her across, and that he has atoned." " I don't understand." " Nor will she—but that does not matter. She need never know. Angelo is dead, and she gets the child. Look at me, doctor. You do not know the wicked sort of person you have on board. I killed Angelo." "What !" I cried.

" Yes' practically I did. I did it on purpose. I hated him, he and I were partners in the same business, up country about two hundred miles beyond Bombay. The plague came, Und I brought some infected sheets from a man who died of it, and put them on Angelo's bed. He took it and died; I killed him. I did every bad thing I could to that man, defrauded him, stole his property. The reckoning day was near, and I had to get him out of the way. It was either he or I to go under, and I had the choice, and I chose him. He is dead, and I was taking the little one back to her mother. Now, I will tell you something strange. You see a devil before von, a devil neither more nor less, but that mite 'fell in love with me—would not be happy with anybody else—liked to stroke this awful face of mine, liked to get into my arms, liked to kis', well, she bowled me over, Doctor' I can't tell you how or why. I can bear a good bit, but just the love of that little innocent was the straw too much. The mother had gone to England year ago, broken down by the climate. but An gelo would not part with the child. That Ail( could bowl any man in all the world over. Well, my punishment and my redemption too was tc bring her home, and put her into her mother's arms. But it is not to be. I hoped that I might have reached Malta before the disease broke out, for 1 guessed of course that I was infected. lam dying now, .1 never see that little angel again. I atone for everything when I die with- out seeing her. Oh, God to a man like me cmd,l any punishment be more ? She is the ono bit of lminanity that ever touched me."

Hi s voice railed away to the faintest whisper. gate Mtn a stimulant, awl after a little be said : " Do you ask if I repent —no, not a bit of it." I vat with Stirling for boore. By and bye, I went back to thy cabin. Mrs. Harris met me with her face quite white, and tears in her eyes. 4, We ertmt,,i 6,,11 nny,v)wro. Doctor. Do yOU mum rue poor utue ut:ar eouicl nave ant),,e,; over board I."'

" 0;1, no, Mrs. Hareis, she must be on the ship." • Well, sir, every sailor on board is searclihig high and low: we are all in a taking.'' The panic about little Victoria spread rapidly, and by lunch time, the saloon passengers were in n sti,t of excitement. They knew that Stirling was ill. although the real nature of his illness was carefully kept from them. One lady came to the Captain with tears in her eyes. My little Doris is Victoria's age. if the poor baby could he found she might come tu my cabin to play with Doris." But Vic's chosen playmates were of a different sort, it broken-down and battered doll, and a broken-down and battered man, black as pitch except for that little streak of gold wYch his loNe for her caused to shine through his nature. Towards evening we entored some of the cross currents off the coast of Malta. The wind rose and the Arethusa ' was tossed on the waves. In Stirling's cabin the motion was felt a good deal. The dying man was now in a state of stupor, and could scarcely be roused to take nourishment. I arranged once again to spend the night with him.

By f.ix o'clock in the morning we should reach Malta. Could he possibly live so long r Night settled down over the big liner, and Stirling breathed heavily. About an hour after midnight, he dropped into a still deeper slumber. His breathing became fainter, and once I bent towards him, wondering if the last moment bad come As I did so. he started up. fresh

div.head: FIRE AT COCKHEDGE MILLS.
div.p: FIRE AT COCKHEDGE MILLS.
Exciting Scenes.

Cockhedge Mills narrowly escaped serious damage by fire in the early hours of Thursday morning. The train of events leading up to the outbreak was somewhat peculiar. It appears that on Wednesday afternoon a fire was discovered in one of the "slashing" rooms lat the factory and an alarm was raised. The works brigade quickly got to work with the powerful fire pump which is kept on the premises, their efforts being directed by the managers. Fortunately they succeeded in confining the fire to the room in which it broke out but some garments belonging to the girls employed there were destroyed. At 12.45 on Thursday morning the watchman on duty at the works found that the debris remaining as a result of the previous afternoon's fire, and which had been piled in the yard, was in flames. The remains had either continued smouldering and been fanned by the powerful westerly gale, or had been ignited by a spark from the adjoining house property. The works fire-alarm roused the neighbourhood and people from the east side of the town hurried - to the mill in crowds, exciting scenes being witnessed. Inspector If owbotham, Sergeant Bell and a detachment of police were quickly on the scene and rendered valuable assistance. The watchman and a few of the company's firemen got a line of hose to work from the fire pump. Mean- while the burning material was blown about the yard by the gale, and a message was dispatched to the Fire Station. The bell was rung and the borough brigade, under the direction of Superintendent Turner and Deputy-Superintendent Turner, promptly turned out at full strength, taking with them two steamers, reels, ladders and escapes. Fortunately the works brigade succeeded in getting the fire in hand, and the borough firemen's services were not required But for the prompt measures taken the fire would undoubtedly have hadslisastrous consequences, but as it was the vorks were not touched. The Borough Brigade deserve credit for their ready response, this being the ninth fire the men have been celled to within a month.

div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
NORTHERN LEAGUE. First
RESULTS OF' SATURDAY'S MATCHES. LEAGUE (FIRST DIVISION).
G. T. I% G. T. P. Broughton R. Salford 1 9 8 Runcorn Batley Widnes Warrington Hull Kingston R. 0 2 6 St. Helens Leigh 0 9 10 Hull Bradford Hunslet 2 1 7 Wigan ‘. \ Warrington v. Leeds.

An excellent contest between these teams was witnessed at Warrington. The homesters were keen to avenge a defeat sustained at Leeds and succeeded. Both teams turned out as selected, in the presence of 5,000 spectators. The weather was fine and the ground in good order. Teams and officials: Leeds—Little wood, back ; W. Evans, T. Llewellyn, P Thomas and J. A. Naylor, three-quarter backs; R. Ward and A. Brayshaw, half backs : F. Webster, H. Moon, J. W. Stead, F. Wright, T. H. Wainwright, E. Watts, A. Lunn, and F. Wormald, forwards. Warrington—Hallam. back ; Fish, Isherwood, Brooks, and Kenyon, three-quarter backs ; Davies and Hocken- hall, half _backs ; Boardman, Thomas, Cook, Belton,

Preston, Naylor, 'Jolley and SinPmrs, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Oakland, Barnsley. Touch judges, Messrs. J. Bruckshaw and J. H. Houghton. Leeds had the wind behind them in the first half, and were quickly on the attack. A good many scrummages were forced on the home line, but Hallam and his col- leagues dealt safely with the scoring attempts of the Headingley backs. For obstruction Warrington were penalised, and Littlewood had a shot for goal, but the ball went outside. Fish from a tall kick snapped up thejball on the bounce, and dashed away, kicking over Littlewood's head. Llewellyn was tackled by Board- man before he could reply, and a passing movement between llockenhal I, Davies, 'lsherwood, and Fish, ended in the latter repassing to Davies, wha transferred to Preston, the latter being tackled by half a dozen opponents. Another bout by the Warrington backs put Fish again in possession, and, after dodging his oppon- ents, he kicked over Littlewood's head, and Boardman dashing up. ran over and scored amidst tremendous cheering. Preston failed at the goal kick. Soon after the restart the Leeds backs started a passing movement i Phil Thomas and Naylor had only Hallam to beat, but Hallam accounted for Thomas, and his pass was mulled by Naylor, who could have walked in had he taken the ball. Leeds now attacked strongly, and Evans was ' thrown into touch by Fish near the line: From a pass from Llewellyn3Evans tricked Fish, but Hallam forced him into touch, and at the interval Leeds were still a , try in arrears. With the wind Warringtoh did not have so much of , the game as looked likely from the run of the first half, the visiting forwards playing with so miich resolu- tion that the Warrington half-backs rarely got the ball. Littlewood again failed at a penalty kick, this time in a fairly easy position, but Leeds at this point were making the rnnning strongly, and looked to have a good chance of pulling off the game, when Warrington scored another try as the outcome of some wonderfully fine back play. Hockenball broke away from the scrummage and got clear away. When fronted by Littlewood he passed to Isherwood; the latter was tackled, but man- aged to pass to Thomas. who transferred to Hockenhall again, and the latter completed a brilliant effort by running over near the post. Fish hit the cross bar with the goal kick. Leeds continued to have innumerable chances, but their backs bungled badly, and the result was :—Warrington 2 tries (6 points), Leeds, nil.

Most Extraordinary Cure of Modern

LIFE-LONG BILIOUSNESS ENDED.

The restoration to health of Mrs. Phcebe May, of Perry's Farm, Snelsmore Column, Newbury (Berks.). by Bile Beans may be regarded as the most extraordinary cure of biliousness and allied ailments which has taken place in recent years. "Ever since childhood," she says, " I suffered from biliousness. Vomiting attacks would continue for hours, and so exhaust me that for days I should be helpless, and unable to move, eat, or sleep. I was told I should outgrow this ailment, but when I became older and went out to service the attacks still came on regularly, making me unable to do my work. My mistress was very kind and considerate, and had to employ a woman to come and do my work whilst I was ill.

"First I would have a fit of shivering, then violent vomiting would come on, and I was so had that I was bound to remain in bed for two or three days. People said I ought to diet myself, and not eat this, that, and the other. I avoided some foods, took others, and tried ,every remedy that was suggested, but it was all the ,same. Even the drops of brandy which they used to give me to stop the vomiting only made me the more sick. l took hot water morning and night, yet all food made me ill. In consequence of this continued illness, I got very thin and weak. "If I went anywhere, I was sure to be bad. I went to Reading to see my brother, and he had to bring me home in a cab. Mother and I went to a circus in Newbury. I was taken ill outside,and a crowd collected. "I had more doctors than most people," said Mrs. May to her interviewer, and counting on her fingers she enumerated no less than eight doctors who had attended her. . .

"One day we read in 'Lloyd's News' how effective Bile Beans were in cases of biliousness, and decided to give them a trial. The first box did me a little good, so I persevered with this remedy. In a very short time I found I was getting rid of the biliousness. The improvement continued; I became able to retain ray food, and in consequence I gradually recovered my strength. After a thorough course of Bile Beans I was completely cured. The cure, I am pleased to say, has been a permanent one. I have not had a bilious attack for over two years, so that it is evident Bile Beans have thoroughly corrected my system." Mrs. Giper, the mother of Mrs. May, corroborated the above details. Bile Beans also cure indigestion, headache, constipa- tion, piles, female ailments, amemia, debility, wind spasms, dizziness, unpleasant feelings of fulness after eating, biliousness, heartburn, .4:c. div.head: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE CLUB. -- -- A "Keen Election" Expected.
div.p: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE CLUB. -- -- A "Keen Election" Expected.

Mr. E. DRAPER presided at the annual meeting of the Warrington Junior Conservative Club which was held at the club in Orford Lane on Tuesday evening. In the course of a brief speech he said that during the four years of its existence the club could claim to have made itself a force to be reckoned with politically in Warrington. It was for the members to see that that position was maintained. He sincerely hoped the club would become still more forward in political affairs and that they would be in the forefront whenever the time came to show that "the good old cause" was still the win- ning side in Warrington. During the last twelve months they had had to encounter adverse circumstances. Trade had been very bad and money had been scarce,and this had had a prejudicial effect. He hoped, however, that they had seen the bedrock,that trade would steadily improve, and that a year hence they would be able to take a much more hopeful view of their position. He was afraid they would not reach that position of great prosperty which they all wished to see until we had some alteration in our tariff methods. Mr. J.SEED presented the annual report of the Secre- tary (Mr. H. Hayes), giving a resume of the events of the year. In the absence of Mr. W. J. Forshaw (hon. treasurer) the financial statement was read by Mr. H.B.HOUGIITON who said the position was satisfactory and they could ' look forward to the coming year with a good heart and renewed vigour. On the motion of Mr. KAY seconded by Mr. J. GERRARD, Mr. Roger C. Parr was re-elected president. Councillor W. J. FORSHAW was re-elected Non- treasurer, on the proposition of Mr. W. L. WILLIAMS seconded by Mr. T. WILKINSON. In moving the re-election of Mr. Herbert Hayes as bon secretary Mr. J. J. Hands said that no doubt they would very shortly have a general election sprung upon them. He did not think it could be more than twelve months distant, and he expected a very keen contest in Warrington. Be hoped no one in the Conservative party would be over-confident, and if they were not he had no doubt they would win. Mr. P. BERRY seconded the motion which was agreed to. Messrs. Kay, Littlewood, W. Jolley, Edwards, and Robinson were elected the committee for the year. A special committee was formed to attend to bowling matters, Mr. 3. Seed being appointed secretary.

Miss Eitzgerald,the daughter of Sir Gerald Fitzgerald The Poles, Crawley, was tined £6 by the County Court judge at Redbili, on Wednesday, for assaulting two bailiffs who had gained admission to The Poles with a view of taking Sir Gerald to Wandsworth Gaol on a commitment order.

DIAGRAM 57.
STRONG RUN-THROUGH TO AVOID A KISS.

Diagram 57 shows a run-through cannon which is only possible by a strong stroke. If the ordinary player will place the balls to the measurements given under the diagram, it will most likely appear to him that no run-through cannon is on owing to the impossibility of preventing the object balls kising. As a matter of fact if the stroke be played • at slow or medium pace a kiss- must inevitably occur. If, however, the stroke be played at high speed the object ball will rebound from the cushion very squarely, and by this means the kiss may easily be a vti,ird. Were the angle of reflection always equal to the angle of reflection as is taught in so nlany books on billiards, such a cannon would. impossible. But except in slow strokes the angle of reflection is never the same as the angle of incidence, and in high-pace strokes the dif- ference is very marked. On tables with elow, hard cuchions, the 44fference is not nearly so great: as on tables with good yielding cushions; still it is always there. Naturally the more yielding the cushion the lees difficult does the stroke become, and it also follows that a stroke which is perhaps somewhat difficult on a table with poor cushions is still easy .enough on a table with resilient cushions, and that in some positions it would on many :tables be absolutely impcesible•to avoid the kiss, no matter at what pace the stroke were played, whereas on other "tables the first •object ball could be made to just clear the eeeond In the positioh shown on diagram 57 the cue bail •should be aimed quite full on to the 0b".4..., ball, 'mid some running side (left hand side in he diagram) sheuld be imparted to the cue ball. Even without side, however, the cue ball will come off the cushion less squarely than the ob- ject ball, for the simple reason that it does not strike the cushion at anything likethe pace that the object ball does, and this difference in the throw-off angle of the two bails is in itself generally sufficient to ensure the cannon being made. It would perhaps be as well for the ordi- nary player to play this strong run-through cannon without side, for it must not be forgotten that when playing a strong stroke it is far easier to strike an object ball as intended when using no side than it is when striking the cue, ball away from the centre.

A run-through cannon that requires ,:xtreme side. Cue ball 8.!-, inches from the top cushion and 11 inches from the side cushion. Object white 21A inches from the top cushion and 9 inches from the side cushion. Red ball 51 inches above a line drawn through the centre of the middle pockets, and in a dead straight line with the other two balls.

Diagram 53 shows the three balls in a dead straight line. Again here many players would think that a run-through cannon must be im- possible owing to a kiss being unavoidable. A really good player can, however, easily avoid the kiss. 'The stroke is played by aiming almost, but not quite full on to the object ball, and im- parting as much running side as possible to the cue ball. The chief thing in the stroke is to send the first ball just past the second, but only just past it, for if it passes too wide of it the cue ball will strike the cushion too far away from the second object ball to allow of the cannon being made, noianatter how much side the cue ball is carrying. If, however the first object ball pass the second ball with not very much to spare the cue ball will strike the cushion near enough to -Eh° second ball to allow the running side to carry it on to it. Such A cannon is waYs a good stroke, as it requires well playing. The cue ball should be struck with a free flowing cue, that is to say, the cue should follow on after striking the ball. Any jerkiness about the stroke is almost certain to cause failure. As the stroke requires a maximum of side, the cue should be chalked for it. Many players, though • they always chalk their cue for a screw stroke, often omit to do so when playing a stroke with extreme side, though the chalking is quite as essential in the latter ca sao as it is in the former. don as a record,for they have made a rule that in order for any break to be recognised the table on which it is made must be tested and found to be a standard prior to the commencement of a match. In my opinion and the opinion of every player amateur or professional with whom I have discussed the matter, the rule is an absurd one. It cmnot be that the Billiard Association think that any respectable firm would put up a very easy table, and after a big break had been mate, change the cushions and make the pockets standard, and then apply to have the table tested. If any billiard table maker could he guilty of such an action, what would there be to prevent them erecting a standard table, getting it passed before the match commenced, and then altering the pockets ? It seems to me that it is simply a question of s. d. with the Billiard Association, and that were they to pass tables after a big break had been made they'would have very few applicatiors during a season, whereas they hope to get every table maker to apply pany times during the season to have different tables tested. lam not aware what charge the Association makes for test- ing a table, but whatever it is its funds cannot be increased to any very great extent by the present system, and the Association therefore could lose very little by altering their rule Besides, it is not always convenient to have a table tested prior to the commencement of a ratch. Sometimes some par- ticular hall is not at liberty until the Monday, on which the game begins. A firm has thus to put up a table the same morning , and cases have occurred in which a table has only bran ready for play a few minutes before the advertised time of startirg. Also is it not a great injustice to the professional who makes a big break and then finds that the Billiard Association will not pass it, though he has had no say,`one way or the other, in the matter ? I remember perfectly well the dismay on Stevenson's face one day last season when he went to the table to continue an unfinished break. The night before, playing with crystalate balls, he had fun to his points with 687 unfinished, the highest break he had yet made and by far the biggest break ever made with composit ‘-‘ll balls. A big crowd had assembled, hoping to see Stevenson beet the then existing record of 722 by Dawson. Jest as he walked to the table a telegram was handeal o him stat- ing that his break could not be passed e' • •i table had hot been tested by the Association. Tv, h the balls were in perfect position at the top ot he table, yet Stevenson only -increased ihe break I,y 10. Is it not possible that he might have made a great many more but for that telegram. With regard to Roberts' great break, I understand that the Billiard Association the following day passed the table as a standard for any future breaks that might be made on it, but would not pass the S2l as a record. Is not their action farcical ? Answ6rs to several correspondents are unavoidably held over till next week.

div.p: HOCKEY.

STOCKTON HEATH v. SOUTH MAitHESTER. Played at Stoat on Heath. Both team were fairly well represented rid a good hard game was expected. From the bully off e Stockton forwards carried the ball into the visitors' 25, but good defensive play by the visiting backs kept them from becoming really dangerous. At length a score came, Eric Fairclough feeding W. Richardson with a nice pass, and this player beating the half in fine style gave to W. Longdin, who scored with a splendid shot from the edge of the circle, the goalkeeper having no chance of saving. Smarting under this reverse, the South forwards now made their presence felt, and Mercer rushed the home defence, and running right between the backs he easily scored a good goal. The visitors still kept up the attack and Leßoy had hard lines in not scoring number two. Half time: Stockton Heath, 1; South Manchester, 1. After the in- terval the home forwards played like a different line, and fairly out-playe.l the visiting backs R. Fairclough in particular playing a fine game. Before the final whistle sounded goals were scored by C. H. Bond, W. Richardson and R. Fairclough, and on numerous other occasions the South goal only missed capture by inches. Final score: Stockton Heath, 4 ; South Man- chester, 1.

GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION.

div.head: Speeches by Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., Mr. A. H. Grosfield, Mr. Frank Roberts, Mr. C. E. Parker, and others.
div.p: Speeches by Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., Mr. A. H. Grosfield, Mr. Frank Roberts, Mr. C. E. Parker, and others.

No local political meeting of recent years has been looked forward to with keener interest and pleasure than the great Liberal demonstration held in the Parr Hall last evening. The reason was not far to seek. The 'fact that such a conspicuous figure in the politi- cal world as Mr. D. Lloyd-George, M.P., was to be the principal speaker was sufficient to invest the gathering with a special interest and importance. Warrington Liberals, in common with members of the party throughout the Kingdom, have been full of admira- tion for the sturdy fights for principle in which Mr. Lloyd-George has taken a foremost part. His unswerving opposition to the Education Act and the marked ability and energy which be has brought to bear in ee-posing Protectionist fallacies and strengthening the Free Trade cause, have earned the thanks of a large section of the community and his career, which gives promise of a great future) is being closely followed. It was but natural that the supporters of Liberalism in Warrington should be anxious to do honour to the chieftain of Wales, and at the, same time avail themselves of the opportunity of hearing an instructiveand vigorous speech on the vital questions of the day. Admir able arrangetoents had been made for the demonstration, which afforded convincing evidence of the vitality of local Liberalism. The hall was crowded in every part and the greatest enthu- siasm prevailed. The proceedings will rank as memt i orable n the history of the progressive party is Warrington and certainly gave one strong hopes that the town will declare for Free Trade and progres when the trial of strength comes. The building had been suitably decorated for the occasion' mottoes expressing the sentiment of the moment being freely displayed. The attention of the visi-ior on entering was first arrested by a long streamer suspended above the platform. In the centre appeared the honoured name of " Crosfield," while beneath were the Liberal watchwords "Peace, Retrenchment and Reform."On either side the feeling of the working-classes were clearly expressed in the sentences "Peers of the people " and " House of Lords ended or mended." Mottoes which kvere arranged round the balconies were " Free Trade and free food," and "No slavery under the British flag." The window cur- tains were embellished with posters bearing the spirited appeals: "Do justice to yourselves and stick Ao Free Trade "and " Let. commerce and industry be fairly represented." Another motto conceived in a prophetic vein read "Bravo Stalybridge and Dorset Warrington to follow !" Other declarations of the Liberal policy were worded " Englishmen love 'liberty and despise Chinese labour ' and "Free Trade with all the world." Some considerable time before the meeting com- menced the hall was filled and the time was pleasantly occupied in singing such choruses as " The Liberal march" and "Stamp, stamp, stamp upon Protection" which went with a fine swing. Mr. W. H. Payton, rkflis. Bac., presided at the organ. When Mr. Lloyd George appeared on the platform he received a great ovation,,the audience rising and cheering. The meeting was presided over by Mr. 'rank A. Roberts, a well-known Warrington Liberal who some years ago rendered valuable service to the party of this town and who now lives at Windermere. Be was supported by Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield and many prominent Liberals- The SECRETARY (Mr. C, Jackson Holmes) read letters of apology from Mr. William Long Mr. Ziba Armitage, and Miss Bessie Dutton of !the Women's I.lberal Association and the Rev. John Yonge. The CHAIRMAN said he was almost overwhelmed at the cordiality of their reception. Those who knew him in the past would know that he was not given to .oratory, and the cordial reception had almost taken any words he might have had to say from his memory. .(Hear, hear.) He was induced to take the position ho occupied because he would hear Mr. Lloyd George, who was doing such yeoman service for the country. N' Applause). He would refer to the past to see what lessons it taught and taken view of theprospects of the future. in 1880 the Liberal party in Aarrington were rejoicing in a political victory. (Applause.) They had just elected to the House of Commons their good old highly respected and dearly beloved Mr. Gordon McMinnies. (Applause). EL, joined the active branch , of the party. In 1885 they had another election and they bad the ex-Colonial Secretary, the Missionary of the Empire, to speak for them and he <the speaker) I afterwards declared that that speech had lost them the I election. (Applause). Afterwards he (the Chairman) left Wartington and he did not know that they had ' improved in election matters very much—(a Voice "We will show you")—(laughter)--but they had now an oppor- tunity of reverting back to the glorious time of 1880. (Applause). He referred to the misdeeds of the present Government sad declared his firm adherence in the principles of Free Trade. (Applause.) Mr. Chamber- lain's policy would increase the already heavy taxation which the workia g classes had to bear and instead of ti tending to bind the Empire together would be a source I of constant irritation and be no benefit to the trade of . the country. (Applause.) MR. LLOYD-GEORGE had a preet ovation on rising to address the meeting, the audience risiag and singing "For he's a jolly good fellow." A voice from the gallery exclaimed " Go on lad ! you are not`la Birming- ham now "to which Mr. Lloyd George responded " Oh, 120. The reception was evenivarmer there." (Laughter). Proceeding he said : I have great pleasure in coming here to Warrington to support the candidature of Mr.
Crosfield—(Applause)—and I congratulate the Liberal Association upon having secured the services of so able a champion as Mr. Crostield in this fight. He and I have

A MUTUAL FRIEND, Mr. Broadhurst. (Applause). He is a very fast friend of Mr. Broadhurst's and so am I, and there is one thing I have discovered about Mr. Broadhurst—that he is an excellent judge of human nature, and the best test is that he is my friend. (Laughter.) But lam per- fectly certain that on the whole he is one of the best judges of human nature I know,and he always tells me that his friend Mr. Crosfield is one of the best fellows he ever met. (Hear, hear.) Although I had not had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Crosfield the recommenda- tion of Mr. Broadhurst was quite enough for me, and I am very delighted to come down here to support him. (Applause.) Your chairman has told you that the great missionary from Birmingham—(laughter)—has recently been making another attempt to convert the English heathen. (Laughter.) He has been at it somewhere near Gains- borough. He has not so far made any attempt to con- vert the Welsh pagans. (Laughter and applause.—A Voice: Give him a bit of revival.) I know he needs it badly. (Laughter.) I have no doubt our turn will come. But he is: trying the less hard-hearted first. I observed the moment I came here an inscription up there : "Remember the sugar tax." That is not the place it ought to have been fixed up. You ought to have sent it to Gainsborough (Laughter.) It is Mr. Cham- berlain who ought to remember that, and so far as I can see at all his meetings there is always some person who takes care he doesn't forget it, and sugar has always

div.head: :VIOST IRRITATING EFFECT
div.p: A :VIOST IRRITATING EFFECT

upon him whereas it ought to have the most soothing effect. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain delivered his usual speech at Gainsborough with variations and his text was that things were going very badly. This time it was " for the empire." The empire, he told us, was going to pieces. There was going to be a dissolution of the empire. One thing is pretty clear, that Mr. Balfour would rather have a dissolution of the empire than a dissolution of Parliament. (Loud laughter.) He thinks pnblicly that from a personal point of view that would be serious calamity. (Laighter). No doubt as a shre Ncl observer, he had come to the conclusion that that catastrophe would be a much more ruinous one than the prophecy of Mr. Chamberlain. Now, Mr. Chamberlain is very hard on false prophets. He is the last man who should say these hard things about false prophets because we know no man in politics to prophesy so falsely. (Laughter.) The Chairman has reminded us that one set of prophecies he has made were prophecies about the war. There was first of all, the prediction that there would be no war. That turned out to be absolutely untrue. There was the other pre- diction that the war would be over in three or four months and that it would only cost £10,000,000, and we know that proved to be very untrue. (Hear, hear.) The sugar tax is there to remind us that Mr. Chamber- lain is a false prophet in that respect. These prophecies failed from being too optimistic,so Mr. Chamberlain thinks "I have been too hopeful and I will just take the other tack on the off chance that T may be right." (Laugh- ter). So instead of saying things are going wrong by being too hope ful,he says things are all going wrong.(Laughter). The Empire is going. Tin and steel are going. Cotton is going. Pearl buttons are going. (Loud Laughter). In fact

EVERTTHING 1., GOING BUT THIS GOVERNMENT. (Loud laughter.) This Government won't go. (More laughter.) That is his present mood, He is a prophet of woe. Well I have been trying to look out Mr. Chamberlain's position in history as a prophet. I am not quite sure what prophet •to take as his model. Sometimes I think it is Jeremiah—(laughter)—or Zadkiel—(loud laughter)—because there is something to be said for Jeremiah. That prophet only started his i wailings when he saw the city was n ruins. There was no room then for repentance. It was too late. Mr. Chamberlain is anticipating it. He is telling us in time. Mr. Chamberlain is more opportune than Jeremiah and more hopeful than Zadkiel. He tells you the thing will happen unless—so there is room for repentance in the prophecies according to Joseph Chamberlain. (Laughter.) He is in fact more often the model of the prophet Jonah. Jonah says that in three days unless they improve matters and join the Tariff Reform League (laughter) Nineveh will fall. So Mr. Chamberlain says that unless the Free Trade Nineveh repents every- thing will be going. You know we have not had much time to test the prophecies. He started his new career of Prophet of Woe about eighteen months ago. WelLa prophet must boa poor one if his prophecies won't last out eighteen months. (Laughter.) But Mr. Chamber- lain's have not panned out to that extent. (Laughter) "Your trade is going. You have reached the climax, won't go any higher." And it has gone higher speedily. (Laughter.) Dukes may join the Tariff Reform League, Mr. Balfour may agree with its principles, the Tory party may subscribe to its views, but there is one thine that will not join the Tariff Reform League, and that is the trade of this country. (Applause.) Our exports have increased enormously since Mr. Chamber] A in's speeches. I think we had better keep him going. (Laughter.) If be made a few more speeches our exports would go still higher. He said eighteen months ago "your trade in foreign countries has largely declined." It has gone up 16 millions since then. (Laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain said "although your trade with foreign countries is going down your ' trade with the Colonies is going up I can see." But it has gone down. (Laughter.) What Mr. Chamberlain I said would be down has gone up, what Mr. Thamberlain said would be up has gone down. , So much for Mr. Chamberlain as a prophet. • British prosperity has gone up steadily. Oh ! Traitorous trade ! Trade refuses to think Imperially. (Laughter.) Trade must be a pro-lker. (Great laughter and applause.) Mr. Chamberlain AU indicated clearly what its duty is. He said so IS mcalitbs ago. It was to go down. It won't. It is anti-National.

It is a little Englander. (Much laughter.) That is the view of Mr. Chamberlain. It is true his prophecy is false, but it is because of the perversity of facts. Facts decline to square themselves to the principles. What are you to do in a case of this sort ? It is sheer per- versity. Facts happen to be stubborn things. You

_ CANNOT ALTER FACTS as you can alter the opinions of a newspaper by buying it. (Laughter and applause.) What we have got to deal with is in spite of all these principles enunciated, British trade is steadily going up with foreign coun- tries and trade with the self-governing colonies has dropped down very rapidly. It is only India that has saved our heads there--2lndia being the only Colony that declines to go with Mr. Chamberlain's preferential notion. (Apple/ase.) There is another prophecy of Mr. Chamberlain Which facts in their rude perversity have declined to testify. That is
