div.head: IRON AND STEEL.
div.p: IRON AND STEEL.

Mr. Chamberlain, ai-Vreen;cif-think, nude a speech in which he said on the authority of a Philadelphia paper—(laughter)--I cannot give you a higher authority than that—(laughter)—and pray observe that Mr. Chamberlain is not a man to worry about Blue' Books, documents with the Government stamp on them,—never quotes them,—but the reporter of an American newspaper that nobody ever heard of is the authority upon which you are to reverse the whole fiscal policy of the Empire and to upset its trade for years to come. For my part lam an old-fashioned sort of man. I would rather stick to Government Blue Books and official documents and figures, (Applause.) On the authority of a Philadelphia paper he said "There is going to be a little depression inAmerica." That was a great admission, because America is a Protection- ist country. it is a great admission that there is such a thing as depression in any country that is Protec- tionist. (Hear, hear.) He said there was going to be depression in America, but this is where Protection came in. The moment depression came in the iron and steel trade in America they were not going to close their furnaces. They were going to keep them all going, keep every man working at the furnace.

WHAT WERE THEY GOIRG TO DO WITH THE STEEL? —Dump it here. What would happen, said Mr. Cham- berlain, was that hundreds of thousands of workmen in 1 the iron and steel trade would be thrown out of employment. As a matter of fact there are nat hundreds of thousands of workmen alto- gether in the iron and steel trade. There are just over 100,000 so Mr. Chamberlain said there would be more thrown out than were!engaged in the trade alto gether. That is a mere detail. (Laughter). You should not allow a little detail of that sort to upset a great argument. What happened? Furnaces were closed ; there was a very great depression in America. Tens of thousands of workmen were thrown out of employment. I have no doubt there is a lack of employment here, but not to be compared with America. Our exports in iron and steel last year went down by 21 per cent. In Germany a Protectionist country, they went down 28 per cent.— (Applause). Our imports of iron and steel were less than they were the previous year by about 11,000 tons.l If you take all the industries that depend upon iron and ' steel, the engineering trades, etc., there was not a country in the world where they were so prosperous as in this country.—(Applause). Cotton, of course, was going, and it is going—to China (laughter), the Argentine Republic, and it is going all over the world. So far froui the cotton trade going down,—it is a remarkable story.

div.head: COTTON
div.p: COTTON

is one of those industries which depends almost entirely on the export trade. We produce a little over 100 millions' worth of cotton manufactures in this coun- try. We used to sell about 70 millions abroad—that is —we sold more abroad than we consumed at home There is no country in the world of which you can say this, except this Free Trade country of Great Britain. —(Applause.) But we had reached the meridian, said Mr. Chamberlain. Henceforth we were to be cut out of the markets of the world by some more fortumately situated country. Germany, blessed Germany, with its Kaiser its armies, and its sausages.—(Loud laughter.)—You send these Protectionists to eat them for twelve months. Yon will cure them of tariff reform. (Laughter.) However, these paradises of Protection were going to cut us out. German cotton exports, which were not very high before, went down very substantially last year. What about our story? Since Mr. Chamberlain said cotton was g improvement we have leapt up in our exports—not in the Colonies, these was no there—we have leapt up from 72 millions to 83 millions. (Applause.) Cotton is going. (Laughter . These are some of the prophecies which the false prophet of Birmingham issued. (Laughter.) He has prophesied now that unless we enter into some compact with the colonies, they are going—with cotton—where, 1 don't know. But they are going ,to leave us. Hard hearted parents! Blood is thicker than water, so Mr. ;Chamberlain said, and so it is, but you can make blood too thick. If you infuse a solution of gold into it you make it so thick that it won't circulate for a while. (Applause). Besides that, you may produce blood poisoning. You had better have the blood pure. I DON'T BELIEVE THE COLONIES ARE GOING TO LEAVE

I don't believe the colonies will say "You are giving the same chance to our butter as to Argen- tine butter. You are giving the same price for our beasts as for Argentine beasts. We won't have it. Unless you give a better chance to us we will go." The colonials are not made of that stamp. (Applause.) But, said Mr. Chamberlain," You must give them a share in the Empire or they will go." I don't believe there is any Liberal who objects to giving them every share which is fair in this Empire. What share do they ask for? They have a share in its glory. They have a share in every profit and advantage which come in its trade. If there is any trade advantage in the British Empire it is as open to the Canadian as it is to the Cheshireman. There is no civil service in the Empire he cannot enter which a Britisher can enter. More than that, this Empire costs a bit of money. You can't run it on the cheap. It cost last year to defend it 104 millions. There is not a position in the army or navy which is open to a British subject which is not open equally to a Colonial. They share the advantages, they share the glory. They share the name. There is only one thing left if they want to share all round, and that is to share the burden. (Applause.) if Mr. Chamberlain's Idea is to complete the share,shall you object to it? (Cries of " No.") Would you object to our colonies taking a share which is in pro- portion to their population ? They are 11 millions, we are 42 millions. Their share would be about a fifth. Supposing they took off our shoulders one fifth of the 86 millions we are bearing ; the army is at their dis- posal, the navy defends their shores, and the last great war we LIM, which cost us 25f) millions, was a war to defend a couple of colonies. It was not to defend England. It was not to defend ,Vales, (Laughter.) We don't want it. We can defend ourselves—(renewed laughter)—and against Chinamen too. (Loud laughter.) It was a war to defend two colonies—British colonies. The British tax payer spent all the money upon it. The oontribotion of the colonies was not worth noting. It amounted to hundreds at the most. I am not going to

div.head: _TAUNT THE COLONIES
div.p: _TAUNT THE COLONIES

but if Mr. Chamberlain talks as if we were doing wrong to our colonies as he does, let us hear the facts in mind. (Applause). Their troops came to help us. But what do you think was paid to the poor British Tommy —ls. a day, but we paid to the colonials out of our own pockets ss. a day. Where was the justice to colonies ? (Hear, hear.) But don't forget the complaint does not come from them. • The complaint comes from Birming- ham. (Laughter.) Mr. Cobden according to Mr. Chamberlain was a crabbed little man,aLittle'Englander Mr. Chamberlain is the man with an Imperial mind. There he looks with his eagle eye from his perch in Birmingham surveying the whole Empire. (Laughter). Mr. Chamberlain says" Look at Canada." Canada has given us preference, and what is thes result of that preference ? Since that preference ha been given our trade with Canada has leapt up by 4% millions. A very clever letter by Mr. McKenna, M.P., inithe " Times" showed that during that time the trade with the U.S.A. hadgone up 10 millions. The U.S.A. has had no preference, and yet its trade has increased more than double. Of course it has nothing to do with preference. It was purely because the U.S.A. is Canada's nearest neighbour. But while we are selling Canada £12,000,000 worth of manufactured goods we are selling the U.S.A. £41,000,000 worth of manufactured goods every year. The fact that we buy so much from other countries makes them buy from us.

div.head: LET US LOOK AT THE FIGURES
div.p: LET US LOOK AT THE FIGURES

_ which Mr. Chamberlain gives. He says there are £30,000,000 worth of goods which come from foreign nations to our colonies. Why can't we supply these goods? If we enter into a bargain with the colonies we will collar all that £30,000,000. Ail! I have got a number of blue books which Mr. Chamberlain shuns as if they were sugar. (Laughter.) I have gone through these blue books to find out what was the trade in manufac- tured goods with the world, leaving out that in the Colonies. I find that it amounts to .C 420,000,000. We are all competing for that huge custom. We have Germany, France, U.S.A., Japan and other counties com- peting with us and Mr. Chamberlain says" don't worry about that but secure the 30 millions."( Loud laughter). And how much do you think we got of the £420,000,000? Remember that we are the smallest country among the big manufacturing countries of the world and yet we have secured of tbat trade over one-third. Over one-third, and yet they talk about Free-Trade handicapping us—as if it was ruining us. Take the Argentine Republic. It buys from us more than from Germany. France and the U.S.A. put together. (Applause.) Mr.Cllmberiain said at Gains- borough" Put a little tax on flour and a little tax on fruit and nobody will feel it." (Laughter.) What a clever man he is ! He is going to give a little profit to I Canada. He will give a little profit to the farmer, and he is of course going to give a little profit to Dukes. 1 (Laughter.) There must boa little putting up of rent. ' All these little profits are to be put together. Then it is turned over to the miller. Surely he must get just a little. (Laughter.) Who is going to pay? Your loaf is going to be just as cheap. Flour will be dearer but the loaf will be just as cheap. (Laughter.) The grain will be dearer and everybody is going to make some- thing out of it. WHO IS TO PAY? The Baker ! (Laughter). Well, bakers of Warrington, bear this in mind next election. (Applause). All these

things are going to happen. That is Mr. Chamberlain's theory of protection. He is going to put a little on just to help the Canadian, the Australian, and the New Zealander, who sends us frozen mutton to London and sells it as Welsh mutton. (Loud Laughter). Then he is going to put something on fruits. Who is it going to hit? The United States of America and the Agriculture Republic ? The United States buys three times as much from us as does Canada and we carry in our ships more than half of the American trade And of course we don't carry for nothing. Are you going to quarrel with a good customer like that just for the chance of getting a monopoly of a trade of 30 millions? Are you going to quarrel with a trade of four times thirty millions ? That is not busi- ness. It is insanity. (Applause.) The Argen- tine Republic is a good customer of ours. We have got all the great enterprizes in the Argentine— railways, gas works, water works, docks—all in British hands. There is nothing German except a shoddy sew- ing machine or two. (Laughter.) The Argentineer is beginning to find British goods, although not of the same shining polish, last better than others. (Ap- plause.) Our trade is going up there, and to-day we beat the German, the American. and the French all put together. It is one of the richest countries of the ' world unlimited in its resources. There is no knowing what will become of the Argentine and are we so insane as to quarrel with an excellent customer? We help with our capital, but they help us with the trade ; and the only thing they send us in return is about the best wheat in the world. (Hear, hear.) Why should not we receive it? hear.)

div.head: IVIIAT-RAPPED LAST YEAR ?
div.p: IVIIAT-RAPPED LAST YEAR ?

There was a failure in Canadian and American Wheat and they could not send us within millions of tons the corn we wanted. What would have happened if you had had your preferential tariffs and the trade of foreign countries had begun to go into other countries? We have established a market here. This is the market for corn and we get the best of everything from every land. (Applause.) Freedom is a good master. He pays well, he feeds well, he clothes well, he treats his servants well. Slavery is a bad master. _ . DON'T CHCHAINYOUR TRADE.

don't put your commerce in bonds. Cobden and Bright shattered them. See that you walk freely throughout the world. (Prolonged applause.) Last year during the wheat failure in Canada and America, the Argentine sent us a bigger crop than ever sent us before. Russia sent us a bigger crop than ever. Once you lock up the wheat crops of the world, a blight would bring starvation to us in England. Now if there is a blight in Canada i there is sun n Argentina. It is never cloudy all over the world. Providence is kinder. (Applause.) Don't meddle with it. (Applause.) T have here not a pamphlet of the Cobden Club, but a book printed by the King's printers. There is nothing biassed here against tariff reform. TAKE OUR SHIPPING. Mr. Chamberlain never mentions it if he can help it. Look at last year. T want to give you these figures. They are most marvellous. The book gives the tonnage of the shipping carried to and from every port in the world. Ninety millions of tons were carried in ships to every country, last year,and from every country. That is a huge quantity. Who carried it ? Where did this miserable little Free Trade country come in? (Laughter). Out of the total tonnage carried to every part of theworld,the British flag floated over 60 millions out of the 90 millions. (Applause). Ah, but there is ' Germany beating us of course. Creeping up, at any rate, rapidly. German shipping, of course, is beginning to beat as. Is it? Where is it beginning? (Laughter) Germany, with all its boasts, with its subsidies, with its low wages for seamen—What did Germany do? Out of the total Germany carried 4,600,000 tons.—(Laughter). But there is America with its scientific tariff. Surely it has got near us ? It got pretty near us once, but that was when the United States were Free Trade and we were Protectionist. Since then it has listened to its Chamberlains. It has fabricated scientific tariffs. There is no more able seaman, there is no more intelligent nor ,skilful race than the American. Where are they? They carried last year out of the total, including their own, only half a million. (Laughter and applause.) We, this country, in a state of decline—(laughter)—rapid consumption—(laughter) of foreign goods—(laughter),—who are going down headlong, nothing for us to do. According to Mr. Chamberlain we shall all be millionaires, with nothing to do, in a very short time. We carried

SIXTY DirmioNs OF THE TRADE OF THE wrorao (loud applause). The United States of America carried half a million. How many times half a million is sixty millions? It used to be 120 millions when I was at scnool but since the Education Act (the sentence was not concluded owing to an to an outburst of applause)-120 times—by so much is Free Trade better than Protection. (Applause.) I have been reading the blue books. There is no novel half as romantic. (Hear, hear.) I tell you that in all seriousness. Carla() said that Englishmen can do great deeds but they cannot describe them. Ah, well, that is not a bad quality in a race. (Applause). Look at this (producing a blue book., I read it and I see long lists. I see a list here of shipping, and' see a list of countries to which it goes. I see great blanks here, where the ships of certain nations never go. But look at Britain; there is not a country where I do not see huge black figures of British ships. (Applause). What you want isa magniflying glass. Throw this on a canvas, see the dense black list of British ships that enter every port, and see the blanks to foreign vessels. What is in that ? It is a great story. LoDk at at all thed earth, China, Japan, the remotest little republics in America, you will find the British mer- chant going there. He is not a pushing chap. He does not send commercial traveller who talks Brazilian and every ling. under the sun as if he was a missionary. (Laughter.) He goes there and talks English to a man who does'nt understand it— (laughter)—and produces an article, and says" If you want it take it. If you don't I will put it in nay pocket."—(Laughter). Ho goes there with his own goods; he meets the foreigner armed with scientific tariffs everywhere, and the British merchant comes with nothing but freedom, and it beats them in every market in the world.—(Applause).
TT IS -A.-6REAT'sTORY.

It is the story of- a-little island in 'ibis seas. It is a romance. I wish it could be written in the language that befits it, not in the language of blue books. A little imagination, and you can write it on your brain. One little island in the seas—that is how it would begin. A little island—one thirtieth the size of America, one half the population of the United States. It is not to be compared in magnitude to Germany or any of those great countries, and yet its ships cover the ocean, and fill every port. They build barriers of tariffs and tolls against them. They ride over them all on the crest of the wave and the end of it is, simply because you have got freedom at the prow, Britain wins and as long as it will stand for this great prin- ciple it will win for itself everlasting renown in the history of nations. (Loud and prolonged applause). THE RESOLUTION,

Mr C. E. PA RICE.Ti—E110;0;"1 ;:i1;11-t- this meeting con- siders that the present Government has forfeited all claim to the confidence of the country for the following amongst other reasons :--:Because it has passed an Education Act which, while placing practically the whole cost of Education upon the people, denies the right of the people to effectual control; has done its best to block the way of honest and reasonable Tem- perance Reform, has encouraged a system of Alien Labour in Sonth Africa under conditions which conflict with the, traditional principles of English liberty and especially because it has thrown the country into a state of agitation and confusion, by its conflicting and reactionary fiscal proposals. This meeting therefore calls upon the government to resign in order that the country may. by a decisive verdict, put an end to this fiscal agitation and unrest."- At the outset he alluded to the Sugar Convention, pointing out that it shut out from our country the sugar of Russia and Argentine which would have done much to save us from the effects of the short crop elsewhere. Continuing he referred to the great change of feeling which had come over the country of late years. Five years ago he did not believe the Liberal Association of Warrington would have had courage to ask Mr. Lloyd George to come and speak to them in Warrington (Laughter and applause). At, the time of the war there was scarcely a meeting attended by Mr. Lloyd George at which a great many of our countrymen did not try to howl him down ("Aame"). He (Mr. Parker) admitted that he was one of those who thought at the time that the war was a painful necessity. The information which had come to us gradually and slowly had gone a very long wsy to undermine the opinion which many Liberals held at that time. (Hear, hear). The forward movement in a nation's progress, continued Mr. Parker, was subject to periods of strenuous advancement, ever followed by periods of pause, inaction, and at times distinct retro- gression. Vhen the great Liberal statesmen of the last century, men like Bright and Gladstone, who thro' many decades ever held the honour of England high, when i these passed out of the activities of the nation's life, there appeared to creen over the pro- gressive forces a torpor, a lassitude. (Hear, bear.) Great ideals were no longer cherished, watchwords such as Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform ceased to thrill, and were looked upon as worn-out shibboleths. Peace gave place to war, and a hunger for extended dominion; Retrenchment to extravagant expenditure, and costly expeditions ; and Reform was hustled out of the way by $ truculent and sordid foreign policy. (Applause.) This spirit invaded every phase of the national life, the people were hypnotized by it, Statesmen were controlled by it, poets sang of it. They should recall the well- known words of Kipling : " God of our fathers, known of old, Lord of our far-flung battle line, Beneath whose awful hand we hold Dominion over palm and pine, Lord God of Hosts be with us yet, Lest we forget, Lest we forget." These were strong thoughts in a strong setting, but in all soberness he asked them if that dominion over those races that dwell beneath the northern pine and southern palm, and those who had their homes and unhappily many of them their graves upon the African veldt— if that dominion which Kipling sang of as a gift from heaven was gained by raid, misrepresentation, and slaughter—if that dominion was followed as in the case of South Africa by the institution of conditions of labour, which conflicted with all the cherished and hard won tradition of English liberty and personal freedom —then he said this appeal to the "God of our fathers"

div.p: to forward and favour the British cause was a mockery. (Applause,) Happily the spirit of freedom of reform which vitalized the nation during the early Victorian ern was not dead, but only asleep. There were signs that the nation was awakening as from a troubled night- mare, was casting off its lethargy, and once more girding itself to further advance along the same paths of national progress. (Hear, hear and minimise). in contrast with the florid appeals which Kipling made to heaven about what he conceived to be our Imperial destiny, he would quote the words of a sane but no less patriotic writer. One whom he sup- posed would be called the poet of the little Englanders, William Watson sang:— Friends 0,11 me what you will; no iot care I that shall stand for England till I die. The England from whose side I have not swerved. The immortal England whom I too have served Accounting her all livine lands above In justice and in mercy and in love. (Applause.) However able their leaders might be, they were Powerless unless supported and sustained by a loya, band of followers recruited from all parts of the country and in the coming conflict theirs was the part by strenuous work, and enthusiastic support to rally round the one who in our local fight would be the man to carry the flag and might it be to victory. (Loud applause.) Mr. Cnospixf,p,who hada splendid reception, alluded to the great pleasure one felt at seeing in the chair so good a friend of Liberalism in Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. Frank Roberts was an old friend of his father's,and was a personal friend of many of them there that night. To deal with the shortcomings and misdemeanours of the Government and the manifold follies of Protection in the space of ten minutes seemed to him a task as difficult As Mr. Balfour's attempt to explain his views on the Fiscal Question on two sides of a sheet of note- paper. Whether he succeeded, or whether he simply skated, very skilfully and delicately over very thin ice without attempting to cut anything like a distinct figure was a question about which some of them have not a shadow of doubt. Mr. Balfour was an adept, and showed great agility in that nicely balanced art. (Applause.) But unfortunately it was not only his opponents who were mystified. There was a dignified protest on Thursday night in Liverpool by Lord Balfour of Burleigh, and even his own special supporters in the press were just as much at sea as they are—excepting perhaps the "Morning Post" which said it daren't add to or subtract anything from the Prime Minister's fabric lest it should all tumble to the ground like a house of cards. (Hear, hear.) But putting aside the played out attempts that were made to mystify opinion, he would venture to put on a quarter of a sheet of paper questions which he had asked at greater length in the press here, but with never an answer to them that would hold water :—"Do you increase the wealth of an individual by adding to the all round cost of his living? if not are you more likely to do so in the case of a nation? If you increase the cost of living you reduce the purchasing power of wages throughout our home market, which is seven or eight times larger than our export market. And if you reduce the consumption that way you reduce trade and the demand for labour. Very well :ken, are workingmen under those conditions going to believe the promise of higher wages held out to them ?"—The answer England was giving was pretty emphatic all over the country, and would be most em- phatic of all when the time came in Lancashire. (Loud Applause). And Mr. Balfour knew this well. He knew that the country would never assent to Mr. Chamberlain's reckless, and "crude "proposals, and so he sought to tide over bad times with a little bit of' skilful legerdemain when he referred to the fiscal con- troversy. And then he tried to carry the war into our quarters and charged us with having nothing but a negative policy. (Laughter). Our policy was the very opposite. (Hear, hear). There never was a time when more serious and earnest and positive work was needed by the Progressive Party. We meant to go forward,but we meant also to take care that before taking a step forward we did not take a step backward. He said "more" advisedly, because in the last eight or ten years in some ways we had gone back a great deal: in wild cat schemes of adventure, in reck- less extravagance which had squandered the National resources and increased taxation, and in that kind of political dissipation which made the " Jingo Rake's Progress." (Loud applause.) In all these things we hat' lost ground and the time had come to put an end to it. That was the first thing to do And then as to our positive policy, there were many things waiting. He should only allude to one, and that was surely at the very root of what Carlyle used to speak of as the ‘' Condition of England b question. Many things to day demanded the attention of every man who really loved his country and hoped to see it, advance in prosperity of its people and its power as a civilising force in the world. But of all things surely the most crying need was to get rid of our centres of depravity and stagnant misery. (Hear, hear.) How else would they steadily and surely cure the worst com- plaint of our nation,excessive drinking ? Did not misery and drunkenness, like squalor and disease go hand in hand? Better housing and less drunkenness would raise the stamina and well-being of the nation more than anything else. But they could never deal effec- tively either with the one or the other till they had grappled with that great fundamental question the taxation of land values. (Applause.) Do that and the rest followed. Without it they would but fence and skirmish with this great and urgent question, the hous- ing of the poor on which the health and strength and welfare of our race so vitally depended. And if they said that our energy and endeavour in the matter would be frittered away because the House of Lords would never let us get to work in good earnest, then it was plain that they must reform that House at the same time. (Applause.) Housing, Education, Temperance, the question of Chinese Slavery, of Trade Union Law, and last but far from least, that Army Reform and strengthening and better equipment of our auxilialy forces which was so vitally important, were it only that we might check the frightful rate of increased expenditure on our Army and Navy, though there were other paramount reasons for it—Nl ere these things not a positive policy? (Applause.) Yes, but they were more than that. They were a gospel of justice, and he would say, of mercy to those dumb millions who had yet to be lifted out of their wretched social quagmire (Applause.) It was a great task which lay before us in our work for social reform. And if there were obstacles and financial diffi- culties in the way it ill became Mr. Balfour to taunt us with these difficulties which he had been the very man in large measure to create. But we did not fear such difficulties. The steady trend of public opinion was with us and would enable us to overcome them. (Hear, hear.) And so we might go forward with prudence and resolution determined to do our best to support these great causes, so that each of as in our own sphere of action might help to swell that great tide of new hope, effort and energy, on the force and set of whose currents so largely depended the prosperous voyaging of humanity. (Loud applause.) The resolution was put to the meeting and carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: -ATR7-1.-I.OYD GEORGE THANKED.
div.p: -ATR7-1.-I.OYD GEORGE THANKED.

The REV. H. DUNNICO said it was one of the proudest moments of his life to propose a vote of thanks to Mr. Lloyd George for the instructive and eloquent address he had just given. He thought it was most appropriate that he should move that resolution. Mr. Lloyd George was a Welshman. So was he (laughter). Mr. Lloyd George was a Baptist deacon. He was a Baptist minister, so that they could not have had a better speaker and a better man to propose that motion. (laughter). Mr. DtiNNlco went on to speak of the Progressive Labour League, which be said, was the genuine league of workingmen and they were determined to return Mr. Crosfield to Parliament.

COUNCILLOR BURTON seconded- the motion, which was heartily carried. MR. LLOYD GEORGE, who was greated by a member of the audience with the exclamation "R. A. Naylor's opponent," said he simply rose to acknowledge the hearty vote of thanks they had been good enough to pass. He felt he was already rewarded. He had actually received promotion since he had appeared on the platform at the hands of one of his countrymen. He was a humble member of a Baptist congregation and Mr. Dunnico had made him a deacon on the spot.— (Laughter). He earnestly entreated the Warrington electors to set to work and return such an excellent candidate as they possessed in Mr. Crosfield, who would be an acquisition in the House of Commons, as he expressed his ideas so clearly and concisely. His presence would be of enormous advantage to the younger section of the party. It would be a source of great oy to many members who knew Mr. Crosfleld to see him win a great victory at the next general election. —(Applause). VOTE OF THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN. ALDERMAN PIERPoLST proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and alluding to the candidature of Mr. Naylor, 116 Said he wondered however he had thought of contesting the seat against Mr. Lloyd-George. As they said in Lancashire he had "taken on a job," (Hear hear, and laughter). Counitton Er,r,tsoN seconded. In response to calls, Mr. HENRY ROBERTS sup- ported the vote of thanks. He expressed his thanks to the audience and said that he had received adequate compensation for the trials through which he had gone during the last few years. He felt he could no longer remain outside the ranks of the Liberal party (applause), and he could not resist the temptation of listening to his most eloquent country- man, Mr. Lloyd George. (Applause). He intended to to do his utmost to promote the interests of the party and put his shoulder to the wheel and help to return his friend and colleague Mr. Arthur Crosfleld. The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. F. A. Roberts briefly replied. The meeting closed with the singing of the National Anther, .

div.head: Sudden Death in Church-street.
div.p: Sudden Death in Church-street.

A painful incident occurred in Church-street on Sunday night. Mrs. Hart, wife of Mr. William Hart, who resides at 33, Helsby-street, was walking down the street at about eight o'clock when she fell and died before any assistance could be procured. Her husband, it is stated, was attending the service at the Parish Church at the time.

div.head: TRADE UNIONS. Their History and Present Legal Position.
div.p: TRADE UNIONS. Their History and Present Legal Position.
INTERESTING LECTURE.

"Trade unionism" was the subject of the second of a course of University Extension lectures on "Social questions" which was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Thursday evening by Mr. S. J. Chapman, M.A. (professor of political economy and dean of the faculty of commerce in the University of Man- chester). There was only a small attendance—a fact which occasioned an expression of regret from Coun- cillor J. Fulton Smith who presided. The question of trade unions, he said, was one which was coming very much to the front at the present day and he was sure they would all be very pleased to hear something of the history of those wonderful organizations which were such a force in the country. The LECTURF.R said the field before them for examination that evening was a vast one and therefore he could not hope to do much more than glance at it very cursorily. He concluded the first lecture by describing the beginnings of workmen's combinations in this country. These combinations were formed by the people who found their callings had been taken away from them by the changes which came with the industrial revolution. The first demand was for a move- ment back to the old state of affairs, but that demand gradually disappeared and they came face to face with trade unionism proper. It was in the first ten or twenty years of the nineteenth century that trade unions as a combination of operatives against the masters appeared. At first they were closely associated with the friendly societies, but they gradu- ally dissociated themselves from those organizations and became independent. The trade unions of distinct trades very soon merged into general labour movements and the reason of that no doubt was that the trade union in the one trade felt itself powerless when opposed to the new capitalists. The first general trade union of any force was the union established in this county in 1830 with the title of" The national society for the protection of labour." Even this strong federation was not strong enough to cope with the masters combinations which were forming themselves on the other side, because it must be remembered that it was an undoubted fact that the movement in the direction of combination was not confined to the workpeople but took place on both sides. It was no doubt this non-success, united with the dissatisfaction at the new state of affairs brought about by the indus- trial revolution.which merged the early trade unions in socialism and they found in the middle thirties that trade unionism was almost completely swallowed up in the socialism that was connected with the name of Robert Owen who established the general trade union federation of all the trade unions of the country. That union also failed and from its embers Chartism appeared. Many of the early leaders of the movement were fol- lowers of Robert Owen and they came to the conclusion that Owen's schemes were too large to be brought about suddenly : they must be accomplished by political action. Chartism had an ancestor in the Radical move- ment which appeared in the country shortly after the French revolution and caused a great deal of excitement while it lasted. Chartism was a failure that was not altogether a failure. because many of the aims of the Chartists had been realized since. It was, however, a failure regarded from the achievements of that time. Then came a period of quiescence and in that period trade unionism in its modern form, unrevolutionary, sane, serious, confining its operations to its particular trade and accepting the new order of things, emerged. The most interesting part of the lecture was that which dealt with the state of the law relating to trade unionism. Between 1791 and 1801 saw the passage of extreme repressive laws directed against all combinations which naturally emerged from the industrial revolution. They were removed partly as the outcome of agita- tions among the working classes, but more particularly as the result of the very clever wire pulling of a tailor named Francis Place. It was in Place's back shop that the evidence was prepared which led to the repeal of the trade union laws. Trade unions'at that time had no legal personality • they were not recognized by the !law ; they could note pro- perty and they could not sue in a court of law. On the combination laws being repealed, the country had a troubled time. Unionism appeared all over the country and strikes broke out in every county. Those who had secured the removal of the combination laws expected that trade unions would disappear, but that did not happen. The Government was so frightened at the turn of events that another committee was hastily appointed, the intention of the Govern- ment being to reinforce the combination laws. The working classes were so excited at the mere suggestion that the Government was convinced that the laws were gone for good and their reimposition might moan nothing less than a revolution. The immediate amend- ment of the law was only slight, but in the sixties the demand for legal recognition and improved status on the part of the unions led to the opening of a third commission on combinations. Legislation favourable to trade unions followed. On the one hand the Govern- ment decided to give to trade unions the right to sue, but an exemption from being sued. It gave the trade unions control over their funds, because it gave them the power to sue defaulting officials, and it spared them from the constant trouble of actions that might I have been brought against them by employers. That Act was passed in 1867. iThat he had described was obviously the intention of the Government and it was thought until a few years ago that that was the law. As a matter of fact it appeared that it was not and that through a fault in draughts- manship the Government. although it intended to give those powers to trade unions, had never really given them and for over thirty years we had been mistaken in what the law was. The Act of 1875 apparently gave trade unions a right to "picket" and to pursue their interests by combined action. The points now to be considered were (I) whether a trade union can be sued; (2) what is legal picketing? (3) what mayacombination do? The last question did not arise until after the Taff Vale decision for the very good reason that it was supposed a trade union could not be sued. The effect of the Taff Vale decision was that a trade union might be sued for damages and could not escape by failing to register, because the House of Lords held that even in the case of an unregistered union damages could be obtained by bringing an action against certain qf the officials. That was certainly con- trary to the intention of the Government in 1867. (Hear, hear.) In regard to picketing it was thought that by the Act of 1875 a trade union could post pickets, provided they did not proceed to acts of violence. They were not allowed to watch or beset but they were allowed to stand about the entrance to a works to give and receive information. The question had recently arisen, "Is persuading watching and besetting, or is it attending to give and receive infor- mation ? " It had been decided by the Court of Appeal that persuading was illegal, and constituted a case for action for damages. The question of what a combina- tion might do was exceedingly intricate. In a very famous decision relating to a shipping ring it had been decided that a combination might do anything which was not illegal in itself in pursuit of its own interest, providing that its action was determined entirely by its interest. If it incidentally damaged other people that was not to be laid to its charge, providing that the damage to the other person was incidental only. Three cases on that point had gone against trade unions and a commission was sitting to consider the matter. The law relating to combina- tion would be altered ; there was no doubt about that. There was confusion even among distinguished lawyers as to what a trade union might and might not do at the present time. Trade unionists as a whole wanted the state of affairs that existed prior to the Taff Vale decision to be restored while other people wanted trade unions to be incorporated. With a modification of the law relating to combination, the incorporation of trade unions would not be so undesirable as it at flist appeared. It would, however. be very undesirable in the present state of the law. It certainly seemed to him to be more desirable that a trade union should be incorporated than t that its legal position should be as it was to-day. It was a more difficult question as to whether it was better to be incorporated or to be in the position in which the Government intended to place trade unions in 1867. The lecturer concluded by giving interesting descriptions of the state of organized labour in France and Germany. Questions having been invited, Mr. W. HAIGH asked what the lecturer's personal opinion was regarding the recent decisions. The LECTURER said he was not a lawyer so he could not answer the question. He was informed that accord- ing to the drafting of the Bill the decision was right. If anyone was to blame it was the man who drafted the Bill. Mr. NIGHTINGALE said the surprising feature was that the deciSion had been come to at such a late period. It was the determination of trade unionists to change the law by changing the law-makers. The Lecturer was asked if he thought there was a possibility of Germany taking the premier position with regard to trade unions. The LECTURER : Very far from it. Trade unionism in Germany is merely an infant as compared with trade unionism here. Mr. NIGHTINGALE asked if conscription would pre- vent workingmen's combinations in Germany. Ile believed one reason we were so far ahead of Germany in regard to trade unions was because we had more liberty. Mr. S. WRIGHT asked if the labour movement had raised the social standing of the community in England. • The LECTURER : I think there is no doubt about that. This country is in a Very happy state because the labour movement got on trade union lines instead of Socialistic and revolutionary lines. (Hear, hear.) The subject of the next lecture on Friday, February 17th will be" Methods of settling disputes."

A specimen of a coreless apple has arrived in this country from America, and was despatched from Covent Garden to the King. A first quarto 'edition of Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus ' has been purchased in London for £2,600, and its destination is believed to be America.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITORr
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITORr

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENT. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases sent their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matters intended for publication must be written on sitleonly 2„ the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday.

Lectures on " Social Questions."' Sir,—.The manifest industrial interest in Warrington and elsewhere mainly arising out of a dissatisfied state of the workmen's mind would surely lead one to suppose that this interest is paramount, and far exceeding all others, in importance. Warrington is by no means lacking in its Labour representatives, as witnessed in our local press from week to week. I hear meetings are held very frequently. Judge, then, of ray surprise, when attending the above lectures given by a recog- nized authority, to find a mere handful of an audience, mainly composed of men and women, who are not directly associated with the labour movement, but whose interest goes without saying. This leads one to ask "Where are our labour men and workingmen gener- ally "! The Education Committee have generously laid before them a lecturer of high standing, and a series of lectures dealing with the most vital questions of labour and yet scarcely a half-dozen workingmen are present. It cannot be said that the lectures have not been freely advertised. Let me plead with the workingmen of this town to attend and give an intelligent hearing to one who can and will help them towards the solving of their diffi- culties. With thanks for insertion of my letter.—Yours truly, G. H. WALKER. Warrington. Mr. Pierpoint, MP., and the Sugar Convention. Si r,—l was very pleased to see in your last Saturday's issue that Mr. Parker had taken up the statement made by Mr. Pierpoint on the Sugar Convention, but even Mr. Parker has not dealt with the question as deeply and as fully as it deserves. This is one of those ques- tions upon which the man in the street is easily gulled and led away by such statements as was made by our Borough Member, especially when he does not take the trouble to look up the facts of the matter. Sugar is going" said Mr. Chamberlain at Greenock last autumn, but how does this fall in with Mr. Pier- point's statement that the rise in price of sugar is only temporary? Certainly,one of the greatest of our indus- tries is brought to the verge of ruin by the criminal folly of that Government which our Borough Member supports, and of which Mr. Chamberlain is the evil genius. There are in the Britith West Indies a few wealthy sugar planters, noted amongst other things for their insatiable greed. These gentlemen made the very important discovery (to them) ti,-' s '-:c was too cheap. Cheap sugar is good for the Britis4 nuinufacturer and working man. but "bad "for the West Indian sugar- planter. On behalf of the "distressed " planters an appeal was made to our Government to take steps to raise the price of sugar. Joseph inclined a willing ear and the result wasa tax on sugar, followed soon after by the now famous Sugar Convention, by which the British Government undertook to exclude sugar impor- ted from Russia and the Argentine Republic. When anyone ventured to express the opinion that this attempt to enrich half-a-dozen persons in the West Indies would have the effect of beggaring thousands in. the United Kingdom, they were denounced as "Little Englanders" and told to" think Imperially." What has been the result of these clumsy experi- ments, that our Tariff Reform friends call " scientific taxation" ? It has been fraught with disastrous con- sequences as far as the confectionery and kindred trades are concerned. Sugar is indeed "going," nay it has almost gone. The first move in this clever game to benefit the few at the expense of the many was made in 1900 when the sugar tax was imposed. Since that year the price of sugar has risen from lls. 9A to 20s. 43d. per cwt. Here are the actual figures showing the wholesale prices : s. d. July 1900 to April 1901 April to June 1901 1901-1902 1902-1903 1903-1901 Present price 2O 4f In home markets our manufacturers are unable to compete with their foreign rivals who are able to ob- tain cheaper sugar. All over the country works are being closed and workmen are being discharged almost daily. One auctioneer asserts that he 'has sold up, in London nlone, six large manufacturing con- cerns employing over a thousand hands, and that it is now impossible to sell a confectionery business as a going concern. In London, out of 100,000 engaged in the sugar trade as a raw material, 12,000 have been dis- charged 50,000 are on short time, and this was, at what should be the busiest time of the year. This is the price we are called upon to pay for our folly in allow- ing ourselves to be duped by designing politicians who comniand us to "think imperially" and talk glibly of "scientific taxation." In our anxiecy to tax the foreigner, we have only succeeded in taxing ourselves, Yours respectfully, OSWALD BUCKLEY, Sec., L.R.C. The Late Mr. Percy Randall. In the course of his sermon on Sunday morning, the Vicar of Holy Trinity (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) briefly alluded to the sudden death of the late organist of the church, Mr. Percy Randall. They were all, he said, more or less mourners on that occasion,saddened by the recollection that one who was amongst them on Sunday last had been so suddenly called away by the mysterious visitation from God. It was indeed, an'overwhelming instance of that mysterious Provi. deuce which ordered their lives. It was in an occurrence like this that their faith found its hardest trial. They must submit to what God appointed, feeling sure that love was not wanting on His part. The Rev. T. W. Barber, who as curate preached his final sermon the same morning at St. Paul's Church, also alluded to the deceased gentleman, whom he had known personally during his curacy at Holy Trinity. Warrington people in general, and Church people in particular, had, he said, seen how uncertain the tenure of life was on earth. One who had for years led ths services in God's sanctuary had been suddenly removed. Though not a member of St. Pa al's con- gregation he (the preacher) felt it his personal duty to voice the sympathy which all who had come in con- tact with him felt for the bereaved family. He was ever ready, especially when the cause was a good and • noble one, to give his assistance, and he was certain there were few who could deny that such a life as his cut off so suddenly, and seemingly without prepara- tion, so-called, had not been lived in vain, and would at the last great day receive a righteous reward.

The Street Crying of Newspapers. On Monday evening a meeting of the Warrington and District: Newsagents' Association was held at the headquarters, 3, Scotland-road, some 20 newsagents being present. Mr. A. Downes, president, occupied the chair. Strong remarks were made concerning th& manner in which some publishers supplied back num- bers of novels, periodicals, &c. to outsiders, allowing them to sell at a considerably less price than the newsagents could buy them for, and a resolution was passed that those publishers should be approached on the subject. It was further proposed that a subscription list be opened, so as to enable the newsagent to have one complete day's holi- day in the summer, and to have a social outing. A letter was read from the Chief Constable regarding the street sale and crying of newspapers by boys on Sundays. In the course of his report, the Secretary- pointed out the very great disadvantage that news- agents who paid rates and taxes were being placed at through boys constantly standing opposite their shops and crying papers, and when told to move were insolent. However, he was pleased to say that any cases of obstruction in this manner were to be stopped, and by the combined efforts of the news- agents, assisted by the polir.e, he felt sure that greater benefits would be felt in a short time. The Chief Constable, in the course of his letter, said that street crying' of newspapers was very much depre- cated, and that any cause of complaint would be dealt with by him.

Junior Conservative Ball. Last evening the annual ball in connection with the. Junior Conservative Association was held in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club, Sankey. street, about 200 persons being present. Music was supplied by the band which the late Mr. Percy Randall formerly conducted, and the duties of M.C's were discharged by Messrs. Draper,Mather,Sme thurst,. and Houghton. The room had been decorated by Mr. Ralph Johnson.

strength animated his frame, he opened toe eyes and looked around him—then he uttered a laugh. 66 It is time for the Pussy-call," he said, " How queer that I should have forgotten. Little Vic- toria will wonder ; well never mind, Victoria, ! better late than never." He half raised himself on his pillow, and form- ing his lips into an ' o,' he began to make the queer purring sound of a large cat. This curious noise had nut continued more than half a minute, before there came a rustling from under the berth, and the next instant, to my horror, a little white face, and a dirty white frock appeared in view, and a baby girl, clasping a broken doll in her arms, looked straight into the ghastly face of Stirling. " I'se come, Beauty Dear," said little Victoria. 6' Pussy's come; take I in your arms, Beauty Dear, 'cause Pse so tired." Before I could prevent him, the man leapt forward, snatched at the baby, got her into his arms, and pressed her to his heart. 'Stay close to Beauty Dear, little Vic," he said. " Send Beauty Dear to sleep." - "Hash, hush, Beauty Dear. Go sound as'eep," said little Victoria. But with that last embrace, and those last words, Stirling's spirit departed. It was with some difficulty I could take the child from his arms. Wonderful to relate, the poor baby meter took the plague. We readied Malta the next morn- ing. Owing to quarantine laws, no one could come on board, and Victoria's mother could only be teen on the neighbouring quay. But all in good time the little girl, well and hearty, was pressed in the loving arms of Mrs. Angelo. When this took place the child looked very solemnly at her mother. " Beauty Dear ;Weep. SECOND DIVISIoN, I WARRINGTON CENTRAL V. ST. MARY'S RESERVE. I This match was played on the ground of the first- named team on Saturday. After very vigorous and even play Allen scored the home team's first goal. By good combination the visitors got .to the other end but the home backs proved sound. Play continued in the home quarters, until Central got away again, and the ball was shot over the "Saints" cross-bar. Central ' were awarded a foul, but the kick proved abortive. Half-time : Central, one goal; St. Mary's, nil. Turning round. Central attacked and Brown scored the second goal from a penalty. Milton added the third, the game ending with the score : Central, three goals ; St. Mary's Reserve, nil. WARRINGTON AI,RIONS V. ST. BARNABAS. Played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and was keenly contested. A rush on the home goal led by Jump ended in Harrison scoring. After this the Albions broke away and were nearly scoring, but Whitfield was robbed. Another bit of clever combination by the visiting forwards was spoiled by Jones fouling a player After the kick the Saints forwards combined and pass- ing the home backs, succeeded in beating Hall with a good shot. Half-time score : St. Barnabas, two goals Albions, nil. On the restart the Albions at once forced the visitors to their own goal and kept them on the defensive. Whitfield and Dutton combined well and easily beat Tilley.lllThe Saints could not get!past the centre, but kept the home forwards from scoring. Appleton scored from a penalty.
